Over 900 flights canceled on Sunday
Some travelers on Sunday could be in for another rough day -- with over 900 flights already canceled.
According to FlightAware, 910 flights have been canceled Sunday, and the number is rising.
American Airlines is extending its travel alert and waiving change fees for travel scheduled through Wednesday, Nov. 18.

"American’s recovery from yesterday’s FAA nationwide ground stop continues to move forward," the company said in a statement. "All planned cancellations for tonight and tomorrow have now been completed, though some individual flights may still be canceled as we continue working to fully restore the operation. Our focus tonight is on setting up the operation for a strong start tomorrow, with our crews and aircraft positioned to get customers on their way."
Delta Airlines is encouraging travelers with flexible plans to move their flights to Monday or further out.
Overall, more than 6,400 flights were canceled on Saturday, according to FlightAware, on top of more than 9,000 flights canceled on Friday.
-ABC News' Clara McMichael
FAA union: Technicians not included in upgrade that caused ground stop

The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union, which represents more than 11,000 FAA employees, issued a statement saying its technicians were not involved in the upgrades that resulted in Friday’s ground stop.

"Historically, contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment. PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop yesterday," the union said in the statement.

The union is also saying its members should have a bigger role in the FAA’s air traffic control modernization efforts, arguing that their skills and expertise will help minimize disruptions and make the process quicker.

"PASS fully supports the administration's efforts to modernize the nation's air traffic control system," the union said. "It must be recognized by the FAA that modernization will move more quickly with fewer disruptions if PASS is fully engaged. The employees represented by the union are on the front lines and they have the skills and expertise to make the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) a reality. These employees should receive training on new equipment and could ensure more robust installation and optimization—if the workforce were properly staffed."
-ABC News' Ayesha Ali
Rock bands entertain passengers
Members of rock bands that were traveling to the Vans Warped Orlando concert helped to ease the stress and tension for passengers during flights Saturday.
Videos circulated online of Simple Plan, Hoobastank and The Used performing their hits using the plane's PA system to amused passengers.
Some of the passengers sang along to their songs.
"It felt like a tube of happy people," Hoobastank vocalist Doug Robb said in an interview with Rocksound Saturday.
-ABC News' Malcolm Caminero
Saturday flight cancellations top 5,200 as airlines work to get operations back up
Over 5,200 flights have been canceled on Saturday as airlines continue to work around the clock to get operations back up on Saturday.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system will be fully recovered on Sunday. As of 3:30 p.m. ET, 160 flights have been canceled on Sunday.
"Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," he said.
Nearly 9,200 flights were canceled on Friday.

title: UPS plane, Copa Airlines flight collide on taxiway at Miami International Airport
summary: Two people were treated on the scene for minor injuries, airport officials said.
story: Two people were treated for minor injuries, airport officials said.
A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, according to airport officials and the Federal Aviation Administration.
Two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, but did not need to be taken to the hospital, according to Miami-Dade Aviation.
It happened at approximately 9:15 p.m., the airport said.

The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737, which was taxiing to the gate, struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767, which was taxiing for departure to Bogota, Colombia, according to a statement from the FAA.
Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, the FAA said.
The FAA is investigating the incident.
One pilot is heard on air traffic controller audio saying, "Somebody hit us."
Photos showed damage to the nose of one of the planes.
The airport said flights were being directed to other taxiways, so there was no impact to airport operations.

"We are aware of an incident involving one of our aircraft on the ground in Miami," UPS said in a statement. "Our crew is safe, and we are committed to working with authorities to determine what happened. The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority."

title: Meta fined $887M in Italy over Android gallery photos, videos on Facebook
summary: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.
story: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.

ROME -- Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law. The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
Meta made no immediate comment.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

title: Congressional Republicans push Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia
summary: Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee
story: GOP Sen. Tim Scott sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify.

House and Senate Republican leaders are demanding answers from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and whether that relationship may have influenced business dealings involving Nvidia and China.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee. It comes after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," said Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer.
It's not yet clear when Lutnick will appear before the committee.
The committee is requesting Huang to appear on Dec. 3 with Chairman Scott threatening to subpoena Huang if he fails to voluntarily appear in front of the committee.
Meanwhile, top House Republicans have asked Huang to come in for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 as the two sides have been in active negotiations.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Select Committee on Chairman John Moolenaar requested a written confirmation of Huang’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, under threat of subpoena.

"Failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing. Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony,” Thursday’s letter to Huang states.

Mast, Crawford and Moolenaar wrote in a statement that as "reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately."

The three chairmen also asked Nvidia’s General Counsel Tim Teter to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 2 "regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of NVIDIA products, and recent public reporters regarding NVIDIA’s interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving Megaspeed." Republicans requested a written confirmation of Teter’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, saying they will issue a subpoena if they do not.

The requests for both men to testify come amid growing concern over potential Chinese espionage and whether any protocols at the Commerce Department were broken in their oversight of Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Lutnick is being accused of delaying placing Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia and Alice Huang's employer, on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, even as U.S. intelligence indicated that Megaspeed may have been diverting purchased Nvidia chips to China, something the company denies.

"Well, I want to wait and see if the allegations are true and what he has to say about it. But I'd be concerned. You know, the rumors are very concerning. The reporting is very concerning about it,” Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer told reporters on Thursday.
Republican Sen. John Curtis said "we need answers and accountability" from Huang and Lutnick "immediately."

"Jensen Huang's gross negligence exposed cracks in our national security, but Secretary Lutnick's reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people," Curtis wrote in a social media post.

House Republicans are seeking testimony on Dec. 3 from Jeff Kessler, the under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security "for a hearing on chip smuggling, adversary use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations, and Megaspeed."

title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders receives 2028 presidential encouragement
summary: Supporters and donors have been encouraging GOP Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, sources told ABC News.
story: Georgia GOP Gov. Brian Kemp is also said to be getting encouragement to run.

Supporters and donors have been encouraging Republican Arkansas governor and former White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, according to multiple sources with direct knowledge of the situation.

​When asked about the outreach Sanders has been receiving, her communications director Sam Dubke told ABC News that “Governor Sanders looks forward to serving the people of Arkansas for the next four years.”

​Sanders, the daughter of Mike Huckabee, himself a former Arkansas governor, Repubican presidential candidate and current U.S. ambassador to Israel, won re-election as governor last week. She became the first woman ever elected Arkansas governor in 2022.

Before becoming governor, Sanders served as President Donald Trump's press secretary in his first term from July 2017 to June 2019 after having served as deputy press secretary. She was also a senior adviser to Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.

​While Sanders formally briefed the White House press corps less than her predecessors, she became one of Trump’s closest and most trusted advisers and has maintained a close relationship with him, having worked for Trump in the White House for 3 1/2 years.
Sanders has long been viewed as a rising star in the Republican Party.

In 2023, a few months after winning the gubernatorial race in Arkansas, Sanders delivered the Republican response to former President Joe Biden’s State of the Union address -- remarks usually reserved for individuals seen as on their way up in the party.

Georgia's retiring popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp is also considering a presidential bid after he leaves office in January and has been encouraged by donors and other Republican officials to run, a source familiar with his thinking told ABC News.
​In the days leading up to the midterm elections, Kemp traveled to South Carolina, one of the early nominating states for Republicans, to campaign for Gov.-elect Alan Wilson.
ABC News has reached out to Kemp's political operation for comment.
​After Republicans' midterm losses, the party is reflecting on what went wrong and how to move forward, with some of those conversations happening publicly.
​Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, called Republicans' performance in the midterm elections a "Watergate-level repudiation" of the party.
​Outgoing Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis described the election results as a "meteor strike," arguing that even a "wave" fails to capture the scale of the Republican losses.

​DeSantis is keeping his options open for another presidential run, two people familiar with his thinking told ABC News, after the governor said Florida fended off a blue wave in this year's midterm elections.

title: Schumer and Van Hollen face off for Senate majority leader. What do Democrats think?
summary: Within moments of Chris Van Hollen announcing his intent to challenge Chuck Schumer in a race to lead next year’s Senate Democratic majority, endorsements began flying.
story: Van Hollen says he has support, Schumer says he has the votes to remain leader.

Within moments of Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen announcing his intention to challenge Minority Leader Chuck Schumer in a race to lead next year’s Senate Democratic majority, endorsements began flying in favor of both candidates.

Van Hollen branded himself as an “underdog” while announcing his candidacy during an interview on MS Now Thursday night. But he also said he’d garnered the support of at least 10 senators -- enough to raise eyebrows about his potential to shake up caucus dynamics.

"We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people, and we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up, and that is why I'm running for the majority leader in the United States Senate,” Van Hollen said during a summit event in Denver, Colorado on Friday.
Already, Van Hollen has garnered critical support among some members of the incoming freshmen class.

“The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night.
Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan also threw her support behind Van Hollen.

“Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership. I believe @ChrisVanHollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind,” Flanagan posted on X on Friday morning.
It’s not just new members backing Van Hollen. Sen. Bernie Sanders, a longtime face of the progressive movement, called for a change in leadership before backing Van Hollen.

“This election was about CHANGE. The Democratic Party must CHANGE. Now is the time to take on the oligarchs and fight for working families,” Sanders posted on X. “That is why I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen for Majority Leader.”

Sanders’ endorsement went further than a handful of other Democrats, who have called for a change in the party leadership without endorsing any particular candidate. Sen. Elissa Slotkin along with a number of other incoming Democrats, fall into this category.
But Schumer, who led Senate Democrats for nearly 10 years, doesn’t seem to be sweating it.

In a post on social media Thursday night that came within seconds of Van Hollen announcing his intent to challenge him, Schumer said he’d already clinched the necessary votes to be re-elected as leader for what would be a sixth two-year term.

Democrats picked up a whopping eight seats during the midterm elections, something Schumer claims partial credit for. When the new Senate is sworn in in January, Democrats will go from being the minority party to holding at least a 55-45 seat majority. The Senate race in Alaska has yet to be projected, but a Democratic victory there could secure Democrats an even larger share of seats.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together -- 55 seats and counting is an amazing result -- and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said.
Endorsements for Schumer followed almost immediately after.

“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”
Sen. Jacky Rosen of Nevada joined King and a number of her colleagues in highlighting Schumer’s role in helping Democrats to secure their resounding majority in the midterms.

“I’ve seen up close how hard @SenSchumer works for our entire caucus. He did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds, and I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment. I’m proud to support him to be our Majority Leader,” Rosen posted on X.
Her fellow Nevada senator echoed that.

“Leader Schumer was instrumental in Democrats flipping 8 -- soon to be 9 -- Senate seats and securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto said in a post.

To clench the majority leader title, a candidate will need to amass a simple majority of conference votes during a closed-door leadership election. Though no date for the election has officially been announced, Democrats are expected to hold it in early December.
The leadership election is held by secret ballot. Newly elected senators will get a chance to vote in that election but outgoing senators will not cast ballots.
Depending on the results in Alaska, either 55 or 56 Democrats will vote in the election. The winner of the election will need either 28 or 29 supporters, depending on the Alaska results.

Senate Republicans elected their new leadership following a lengthy closed-door discussion on Tuesday. Current Majority Leader John Thune will remain the top Republican in the Senate leading the GOP minority for the next two years.
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa and Hannah Demissie contributed to this report.

title: Iran live updates: Bessent blasts Iranian threats
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: The secretary attacked Iranian leadership after moving to a military base.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

Iranian foreign minister calls US attacks violation of international law

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. attack on Iran saying if states were free to attack one another "based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" in an opinion piece released in Japanese Outlet Kyodo News.
"Use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," Araghchi wrote.

"The military attacks launched by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran constitute a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty. Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun," Araghchi wrote.
Bessent says economic campaign against Iran is working, he moved to military base due to Iranian threats
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply attacked Iranian leadership on Friday in response to his recent move to a military base because of Iranian threats.
"'F' the Iranian leadership," Bessent said on CNBC this morning, when asked about the recent news and his current safety.
"I'm not going to be cowered that they have initiated death threats against me. The other members of the cabinet were not going to be cowered," he said.
Bessent claimed that these threats against him mean the economic campaign Treasury launched in August against countries and entities that do business with Iran is "working."
"The IRGC, they're like a dangerous, cornered animal. So I follow the Secret Service instructions and have moved from my home to a military base," Bessent said.
Bessent touted U.S. strength during the war through economic restrictions on Iran.

"We are squeezing the regime. I think that they are panicked. In what they're seeing for the first time since they began producing oil, they have no oil on the water. They have no revenues, and we have cut them off," Bessent said.
Asked about next steps in settling the war and if there is concern that Iran will ramp up aggression because they’re "cornered," Bessent claimed Iranians will "eventually want to make a deal."
-ABC News' Isabella Murray
US denies Iran's claim that it destroyed US radar in Bahrain
The U.S. denied Iran's claim that it destroyed an American early warning radar in Bahrain.
"The IRGC launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces. There were no injuries or damage," U.S. Central Command said Friday.

The IRGC claimed its the attack was carried out in response to a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in the southern Iranian port of Sirik, warning the U.S. to cease its hostilities, according to Iran's state-owned Press TV.
The IRGC also claimed a tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, Press TV reported.
White House won't say if talks with Iran have stopped

A White House official would not say whether U.S. talks with Iran have ended, after President Donald Trump posted on social media Thursday morning that "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

When asked whether the president meant there are no more negotiations happening with the Iranians, the official provided a statement highlighting what Trump said this morning -- the U.S. naval blockade and economic pressure against Iran -- adding, "President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon."

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The President has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect. President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," a White House official said in a statement.
The president's post came after he said the war with Iran would end "soon" on Wednesday during his Veteran's Day remarks at Arlington National Cemetery.

title: Republicans push for Jensen Huang's testimony following Nvidia CEO's resignation
summary: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
story: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
Republican lawmakers are continuing to call for testimony from Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday morning following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

GOP Rep. Tim Burchett said it was a "good move" for Huang to resign, adding that the former Nvidia executive should testify as lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Burchett said to reporters at the Capitol Thursday morning.
Rep. John Moolenaar, the chairman of the China Select Committee, told ABC News that lawmakers have growing concerns as details of Huang's affair continue to come to light.

"The concerns are our national security, whether he was being influenced by a Chinese spy, and the Chinese intelligence was gathering information about our crown jewels of American technology, and also this issue of chip diversion," said Moolenaar, who added that he would support a congressional subpoena to compel Huang's testimony.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Brian Mast and Moolenaar both say that they're still in active conversations with Huang to schedule testimony after the former Nvidia CEO had previously signaled a willingness to testify.

"We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us. If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power," Moolenaar said.
Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte said he believes that Huang's affair is a distraction.

"I hope we can keep the conversation centered around the pros and cons of our export policy regarding our most advanced chips, and you know, not talk about, you know, personal peccadillos,” Obernolte said.

Before Huang's resignation, lawmakers had called for him to testify. Last week, GOP Reps. Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and Moolenaar sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing." Moolenaar said Huang responded to that letter and they are discussing a "date that works."

Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Jensen Huang has not responded to ABC News' previous requests for comment about testifying on Capitol Hill. ABC News is working to contact Huang on Thursday -- after he left Nvidia.

On the Democratic side, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media on Thursday morning that despite Huang's resignation, Congress needs more answers from Huang, Nvidia and the administration.
"Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote.

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons are asking the White House and the Departments of Commerce and State to preserve all documents related to the export of NVIDIA's advanced AI chips to China following reports that some senior officials were aware that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spying operation. The two senators wrote a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Wednesday.
Coons and Warren are also requesting preservation of all materials related to the reported intelligence operation and for a briefing to members of Congress.

Some Republicans have brushed aside concerns, however, when asked whether Huang's access to President Donald Trump at state dinners and flying on Air Force One was problematic given his affair with an alleged Chinese spy was purportedly known to the intelligence community.
"I'm not concerned about -- about Jensen's access to the president. I'm sure the president can take care of that," Obernolte said.
Republicans have said they are hoping to bring in Huang before handing over majority control to Democrats in January.

"You know, it's obviously -- with him resigning -- that does change the dynamic," Moolenaar said. "He has stated he's a patriot. He has questioned people who viewed export controls as a sound policy. I would hope he would want to come in and have that discussion with us."
ABC News' Allison Pecorin contributed to this report.

title: Republicans dazed by midterm election defeats grapple with what went wrong
summary: Republicans are grappling with unexpected losses after the midterm elections
story: Republicans are grappling with unexpected losses after the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- Rep. Richard Hudson wanted a triumphant return to Capitol Hill this week after steering Republicans to another majority. Instead, the North Carolina Republican is facing the reality that he and dozens of colleagues will soon clear out their offices.

“It was really people coming out to send a message,” Hudson, the chair of the House GOP's campaign arm, said in a brief interview. “They, rightly so, felt gas was too high, things were too expensive.”
“The mistake Republicans made,” he said, “is we didn't convey to them that we cared about that and cared about them.”

Back in Washington this week for the first time since the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Republicans were in something of a daze. Even as they acknowledged the depth of their defeat, there was little appetite for a wholesale break from President Donald Trump.

Instead, they met behind closed doors to talk about what went wrong. And they scrutinized the calendar to figure out how to push through as much of their agenda as possible before Democrats assume control of the House and the Senate in January.
There was widespread frustration that Republicans who were awarded full control of the White House and Congress just two years earlier had lost touch with voters.

“You cut rural healthcare spending, when you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the poor, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon working people, you’re gonna get your butt kicked,” said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who unsuccessfully sought to delay his party’s leadership elections in the Senate. “And you’re gonna deserve it.”
“We collectively failed,” said Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., who is trailing her Democratic challenger in a district that Republicans carried by more than 18 percentage points in 2024.
“It’s very clear,” she said. “The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress.”

The anger is sharp in part because of the rosy predictions from top Republicans ahead of the election. Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., who is also trailing a Democratic rival, said people kept telling her she couldn't lose. But she knew otherwise.
“I couldn’t get anybody to listen to me,” she said. “People just didn't think it could happen, but we knew it could.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson spent the final stretch of the campaign rejecting the historic headwinds that often befall a president's party during a midterm. He toured the country, insisting the polls were wrong and Republicans would retain their majority even as some incumbents were skeptical.

Back on Capitol Hill this week, Johnson said voters made the “wrong choice” as Democrats flipped more than 40 Republican-held seats. That puts the Democrats on track to hold the most robust majority since the early years of Barack Obama's presidency.

Republicans, meanwhile, are weighing how to proceed, balancing calls for moderation against an impulse for hard-line positions that might reenergize the party's base. Each chamber took different tracks, previewing divisions that may lie ahead.

In the House, the Republicans who will remain in Washington next year largely represent staunchly conservative districts where Trump remains popular. Their decision to elect Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their next leader reflected a fighting stance.

Jordan is a co-founder of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, currently chairs the Judiciary Committee and has previously chaired the Oversight Committee. From those positions, he's waged heated fights against Democrats and become a top Trump ally.
“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla.
In the Senate, the desire for combat was less intense.

The question for Republicans there was less about whether they would stick with John Thune of South Dakota as their leader than when they would make that decision. Hawley and a small group of conservatives spent hours huddled with Republicans in the Old Senate Chamber arguing for a delay in leadership elections to allow the party to consider alternative candidates.

But the problem was that no one would come forward to offer themselves as an alternative to Thune, who has faced criticism from Trump at times for his refusal to abandon Senate rules to make it easier to pass conservative legislation.
“It's a bad job,” Hawley said.
After hours of deliberation, Republicans ultimately backed Thune without so much as a voice vote.
“We're going to let our leader be the leader,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who was also elected to lead the party's effort to regain seats in the 2028 election.

Perhaps the biggest question for Republicans going forward is how to manage their relationship with Trump, whose policies on trade and the war in Iran helped contribute to their losses. He's in the last two years of his second term, and the election defeats have raised stark questions about the durability of his Make America Great Again movement.

But there was no rush to distance themselves from the president as House Republicans, even those who have been critical of his administration, overwhelmingly blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Only Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who led the push alongside Democrats, broke ranks.
“What I found out tonight is they still haven’t broken from the spell of Donald Trump,” Massie said after the vote. “He still controls this conference.”

When asked whether the election was a referendum on Trump, Thune said the results stemmed from “a combination of things,” refusing to directly blame the president for contributing to the party's challenges.
But there were signs that Trump's influence had limits.

Few echoed his argument in a social media post this week that there were problems with the election. In conceding a closely fought Senate contest in Mississippi, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith said she would “respect the decision” of voters.

Several Republicans, including Sens. Joni Ernst of Iowa, Tim Scott of South Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas and Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, posted pictures of Democrats who will either succeed them or soon represent their states, harkening to an earlier era of postelection unity.

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky pushed back against White House warnings to congressional Democrats that planned probes of the Trump administration could amount to “blatant criminality.” Comer, who oversaw extensive investigations of Democratic President Joe Biden and his family as chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said lawmakers have a role in holding any White House accountable.

“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario,” Comer said.
Associated Press writer Kevin Freking contributed.

title: Maryland Sen. Van Hollen says he will challenge Sen. Schumer for Democratic leader
summary: Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader in the new Congress.
story: Van Hollen said the party needs "new leadership."
Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader in the new Congress.
In a social media post, Van Hollen said the party needs "new leadership" following the midterm elections in which Democrats won enough seats to take control of the chamber.
"This isn't about any one person -- it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in the post.

In an appearance on MSNOW on Thursday announcing his bid, Van Hollen, a two-term senator, said: "This is a generational opportunity for the Senate to respond to the call of the American people for change ... They've given us a chance. We have to earn their trust, and my view is that you can't earn that trust with old leadership. You need to move on to new leadership."

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, quickly responded to the news of the challenge, saying he welcomes "discussion about the future of our caucus" while also confidently adding "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together--55 seats and counting is an amazing result--and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people," he posted on X.
The Senate Democratic leadership elections are expected to be held in December. A leader is selected based on a majority vote of the caucus.
Van Hollen acknowledged he was the underdog in the leadership elections but remained optimistic that he could garner support from his Senate colleagues.
"Now people will have to make a decision, one way or the other, and they have to decide whether they want to vote for change or whether they want to vote for the status quo."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: US soldier accused of spying for Russia identified: Source
summary: US officer who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.
story: Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was entrusted with sensitive information, a source said.

The U.S. soldier who officials say was entrusted with sensitive information and was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.

Tyner, 41, was taken into custody Tuesday near Gloucester, England, as part of a British counterterrorism investigation, according to U.S. and British officials. U.S. Army officials said the officer had been entrusted with sensitive information.
ABC News has not been able to reach Tyner. It is unclear if he has retained a lawyer.

Tyner was assigned to Imjin Barracks in the United Kingdom, a military garrison that is home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Response Corps, which manages plans for ground troops in case of a crisis.
Tyner's identity was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Tyner, an Afghanistan war veteran, has held numerous high-profile personnel assignments throughout his more than two-decade Army career, according to a LinkedIn account matching his name. British law enforcement officials said the investigation involves suspected violations of the National Security Act of 2023, a law aimed at combating espionage and foreign interference.

It remains unclear exactly what Tyner is accused of doing. He is expected to be formally charged by British authorities in the coming days and subsequently face separate charges from the U.S. Army, according to a source familiar with the matter.

U.S. troops convicted of crimes in allied countries can serve prison sentences abroad before facing separate prosecution in the American military justice system, according to Army court records, which, could mean a second trial and, if convicted, an additional sentence in a U.S. military prison.

U.S. troops convicted of espionage-related crimes have often been junior or mid-level service members, according to Army data, with financial gain a common motive. Cases involving senior officers are less common, and those ranks typically have greater access to sensitive military information that could be particularly valuable to foreign adversaries, though it's unclear what specific information Tyner had access to.

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement following the arrest that the case is, "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

title: Colom’s historic Senate win could reshape Mississippi’s political future: Analysis
summary: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
story: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
Scott Colom’s victory is more than a Democrat winning in a ruby-red state. It is a breakthrough in who can represent Mississippi and could reshape expectations about who can win there next.

Mississippi sent the nation’s first two Black U.S. senators -- Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce -- to Washington during Reconstruction. Both were elected by the state legislature. After Bruce left office in 1881, Mississippi went nearly a century and a half without another Black senator.

That gap cannot be separated from the violent dismantling of Reconstruction, the rise of Jim Crow and generations of deliberate suppression of Black voters. Mississippi’s 1890 constitution turned racial exclusion into governing policy through poll taxes and literacy requirements.
Now, Mississippi voters have directly elected a Black person to the U.S. Senate for the first time.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom told supporters at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday night.

His slim victory over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith challenges the assumption that Mississippi’s statewide political outcomes are predetermined. Future candidates, party officials, donors and organizers will have to consider whether an electorate that has long been treated as predictable deserves another look.

For Black Mississippians, whose right to vote was obstructed for generations, this victory puts a Black man in a position to help shape the state’s future. Colom will exercise the same authority as every other senator, from voting on legislation to weighing judicial nominations.

But one victory does not establish a lasting realignment. The ultimate test is whether the coalition that elected Colom can outlast him and this political moment. The question becomes whether that coalition will support other candidates, sustain voter participation and make future elections competitive.

Colom campaigned on raising wages, protecting rural hospitals and addressing the cost of living. Those promises now become the standards against which voters will judge him. Delivering will require legislative allies and translating national debates into benefits for Mississippi communities, including those that did not support him.
“My commitment is to be someone that continues to stay in prayer, continues to have faith, and continues to work to make every Mississippian’s life better,” Colom told the audience at Tougaloo.

That promise connects the historic achievement to the work ahead. His victory gives future candidates evidence that a path to statewide office exists. His performance will help determine whether voters see that path as worth taking again.
A state that once systematically denied Black citizens political power has chosen a Black man to represent everyone. The next test is what that representation delivers for Mississippians.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
story: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here’s what to know.
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Rubio acknowledges 'people are struggling' economically in speech after GOP midterm wipeout
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy

WASHINGTON -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a sweeping speech to fellow conservatives on Friday evening acknowledging that Americans are struggling in the current economy, while also railing against what he called the “weaponization” of international law to constrain the U.S. from acting in its own interests.
His comments to the conservative Federalist Society touched on a core issue of the midterm elections — economic pain — that U.S. voters cited in delivering massive losses to Rubio's Republican Party.

“I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There’s no doubt about it,” he said. “The health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need.”

President Donald Trump often points to the stock market as evidence that the economy is doing well. But voters angry over higher costs gave Democrats control of Congress after blaming Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.

Rubio's remarks had the overtones of campaign speech, though the former Florida senator has consistently refused to discuss whether he would seek the presidency in 2028 in a race that could pit him against Vice President JD Vance. Rubio gave another wide-ranging speech last month in Greece that focused on Western values and also appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America’s top diplomat.

Rubio on Friday defended the Iran war, arguing that it was necessary to stop the threat of the Islamic Republic obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he acknowledged that the unpopular conflict has driven up gasoline prices for Americans and other connected costs.

“It’s not easy to address these things because it’s not popular to address them," Rubio said. “It’s difficult. And oftentimes it inflicts, you know, pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that.”

He also pointed to the need for American leaders to continue a tradition of ensuring the next generation is better off than those before them. Economic prosperity is “not self-perpetuating,” he said, but an enormous undertaking that requires years and decades and is not accomplished “election cycle to election cycle."

“That’s the challenge before us now, because I do think there’s a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off, and that can’t happen. That’s un-American,” he said.

Rubio also hit back hard on critics of Trump administration policies such as deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America, the January capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and strict immigration policies.
He accused other countries and international organizations of trying to stymie the U.S. from acting in its own best interests by accusing the Trump administration of violations of international law.

“We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign policy decision or action of this administration,” he said, describing it as “the weaponization of international law.”

Rubio also condemned the United Nations, the International Criminal Court, the “global elite” and organizations staffed by “international activists and bureaucrats,” all of which he said want to weaken the United States.

“They lecture us on the importance of sovereignty, even as they demand that nations surrender control of their borders and outsource their immigration laws to unelected international courts,” Rubio said. "They oppose, they say, all forms of imperialism, of conquest, of domination, but they seek to exercise authority over every country and every government on earth.”
AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed.

title: Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandal
summary: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
story: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump plans to take the world's wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China.

As the head of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk has economic and national security interests that make him a valuable adviser to Trump, according to administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president's plans on a Friday call with reporters.

The journey comes as the fallout spreads from Jensen Huang being ousted as the CEO of Nvidia for having an extramarital affair with an alleged agent of the Chinese government. Beijing denies that Alice Huang is a spy. Her company Megaspeed was accused last year of shipping Nvidia's advanced computer chips into China.

But Trump does not plan to confront Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the matter and administration officials do not expect Chinese retaliation for any follow-up actions to prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips, officials told reporters.

The administration believes the situation with Nvidia should not have any bearing on the trip, as the U.S. does not make its use of export controls subject to negotiations with foreign countries. Trump's aides are discussing the possibility of closing loopholes in existing trade measures, including the use of export licensing and preventing the ability of Chinese firms to use advanced chips over the internet through remote access.

The trip will be capped with a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where efforts to limit nuclear weapons will be a chief topic. Still, there are no plans for Trump to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose nuclear arsenal has been a source of consternation to the U.S. and its allies.

Trump is set to arrive Tuesday in the Philippines to meet with his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While in Manila, he intends to sign a trade deal with Thailand and meet with the Quad, an alliance composed of the U.S., India, Australia and Japan.

On Wednesday, Trump will leave for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he’ll have his third in-person meeting this year with Xi. Afterward, Trump and Xi will hold their joint meeting with Putin.

The leaders are expected to talk about the Iran war, but Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be part of the agenda, officials said — and Musk, whose Starlink system has been integral to Ukraine's ability to fight back against Russia's invasion, will not be part of the trilateral meeting.

title: Investigation says understaffing and unexpected fire behavior led to firefighter deaths
summary: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June
story: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June

Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of highly trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June, according to a report released by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The firefighters, working for the U.S. Forest Service and the newly created U.S. Wildland Fire Service, were part of an interagency response to the Knowles fire that merged with others to form the Snyder Fire on the Colorado/Utah border. The Rifle Helitack crew had been dropped in a remote area to work on a fire line, but became trapped when strong winds blew the fires in their direction and overtook them.

Their deaths came after the Trump administration revived a previously discredited policy to stomp out all wildfires quickly. Decisions on how to fight the Knowles fire were driven by the desire to prevent the spread of cheatgrass and protect sage-grouse habitat and a downwind community, the report said.

These factors “established an organizational posture to aggressively suppress new starts while small,” the report said. “This policy framing drove the decision to insert helitack firefighters onto small wilderness starts on a day with extreme fire weather conditions forecast.”

Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, and Sydney Watson were killed at the scene while Nathan Matthews sustained burn injuries and died on July 24. A fifth firefighter on the team sustained burn injuries but survived.

Ron and Lisa Hutcherson, Nick's parents, said the crew should not have been sent out ahead of the fire because dangerous winds were in the forecast. After meeting with investigators and visiting the site, they said they believe the deaths were preventable and were caused by a failure of leadership and oversight.

“Telling us how the fire reached our son does not answer why he was still there,” Ron Hutcherson said in an email to The Associated Press. “Who was watching the bigger picture? Who was responsible for bringing those firefighters home while there was still time?”
Lisa Hutcherson added: "My son depended on the people responsible for tracking the fire threatening him and making the decisions needed to keep him safe. We want answers, and we want accountability.”
The Serious Accident Investigation report detailed the circumstances that led to the decision to send out the helitack team and the many problems that led to their deaths.
Multiple lightning fires ignited on June 27 in Colorado's Black Ridge Canyon Wilderness. The region was experiencing extreme drought conditions, and the winds were picking up.

An incident team orchestrated coverage of the various fires by calling in aircraft and crews. At one point, the official in charge ordered all aircraft to the Jones fire, but constant high winds challenged all pilots that day, with many saying it was the most difficult flying of their careers, the report said.
By the early afternoon, communication systems broke down, with many trainee dispatchers trying to coordinate operations. There was also confusion over who would track aircraft.

“Dispatchers simultaneously tracked up to 16 active aircraft, three emerging incidents, multiple new starts, county river evacuations, and non-stop media inquiries, leading to severe cognitive task saturation,” the report said. “Due to constant radio congestion and workload strain, dispatchers felt they were unable to transmit the mandatory scheduled 1000 Fire Weather Forecast broadcast across the zone.”
The incident commanders on the Snyder and Jones fires did not have clear information about the location of the firefighters on the Knowles and Gore fires to the east, the report said.

“Because no operational role was assigned to continuously map personnel location against the emerging fires’ trajectories, overhead did not recognize that firefighters were positioned directly in the fire’s line of advance,” the report said.

A large fire about eight miles to the west of the helitack crew was observed three and a half hours before the entrapment, the report said. In less than three hours, the fire ran over complex terrain and reached the five firefighters, who were forced to deploy fire shelters, because a helicopter was unable to reach them in time.

The Hutcherson family met with fire investigators in Grand Junction on Oct. 26 for a three-hour official readout of the report, they said. The review described a failure of lookouts, communications, escape routes and safety zones, they said.

An aging mobile radio system and software crashes compromised official channels during critical operations, the family was told. Overlapping transmissions and confused radio traffic forced firefighters to use cellphones to communicate.

The Knowles fire was in a remote location, the family said, so the central question remains: “What justified keeping this crew exposed as communications, observation, and extraction options deteriorated?”

Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of the nonprofit Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, said the problem can be traced back to the Trump administration's full-suppression policy, which has prompted crews across the country to take unreasonable risks.

“It was outrageous to have a full-suppression policy on a lightning-caused fire in the wilderness to prevent the spread of cheatgrass,” Ingalsbee said. “The policy driving this aggressive attack of all fires is an obsolete paradigm that is just humanly or ecologically unsustainable. And unfortunately this crew paid the ultimate price, ultimate sacrifice.”

title: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
summary: After the Silicon Valley chaos spurred by reports of an AI billionaire's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the Microsoft outage that upended millions of workers' days, Friday's air travel ground stop across the U.S. had many people feeling that s...
story: After the Silicon Valley chaos spurred by reports of an AI billionaire's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the Microsoft outage that upended millions of workers' days, Friday's air travel ground stop across the U.S. had many people feeling that s...

Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley chaos that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.
But by Friday afternoon, when U.S. authorities suddenly ordered every plane across the country to land immediately, it felt to many that something was up. Something was broken.

Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his canceled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.
“There’s a lot of weird stuff going on,” Amasio said. “It makes one think.”
His first thought was dark: “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

Throw in a few more examples just from Friday – a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a U.S. air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Ohio — and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America’s fears for generations to offer his own explanation.
“The aliens have landed,” Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon tweet. “That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”
The official explanations for the thousands of downed jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.

A technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.
By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.

Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world.

Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago’s O’Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.
Gustafson said the week's mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.
“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”
Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.

Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.

“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the government says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”
Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.
She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.
“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.
Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.

He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.
“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.

Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.
It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.
Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.
“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.
Associated Press journalists Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Ali Swenson in Chicago, Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Aron Ranen in Newark contributed to this report.

title: Savannah Guthrie, popular and enduring face of morning TV, renews NBC contract after 15 years
summary: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
story: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
NEW YORK -- Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.

The move by one of morning television's most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.

The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.

In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”
The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: "I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
“The world goes on, things appear 'normal,' ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”

“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”

Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC's election coverage, most recently for last week's midterm elections.

title: Canada’s Carney reports progress in trade talks with Trump as he expands ties with Asia
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. are making progress on a trade deal after talks collapsed in August
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. are making progress on a trade deal after talks collapsed in August

TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that he had a lengthy conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump and senior administration officials before leaving for Europe and Asia and that the two countries are making progress toward a trade deal after negotiations collapsed in August.

The comments came as Carney announced that Canada had substantially concluded free-trade negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a bloc of nearly 700 million people, and completed separate negotiations with the Philippines. Both agreements are part of Canada’s efforts to reduce its dependence on the United States during Trump’s trade war.
Carney was in the Philippine capital ahead of a key three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts that starts Sunday.

“I had quite a long, substantive conversation with President Trump just before leaving for this trip,” Carney told reporters in Manila. “We are making progress. There is the possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal. But we’re not yet there.”
Carney said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Trump’s new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, also participated in the call.
Carney said Canada would not accept a deal that undermines its auto industry, which has been battered by Trump’s tariffs.

Canada suspended trade negotiations in August after last-minute U.S. demands that Ottawa considered unacceptable. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliatory Canadian tariffs in September. The countries have since resumed discussions.
