title: Oregon community suspects foul play when beloved shopkeeper disappears
summary: When Susan "Phoenix" Lane and her two dogs went missing from Welches, Oregon, in the foothills of Mount Hood, her friends and family suspected foul play almost immediately.
story: Tucked in off the road to Mount Hood, the Hoodland Plaza Shopping Center serves as a gathering place for the people of Welches, Oregon, where they sometimes get things that money just can't buy.
Sarah Caswell: It's kind of a — a community hub … if someone needed to vent or talk or … need help, that's where they'd go.
The plaza is home to Sarah Caswell's pizza shop and the neighboring Hoodland Bazaar – the whimsical gift shop where her friend Phoenix Lane worked.
Sarah Caswell: November 22, 2024, we showed up to work … and she hadn't showed up.
Phoenix was supposed to open the store at 11 a.m. that Friday.
Sarah Caswell: She hadn't put the signs out yet. And I was like, that's crazy … she would never not show up.
The search for Susan "Phoenix" Lane
Phoenix's boss tried texting her, but she didn't respond. Sarah became so concerned, she did something unusual. She reached out for help.

Sarah Caswell: … up here we don't have a lot of law enforcement. … Even if you call them and you need them, it can take up to two hours because the county is so big. … so, a lot of the times when we have to deal with things up here, we take it on as mountain justice.
What the community calls "mountain justice" is a kind of self-reliance – lending a hand when a neighbor is in trouble.
Deputy Aaron Clark: It's a very tight-knit community … they definitely, uh, tend to take care of their own problems.

Sarah called Aaron Clark, a Clackamas County sheriff's deputy who often patrols the Mount Hood region. He wasn't working in the area that day and suggested that Phoenix's boss call the sheriff's office to request a welfare check.
911 CALL: My employee did not show up for work today, you know, unexpectedly. And, uh, we were worried about, uh, her well-being.
Two deputies arrived at Phoenix's house that night. The lights were on and the door was unlocked. But there was no sign of 61-year-old Phoenix or her two dogs.
Sarah Caswell: Elrond and Elros were wolf hybrids. … You wouldn't know they were hybrids. They looked exactly like wolves. … They were very, very protective of her.
When Phoenix did not show up for work again on Saturday, Clark drove up to the mountain to talk to her friends and coworkers.
Deputy Aaron Clark: Everybody knew Phoenix. … Everybody really cared for her.

Though everybody there knew her as Phoenix, for many years, she went by her legal name – Susan. She had two adult sons, Jesse and Dakota, who she had raised in California and Kansas with her former husband, Fred.
Jesse Lane: She loved being goofy. She loved being silly, she loved being an artist.

Dakota Lane: A very distinctive memory … was being in kindergarten and her rolling up to the school on a motorcycle to pick me up and all the kids on the playground being really excited. … "Wow. Your mom rides a bike? That's awesome."
Peter Van Sant: The coolest mom in the world.
Dakota Lane: Coolest, coolest mom ever.   Sadly, their lives were upended in 2009 when Fred died in a car accident.
Peter Van Sant: Give me a sense of his death and the impact on — on the two of you.

Dakota Lane: Devastating. … She lost her soul mate. … I don't want to say she lost her way, but she definitely struggled … to realign herself. … There was nothing keeping us in that area anymore. So, she was looking for a way to escape with us.
Several months later, Susan met Michel Fournier, a divorced, French-Canadian long-haul trucker who spent a lot of time on the road.
Mike Lane: That was pretty much his life, running his truck, making a life.
Susan's brother, Mike Lane, says she was struggling to raise her teenage sons alone when Michel came into her life.
Mike Lane: He sees Susan and the kids and he goes, hey, wow, I can contribute to this. This could work.
Susan got her trucking license, and the two began driving as a team, trading shifts behind the wheel. A trip later in 2009 would change the course of their lives.
Jesse Lane: She kind of stumbled across … Mount Hood … and fell in love. She's like, this is where I want to be.
She bought a fixer-upper just off Highway 26, and they all moved up to the mountain.
Jesse Lane: It was kind of a run-down home. … But, I mean, she wouldn't have wanted it any other way. I mean, that's what she really desired was simple life up in the woods.
Susan and Michel married in 2012 and she later adopted her new name, Phoenix.

Sarah Caswell: All the trials and tribulations she had been to with her husband dying and rebuilding her life … that she felt that she had built herself up from the ashes. So … she gave herself the name Phoenix.
Christen Prudence: She was into meditation … and energy work.
Phoenix made deep connections with like-minded friends in the mountain community, including Christen Prudence.
Christen Prudence: I would lead guided meditations. … And we would have these beautiful, restorative women's circles, and we had Phoenix join us and do a sound bath at one of them.
Peter Van Sant: It's the first time I've ever heard of it. What is a sound bath?
Christen Prudence: A sound bath is where participants will relax … usually laying down. … It's channeling the vibrational … frequencies of the instruments … which provide healing.
In 2023, Phoenix began working at the Hoodland Bazaar, where her art adorned the walls. She sold Afghan rugs and Turkish lamps along with crystals and rocks, often dispensing her new-age wisdom.
Christen Prudence: She had so much knowledge with crystals … and just the way that energy works. … It was … almost like a store was made for her to be there.
Mike Lane: She found herself there. … She found her nirvana.

But in November 2024, six days before Thanksgiving, Phoenix was now missing from that special place. Clark started a missing person's report and went to Phoenix's home himself on Saturday to look for her. Dakota, who lived there with his mother and stepfather, answered the door.
Dakota Lane: Deputy Clark said, "Did you know that your mother's missing?" …
Peter Van Sant: Put that into words what that was like for you.
Dakota Lane: Shocking. I was — blindsided.

Dakota told Clark he had worked all day Friday and stayed out late in Portland, an hour away. He and his mother had last texted on Friday morning, and he said he didn't know people were looking for her.
Peter Van Sant: And Michel was still not at the house.
Deputy Aaron Clark: Not at the house, no.
Peter Van Sant: Did Dakota know where he was?
Deputy Aaron Clark: No.
Shortly after leaving the property, Clark got some news –- a member of the mountain community had made an unexpected discovery.
The mountain community takes action
Peter Van Sant (driving with Cari Gesch): Back on November 23, 2024, a Saturday, you were out on this highway. Where were you going?
Cari Gesch
: Uh, I was going up Salmon River Road. … Was taking the dog to go for a little run out in the woods.
That morning, Cari Gesch set out on a hike, unaware that her friend Phoenix Lane had gone missing the day before.   Cari Gesch: We're technically entering the National Forest here right now.

While the majestic Mount Hood National Forest covers more than a million acres, for locals like Cari, their favorite spots are as familiar as their backyard. So, she couldn't help but notice something strange on her way home that day — a white pickup truck parked on the side of the road.
Peter Van Sant: Now, there's hundreds of pickup trucks in this area. Why did this one catch your eye?
Cari Gesch: You know, this is — it — not a normal spot for someone to park that time of year. … It just looked out of place.
As odd as it was, Cari didn't think much of it until she got home, and a post on Facebook caught her eye. Sarah Caswell had asked if anyone had seen Phoenix or her white Ford F-250.
Cari Gesch: And that's when it clicked. I think that was her truck I saw up Salmon River Road. So, I went to the pizza shop.

Word got out that Phoenix's truck had been found seven miles from her home, but with no trace of her or the dogs. Deputy Clark was notified and says the truck's location suggested something could have happened to her out in the woods.
Peter Van Sant: So, there's concern that she may have gone up one of these more challenging trails and that she might be out there injured.
Deputy Aaron Clark: It was certainly possible … that she was out … hiking and had gotten hurt and couldn't get herself back.
Within hours, a search and rescue operation was underway on Salmon River Road. Jim White and Alex Monarch are detectives with the Clackamas County Sheriff's Office.

Det. Alex Monarch: The majority of the effort … are volunteer searchers from a number of organizations that come in … and blanket … these areas … like ants at a picnic. They're all over the place. They're incredible.
Peter Van Sant: And they know these trails. They know the landscape. … They are really seasoned searchers, correct?
Det. Jim White: Yes.
Although the authorities were focused on that area near Salmon River Road, Phoenix's friends were searching elsewhere because they were convinced she would not have gone hiking there.

Sarah Caswell: She liked to have her dogs off leash. … So, she would have never taken her dogs there because … there's too many people there. … And when they said missing hiker, I was like there's –- we all knew.
What they also knew was that Phoenix and her husband Michel had been having problems.
Christen Prudence: She would talk about crystals that she would place behind her husband's chair to absorb his negativity. And … it seemed like she would come alive when he was gone on the road.

Sarah Caswell: I know that she struggled with … paying the bills. … It was a struggle to get the money sometimes from Michel. … The last month-and-a-half is when she really started talking … and the stories were getting stranger.
One of those stories was about some soup Phoenix had donated to the community food pantry.

Sarah Caswell: She said Michel had found out that she had donated the food out of her own pantry and was really angry. So, he put a padlock on her pantry at home, so she couldn't take anything else out of it.
Sarah says in October, a month before Phoenix's disappearance, Phoenix told her she'd grown tired of Michel's controlling behavior and was making plans to leave him.

Sarah Caswell: She had to be secret about how she texts or even made phone calls because he would look through her stuff. So, slowly she was bringing some of her items, even her laptop … to the Hoodland Bazaar and just storing it there.
And that wasn't all she was bringing to the Bazaar.
Sarah Caswell: She started bringing her dogs to work … and she said that it was because … he's threatening the dogs.
Dakota Lane: Her biggest fear was that he would try to do something to the dogs, and that's all she could think about.
When Phoenix went missing, her friends and family shared their concerns with authorities. And they couldn't understand why it seemed investigators weren't focusing on her husband.
Sarah Caswell: I thought for sure he did something.
Investigators had tried calling Michel but got no answer. No one had seen or heard from him until Sunday — two days after his wife had gone missing — when he called the sheriff's office.
MICHEL FOURNIER: My name is Mike Fournier. I – I think they wanna talk to me.
OPERATOR: And why do you think the police wanna speak with you?
MICHEL FOURNIER: I don't know. My wife's been missing for a few days.
Authorities say they found Michel's lack of emotion in that call unusual.
Det. Alex Monarch: He could have been more enthusiastic if he was ordering a sandwich.
Investigators went to the home Michel shared with Phoenix, where he met them in the driveway.
DETECTIVE (bodycam): Let's go chat inside.
A body camera recorded the interview. Michel soon acknowledged the elephant in the room.
MICHEL FOURNIER: I got a big target on my back.
DET. ANDY KIESEL: Why?
MICHEL FOURNIER: My – my wife's gone.
He told the detectives they'd been living separate lives, and Phoenix had served him with divorce papers just days earlier.
MICHEL FOURNIER: … it's been going rough for, uh, quite a while. Uh, you know, can't even talk to her anymore. She won't answer my texts.
Michel said he'd last seen her at home Friday morning and told a strange story about his whereabouts that day.

MICHEL FOURNIER: Probably left around 9:30 … I ended up over at, uh, in – in Halsey.   Det. Jim White: So, Michel Fournier provided … this story that was almost farcical. He said that he hitchhiked into town to get this car part … all the way into Portland, Oregon, to this Halsey Auto Parts. … I believe it's about 33 miles.
DET. KIESEL: How'd you get back? Hitchhiking?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah.

Michel explained that he had been in and out of the house the rest of the weekend and he had not been concerned about Phoenix's absence because he believed she was seeing someone else —  and simply hadn't come home. He allowed the detectives to swab him for DNA and take his cell phone.
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah, important thing for me is I got to get back to work.

It seemed his biggest worry was leaving the next morning on a long-haul trucking job. Investigators were suspicious but couldn't detain him because they still didn't know if anything happened to Phoenix. They continued searching at Salmon River Road, and the mountain community grew more frustrated.

Deputy Aaron Clark:  There are a lot of people who called in who said they thought … Phoenix had been … murdered by her husband. … And I think there was a lot of anger at the sheriff's office … that we were focused … on a search and rescue mission.

What the community didn't know, was that at the same time, the sheriff's office was also running a criminal investigation —  one they were keeping secret for a very important reason.  Deputy Aaron Clark: I think if the sheriff's office had, uh, told the community all the things that we were doing … that would have tipped him off, that would have, um, made it very hard to track him down.
Tracking Phoenix Lane's cell phone  —  and Michel Fournier

On Monday, Nov. 25, with Michel Fournier now back on the road, detectives started collecting cell phone records to build a timeline of the day his wife went missing. They learned Phoenix sent a message to her friend Christen at 10:28 a.m. – half an hour before she was supposed to be at work.
Christen Prudence: She reminded me about her upcoming sound bath on Sunday and to help spread the word.
It was the last time anyone would hear from Phoenix. But investigators were still able to track her phone's location.

Det. Jim White: The cell phone left the residence, and it's traveled west toward Portland. …We got all the detectives together and we went along the route. We went to businesses … and said, "Hey, we're looking for some video."
And when they reviewed the video from those security cameras just after noon, they spotted something significant.
Det. Jim White: Susan Lane's truck was driving with those dogs in the back.
They tracked the phone and truck moving west – all the way to the Portland airport around 1 p.m.
Peter Van Sant: From the airport security video, were you able to tell who was driving?
Det. Jim White: We were not.
They couldn't tell where Phoenix's phone or truck had gone from there.
Det. Jim White: When that cell phone got out towards the airport, it went dead. So, no more location data.
But the airport wasn't far from the auto parts store where Michel had said he'd hitchhiked to that day.
Store security video confirmed he'd been there. But when they checked the cameras in the parking lot — at 1:38 p.m. — just before Michel entered the store –
Det. Jim White: The truck shows up at Halsey Auto Parts. …
Peter Van Sant: And who's driving?
Det. Jim White: Well, we believe Michel Fournier is driving.
Detectives found even more video of the truck two hours after Michel left the store — this time with one noticeable difference.

Det. Alex Monarch: We caught … more surveillance video … driving back towards the mountain … without the dogs. … The only conclusion … is that he disposed of the dogs somewhere and was driving back … to his home.
Detectives now knew Michel Fournier had not told the truth about hitchhiking that day. But they still hadn't found Phoenix, so they went to look for her phone at its last known location.

Det. Jim White: We went roughly shoulder to shoulder down that runway, and we looked for that cell phone. … No dice, no cell phone. … So, we decided to do a search over by the river. … We were just trying to get organized … when all of a sudden, one of our detectives said, "I think I can see it in the water."
Peter Van Sant: This is extraordinary. And what happens then?
Det. Jim White: Sure enough, we went down there and you could see … there was a rectangular device that … looked like a cell phone.
Det. Alex Monarch: Yeah.
Detective White waded into the frigid waters of the Columbia River and retrieved the phone … but found it was too damaged to provide any more information.
Det. Alex Monarch: The phone had been broken apart intentionally with … pry marks. So, not only was the phone thrown into the river … there were efforts made to … destroy it more than that.

They continued their investigation but stayed tight-lipped about what they had found, leaving Phoenix's sons Jesse and Dakota desperate for answers. Jesse, who lived out of town, had come back to the mountain. On Thanksgiving Day, he was driving down Highway 26 when he caught sight of Michel.
Jesse Lane: I see his semi-truck coming up the mountain. And instantly I'm like, "I'd like to talk to him," you know? She's missing. Let's see what he has to say. … So, I just turned the car around.
Jesse says he got to the house a few minutes after Michel. Both men stood in the driveway.
Peter Van Sant: What do you say to him?
Jesse Lane: Uh – I mean, at first, it was nothing. It was a long, long silence. I just stood there and stared at him for a good three, four minutes.
Peter Van Sant: You're serious?
Jesse Lane: Yeah …
Peter Van Sant: So, you're standing there in the driveway … and no one is saying a word.
Jesse Lane: Yeah.
Peter Van Sant: Who breaks the silence?
Jesse Lane: He did. He did.
Peter Van Sant: What'd he say?
Jesse Lane: Um, he said, uh – he said, "I wish I had answers for you." … I didn't really push. I was just expecting him to come clean. …
Peter Van Sant: Did you ask him directly,  "Did you kill mom?"
Jesse Lane: I did not. … I kept trying to get him to open up, and he just wouldn't participate. And I just finally left.

Jesse says it was clear he wasn't going to get any answers from Michel. And it seemed the sheriff's office was no closer to finding Phoenix. By then, after days at Salmon River Road, they had called off the official search and rescue operation.
Christen Prudence: I was devastated that they had spent that time searching in what I felt was the wrong area. And why not broaden that? Why give up and not pivot? …
Peter Van Sant: What do the locals do?
Christen Prudence: We did not give up. We kept broadcasting her flyers on social media … James Evans was forming a search party.
Peter Van Sant: Hey, James. Peter Van Sant, "48 Hours."
James Evans: Nice to meet you
Peter Van Sant: Thanks so much for coming out here.
James Evans: Yeah.

James Evans had been out searching for Phoenix on foot and even in a kayak. But he says when he learned no one had looked in these woods off Highway 26, just a few hundred feet from her house, he posted on Facebook to get a search party together here — even if there was little hope Phoenix would be found alive. He arrived before anyone else the day after Thanksgiving.

James Evans: So, I just … got out of my truck and surveyed area and – and walked back through this way … And so, I started coming through the woods here … and I seen this like a pile of garbage and a couple of tarps …
Peter Van Sant: Right in this spot here?

James Evans: Yeah, right in this spot right here … so I'm like, "oh, let me get this tarp out of the way" … So, I went down, I picked up the tarp, and that's when I seen … boots and legs … and I knew it was Phoenix.
Michel Fournier's accusation, denials – and a confession
Soon after James Evans found his friend Phoenix's body, word spread through their tight-knit community that she was truly gone.
Christen Prudence: She was face down in the dirt under a tarp next to a heap of trash … she was just left out like garbage. … my heart broke.
Within hours on that Friday, Nov. 29, 2024, investigators approached the home Phoenix shared with Michel Fournier with guns drawn and found him outside.
DEPUTY: Hey Michel. Hey, come here. Sheriff's Office. …
DET. MONARCH Well, OK. We're just gonna head that way down the driveway, OK?
MICHEL FOURNIER: OK.

They did not tell Michel his wife's body had been discovered, and he agreed to go to a nearby police station with Detective Monarch and another investigator for an interview. He was not yet under arrest.
MICHEL FOURNIER: When you do these interviews, are you supposed to have attorneys around here or something like that, or?
DET. MICHAEL ZACHER: Well, I'm gonna go ahead and I'm gonna advise you of your rights … Anything you say must be freely and voluntarily said. Do you understand these rights?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah. In other words, shut up.
Despite his attempt to lighten things up, Michel agreed to answer questions.
MICHEL FOURNIER: Let's see what you got …

After again saying his marriage was over, Michel took the interview in a different direction. He claimed that just a few days before Phoenix went missing, he'd gotten sick at home after taking heart medication with an open bottle of Gatorade.
MICHEL FOURNIER: … I was itching all over the place. I was welted up, face, body, everywhere ...

Michel said his heart was racing, so he drove to the hospital — but said that while in the parking lot, he began to feel better and never went inside. He told investigators that he thought there was something wrong with the Gatorade.
DET. ZACHER: Did you think that you'd been poisoned?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah. I've been poisoned.
And Michel Fournier suggested that Phoenix was behind it.
DET. ZACHER: Did you think that she – I mean, who do you think did it?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah. There would have been no one else.
Detectives then asked Michel again about his whereabouts the day his wife had gone missing.

Det. Alex Monarch: We walked through everything. … "is there any way that – that any – that you drove her truck?" "Oh, no, I never drive her truck." OK. … All of those things that we knew he had done, and he denied all of those things.
After nearly three hours, Monarch decided it was time to reveal what they knew.
DET. MONARCH: … Is that you at the auto parts store?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yeah. …

DET. MONARCH: The problem we – we found … is the auto parts store also has video cameras in the parking lot. … there's her truck and her dogs. And there's no one else in that truck. And you obviously drove the truck there.
Det. Alex Monarch: His physical demeanor significantly changed as he was being confronted with the information that we had.
They urged Fournier to come clean.
DET. ZACHER: You do have the ability to make this right. …
MICHEL FOURNIER: I'm void. I'm empty. … I can't help you. …
DET. MONARCH: Did you wrap her body in a blue tarp, Mike?
MICHEL FOURNIER: I don't know.
Det. Alex Monarch: He decided that he no longer wanted to communicate with us. So … we notified him that he was under arrest for murder.
An autopsy later found that Phoenix had been shot three times: in the head, neck, and chest. Investigators determined she was shot with a .22-caliber weapon, likely from the side and behind.
Peter Van Sant: This sounds like an execution.
Det. Jim White: Any one of those bullets was fatal. … We believe that she was likely ambushed as she … left the house to go to work
Michel Fournier was charged with second-degree murder. He pleaded not guilty.

But what had happened to Phoenix's beloved dogs, Elros and Elrond? Fournier told investigators he didn't know. But soon after he was taken into custody, word came that their bodies had been found – off the highway along the Columbia River, on the way out of Portland.
Det. Jim White: The dogs were found down a steep embankment and they had zip ties … fastened around their neck tightly. …
Peter Van Sant: … What did this suggest about … who could do something like that? …
Det. Jim White: Cold-blooded.
Detectives continued to shore up their case, processing evidence from the property including Fournier's Volkswagen truck.
Det. Jim White: It is our belief that … her body was stored there … or her body was moved using that truck.
In January 2025, almost two months after his arrest, detectives got a message from the Clackamas County Jail: Fournier was ready to talk again — and his story had evolved.
MICHEL FOURNIER: I verily believe that I've been … poisoned.
Fournier was now claiming that Phoenix had actually handed him that Gatorade bottle laced with poison which caused him to  "lose it" for days.
Det. Alex Monarch: Now this was the reason for everything …
DET. MONARCH: You believe that your behavior and your actions were result of being poisoned?
MICHEL FOURNIER: Yes, sir.

To back up his claims, Fournier said he had left the Gatorade bottle on the passenger seat in his truck. But since he never entered the hospital, there was no record he had been there. He did, though, give the detectives a helpful suggestion.
MICHEL FOURNIER: You guys did a fantastic job tracking me, uh, with the pickup truck. OK. …  I believe that you can do the same tracking … and – and find me at the hospital.
After some time, Fournier's tone shifted – and he finally was ready to say what he did.
MICHEL  FOURNIER: It was the hardest thing in my life …
That's when he confessed — not to murdering Phoenix, but to killing her dogs.
MICHEL FOURNIER: They had the zip ties on. It wasn't working. So, I suffocated them with the leash.
Det. Jim White: He justified it in a very strange way
Michel Fournier seemed to be implying he knew Phoenix was not coming back and wouldn't be able to care for them anymore.
Det. Jim White: He discussed the dogs as if … they would suffer more by … being taken to the pound … or even being euthanized there.
After Fournier's unusual interview, detectives set out to verify some of his claims.

Det. Jim White: We took that Gatorade bottle, and we sent it to the Oregon State Police … forensics laboratory, where they did testing on it for basically known poisons and heavy metals. None were found.
They did, however, find something they believed gave Fournier a reason to want his wife dead. It was a detail in those divorce papers he had been served.
Det. Jim White: Well, Susan Lane was requesting the property that they lived on. …
Peter Van Sant: Do you believe that … the realization that he could lose everything, for him became a motive for murder?
Det. Alex Monarch: Oh, absolutely. Absolutely.
With that motive in mind, Clackamas County deputy district attorneys John Millar and Alexander Hayes prepared for trial.
John Millar: Because this is a circumstantial case, there are certainly things that we don't know … We never gathered … the murder weapon.
But forensic testing had revealed Phoenix's blood was in the back of Fournier's Volkswagen truck. They also found .22-caliber ammunition in the house, and a shell casing in the driveway.
Peter Van Sant: Did you feel you had a … powerful case?
Alexander Hayes: Most definitely. … but there are no guarantees in the criminal justice system.
And indeed, within months, Michel Fournier — dressed in clothing from the jail medical unit — asked to speak with detectives one more time … with a proposition.
MICHEL FOURNIER: … I wanted to see you folks here. If we can work something out together …
Michel Fournier has a request
On March 24, 2025, four months after his wife's murder, Michel Fournier welcomed detectives White and Monarch back to the Clackamas County Jail and asked for a favor.
MICHEL FOURNIER (to detectives): … it's a bit of a long shot, but I need some time out to take care of my personal affairs.
Det. Alex Monarch: He basically asked that he be allowed to leave jail for a period of time … He's like, "you can put an ankle monitor on me … and I'll stay – I'll stay around."
Fournier said he needed to get rid of his trucking equipment and liquidate assets. In return, he indicated he might be willing to give Phoenix's sons some more answers.
MICHEL FOURNIER (to detectives): I'm trying to bring a closure, so we can move on.
Peter Van Sant: Was that actually considered?
Alexander Hayes: No, it wasn't considered at all. … that request is absolutely absurd.
In February 2026, Michel Fournier went on trial for the murder of his wife, Susan "Phoenix" Lane. The prosecution began by presenting its theory of the crime.

JOHN MILLAR (in court): The evidence is gonna show that Ms. Lane … wanted to get out of a bad relationship, had the defendant served with divorce papers, and then about 41 hours later, he shot her three times in the head, in the neck, and in the chest.
Fournier was given court-appointed lawyers. They — and Fournier — declined "48 Hours"' request for interviews.
Peter Van Sant: What was the defense team's strategy?
Alexander Hayes: So, the defense team strategy is to hold the State … to its burden … to, uh, prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
Fournier did not testify, but his voice was heard throughout the trial.
John Millar: We ended up at trial playing about eight hours of interviews.

Fournier's attorneys had claimed he was in poor health during those interviews and should have had a lawyer present. And they argued that detectives never searched for security camera footage that could have substantiated Fournier's story about being poisoned. But the prosecution maintained that Fournier spoke to them freely each time, and searching for video of him driving to the hospital would not have proved he was poisoned.
ALEXANDER HAYES (in court): There's no evidence to support that he was, and it was tested by a forensic scientist. It's irrelevant. … What matters is what happened on November 22 of 2024.
After seven days of testimony, the defense did not call any witnesses, and the case went to the jury.
Alexander Hayes: The jury deliberated approximately three hours, and that included lunch.
Michel Fournier was found guilty of second-degree murder.

Jesse Lane: I'm very grateful for how much effort and work everybody involved has put into it. … from the community to law enforcement … countless hours of effort and resources to see that he didn't get away with it.
That same day, he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 25 years.
Peter Van Sant: At his age, this is essentially life in prison, right?
John Millar: Michel Fournier talked about his poor health … we don't know his specific medical condition. But he's in his 70s, and … he'll … probably never … get out from behind bars.
For Phoenix's sons, moving forward brings new challenges. Jesse, his wife Gina, and two young daughters adjust to a future without their free-spirited grandmother.

Jesse Lane: The hardest thing is … she doesn't get to see my girls. She doesn't get to see my kids. … we've gone through so much together. And now it's this time where we can really enjoy something beautiful. … and she's gone.
Dakota now owns, and is fixing up, the property his mother loved so dearly.

Dakota Lane: It's her legacy. And it might go into a trust where if eventually I have kids, they can benefit from it. My nieces … can benefit from it. Use it as a seed to make a better life and let something good grow … from this tragedy.
And up the road at the Hoodland Plaza, the Mount Hood community holds Phoenix's memory close.

Sarah Caswell: I just, I miss her being next door. I miss her light. … she made a huge difference in a lot of people's lives up here. … she was able to bring, even in her death, bring so many people together.
Weeks after the trial ended, the community gathered at the Hoodland Bazaar to rename the room where Phoenix led her sound baths as The Phoenix Room.
CHRISTEN PRUDENCE: … want to welcome everybody in … Our intention is to celebrate that justice has been found, that her story … will continue to be spread and shared.
Christen Prudence: I hope that this space can be a place of healing and safety. … just to continue her legacy. … This place is special. … her presence is still in here. We can still feel her spirit.
In May 2026, Michel Fournier was charged in connection with the killing of Phoenix's dogs, Elros and Elrond. He pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

Lourdes Aguiar is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.

title: How Trump administration responded to FAA ground stop
summary: President Trump was informed within 30 minutes after the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, according to U.S. officials.
story: President Trump was informed within 30 minutes after the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, according to U.S. officials.

The ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers across the U.S. The FAA announced that all planes would be grounded at 3:36 p.m. ET — while 3,500 flights were in the air.

Within minutes, the FBI, director of national intelligence, Department of Homeland Security, Transportation Department, Justice Department, Defense Department, Joint Chiefs of Staff, U.S. Cyber Command, FAA and Federal Emergency Management Agency began looping each other in.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement at 4:16 p.m. ET that the ground stop was necessary due to "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," and that FAA technicians were investigating. Within minutes, the White House led a call with the agencies to determine what had happened. A game plan was put in motion.
The intelligence community soon preliminarily ruled out the likelihood of nefarious activity after searching through its various channels for chatter or pings. Nothing came up.

Senior staff briefed Mr. Trump, who was in an economic policy meeting, one U.S. official said. The staff relayed his directives to others on the multi-team call, led by White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Later Mr. Trump met with Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Mr. Trump started calling congressional leaders on Friday to work on getting the FAA more funding. The White House congressional team called key congressional members to work with them on air traffic controller modernization.

The Homeland Security Council invited key members of the government and some outside stakeholders to a meeting Monday to discuss the next steps and what should be done to prevent a recurrence as modernization efforts continue.

The council is an interagency government body responsible for coordinating national homeland security policy. Established by President George W. Bush in 2001, under the current White House structure, the Council operates through the National Security Council framework and can draw on senior officials from agencies like the Transportation Department, FAA, DHS and Defense Department.
But not all planes were grounded during the four-hour stop: medical services flights were green-lighted to proceed to their intended destinations.
By the fourth hour, the problem in the system had been identified, and the grounding was lifted. Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware.

At a news conference on Saturday, Duffy said the trouble apparently began as FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies performed maintenance updates at a remote facility, replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. During that work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming routers across the entire FAA network.

Mullin and Duffy were more than 30 minutes late for a 7:45 p.m. ET press conference on the ground stop Friday because they were close to getting the grounding lifted and didn't want to interrupt the effort to hold the presser, U.S. officials said.
While federal officials have identified a likely sequence of events behind Friday's disruption, key questions still remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

Zak  Hudak

title: Federal judge blocks Trump from closing historic D.C. golf course, for now
summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ruled that the Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., for now.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Saturday temporarily blocked the Trump administration's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington, D.C., that President Trump wants to overhaul into a new "world class championship" course.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ruled that the Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park and its golf course, but said that the Trump administration was not required to actively manage either.

She sided with a D.C. preservation group and two local golfers who argued that closure of East Potomac Park, set for Sunday, Nov. 15, was part of the Trump administration's plan to redesign and replace the course with a championship-style venue designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio.

Reyes said that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and said, "the Government reverse-engineers additional justifications for the Park's closure… All while it continues to assert that it will close the Park to follow the President's directive."
Her order will last until Nov. 28.

"We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," said Catherine Carroll, senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced, and we are honored to work with this coalition to secure this temporary relief."

"The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm," a Department of Justice spokesperson told CBS News. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue. The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."

Reyes has for months been overseeing a challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, a public course in Washington that opened in the 1920s. The dispute escalated last month when the National Park Service notified the judge that it would be removing trees on the course and went on to cut down more than 500 trees in the span of a weekend.

Reyes then issued an order blocking the Trump administration from felling any additional trees, and required the Justice Department to provide her with notice of any future actions the National Park Service planned to take at the golf course.

Mr. Trump, meanwhile, announced last month that East Potomac would close Nov. 15 to allow work on the new design by Fazio to begin, with the renovated "world-class, championship course" expected to open in roughly 15 months.

But in a court hearing Friday, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said he "would be shocked to learn there is a contract" with Fazio or any affiliated entities finalizing the new course plans and future construction.

Following Mr. Trump's announcement, the Justice Department notified the court late last month that the Interior Department was working on a plan to close the course and would also temporarily shut off the public's access to all of East Potomac Park, which encompasses not only the golf course, but also a road, playground and recreational space.

The Trump administration argued that the entirety of the park had to be closed because of a deteriorating sea wall, safety risks at the golf course, and because the organization that was overseeing the course, the National Links Trust, would cease operating it as of Nov. 15.

There is no plan currently in place to fix the sea wall, according to the National Park Service, and it's unclear how long East Potomac Park will be closed for. The new sea wall is expected to cost more than $300 million and take at least two-and-a-half years to complete, according to a proposal for the new golf course that the National Park Service submitted to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts last week.
The Trump administration said in a notice published Friday that it will be soliciting a contract for work related to 20,700 linear feet of shortline and sea wall infrastructure.

Lawyers for the preservation group and golfers said the Trump administration had manufactured a situation where the course would no longer have an operator, the National Links Trust, as of Nov. 15, and found areas of disrepair in East Potomac Park that needed to be fixed, effectively reverse-engineering the decision to close the area.

Reyes, too, pushed the Justice Department on whether Mr. Trump's order to shutter the park to overhaul the golf course was the real reason for the Nov. 15 closure date, or whether it was because of a longstanding need for repairs at the park, and the Trump administration was simply closing the park to effectuate those fixes.

"If this is such an emergent situation… why wasn't [East Potomac] closed immediately?" Reyes asked the government, noting that thousands of runners participating in the Marine Corps Marathon ran through East Potomac Park just last month.
Fazio's new course design shows it taking up the entirety of East Potomac Park, eliminating the existing road around the peninsula and recreational space at its southern end.
Adam Gustafson, a Justice Department lawyer, said that the government has "limited resources and discretion" and "when the president talks, the agencies listen."
"The agency has said consistently that it will comply with the law in reaching a final position on the deposition of this park," Gustafson said.

He argued that closing the park does not mean the Trump administration will immediately begin renovating the course, since the National Park Service still has to continue a legal analysis and assessments under federal environmental and historic preservation laws. The Commission of Fine Arts and National Capital Planning Commission must also conduct their own reviews, Gustafson said.
The NCPC is set to consider the proposal for the new course at a Dec. 3 meeting.

Separately, Reyes has also opened an inquiry into whether top Trump administration officials in the Department of Interior, Justice Department, and National Park Service misrepresented facts to her in recent court hearings and documents and violated ethics rules.

Reyes said she intends to appoint a former U.S. attorney in Washington, D.C., Jessie Liu, to lead the probe, which will include whether government lawyers told Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, and Kevin Griess, superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, to omit or include certain information in declarations about work at the golf course.
The Justice Department opposes the appointment of a special master.

title: Evacuation lifted after bomb threat near industrial plant in Illinois
summary: Police said the device had been rendered safe and residents were allowed to return to their homes.
story: An evacuation order was lifted Saturday and residents were allowed to return to their homes after a bomb threat near an industrial building in Peoria, Illinois.

The city of East Peoria said in a statement that, as of 1:00 p.m. local time, residents in the 1-mile radius evacuation zone "can return to their homes and all businesses can resume normal operations."
Peoria police said a suspicious package was found near a BioUrja ethanol plant at approximately 2 p.m. on Friday, and that hours later it was determined to be a "credible threat."
Police Chief Brad Dixon said Saturday at a press conference that there was still "no explanation on what the device was." He said the investigation is still ongoing.
"Law Enforcement will continue their investigation into this incident, and updates will be provided," the police department said in a statement.
Dixon added the package was "rendered safe" at 9:12 p.m., but searches continued for other possible devices throughout the wider area.
"The area of BioUrja has not been rendered safe, just the package that was on site. It's a large facility; there's going to be an exhaustive search," he said at a press conference.

FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley told reporters his office deployed personnel to work alongside the Peoria Police Department, Peoria Fire Department, Peoria County Sheriff's Department, the Illinois Secretary of State's Office and Illinois State Police.

"We are currently investigating this incident with all of our partners. While it is early in the investigation, know this: we will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," Presley said.
Gov. Pritzker said on social media, "I am actively monitoring the bomb threat in Peoria, and I have directed the Illinois State Police to coordinate with local authorities."
The mayor of Peoria, Rita Ali, said in an interview with WMBD News late Friday that the facility is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."
Country music singer Jon Pardi had to cancel his concert because it was in the area, saying, "Peoria we're disappointed we won't get to spend tonight with you..."
In a post on Facebook, the Peoria Police Department advised those needing shelter to go to the nearby Manual Academy.
Peoria is located in central Illinois, about 75 miles north of Springfield and 150 miles southwest of Chicago. The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River in the southern part of the city.

title: Travelers stranded, flights canceled after ground stop. Here's what we know
summary: Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
story: Airspace across the United States slowly began returning to normal on Saturday after a rare national ground stop canceled thousands of flights and stranded travelers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference Saturday, "We are back at full operations."
He thanked the pilots, airline staff, air traffic controllers and the FAA for their professionalism during the ground stop.
"They safely landed all of our aircraft," he said, also thanking the passengers for their patience during the significant disruption.

"Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Duffy said earlier in a social media post on Saturday. He's scheduled to appear on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."
More than 5,000 flights were canceled Saturday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 5,300 others were delayed.
How did the FAA ground stop happen?
The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. EST Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.
"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.
It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. EST Friday.
This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.
Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.
Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said.

Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service." He also said that L3Harris, a technology and defense company, owned the system.
L3Harris said Saturday the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the company said in a statement, adding they take the nationwide ground stop and "its impact" seriously.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.
"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.
Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.
Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."
Request for more FAA funding
Duffy said in a post that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH."

"I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money. I've asked for a lot of money," he said Saturday. "Now, the Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me 12 and a half billion dollars. And one of the problems that we had was they weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money."
The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $30 billion late Friday.

Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and Rep. Andre Carson, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a joint statement Saturday that FAA and DOT staff will brief the committees on Monday about the additional $30 billion requested by the Trump administration.

"This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share," the two Democrats said. "The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."
The pair said the Trump administration has only used $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress.
"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money," they said.
Can Americans still travel safely?
Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said Friday.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.
Bedford said there will possibly be 5,000 flight cancellations on Saturday, but airlines should be fully back on schedule by the end of the day Sunday.

"We do anticipate somewhere between four and 5000 of the 41,000 flights that are scheduled today likely will cancel, so we will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow," he said.
Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.
"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.
American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."
Southwest said Saturday the airline instituted a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty.
"We are working to get our Customers to their destinations as quickly as possible," Southwest said.

title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
summary: A tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans Friday, partially submerging the passenger boat.
story: A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water.
Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.

The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said in a news briefing late Friday afternoon that 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.
Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday afternoon, with two in serious condition, Moreno said at a news conference.
There were 191 passengers and crew members aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the mayor.

Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.

Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Moreno said at a news conference Saturday that rescuers pulled approximately 100 people from the water. Nearby boats had reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water.

Emergency responders, including Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, conducted rescue and response operations, Port NOLA said. Moreno said that along with local and federal agencies, private vessels that happened to be on the river at the time responded "as volunteers to try and get people out of the water."
Moreno described the successful rescue operation as a "miracle on the Mississippi."

One witness, Jamie Holford, told CBS News he saw the American Heritage hit the dock after the collision. He described seeing people hurrying off the boat. Then, as it rolled over, some were climbing over the railings of the boat, he said.
"It looked like something off the Titanic," he said.
Asked what the collision sounded like, Holford said, "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like."
U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Coast Guard investigators were on scene working to determine what caused the tanker to lose control.
"The investigation is still ongoing, there seems to be some kind of a loss of steering," Burnham told reporters. "The exact reason why, we don't know that."

The National Transportation Safety Board sent a "Go Team" to the scene Saturday to begin its own investigation into the cause. The agency said at a news conference that investigators have recovered a Voyage Data Recorder (VDR) from the Atlantic Asphalt and asked the public for video and information. A VDR captures the vessel's speed through the water, direction, course and audio from the bridge of the vessel, according to the NTSB.

Burnham said at a news conference Saturday that approximately 16,000 gallons of fuel remain on board and that officials are assessing how to address the potential pollution. She told reporters it is too early to give a timeline on salvaging the wreckage, saying, "We're talking weeks."
Burnham noted Friday that she was working to reopen the river, which the Coast Guard had closed when the collision occurred.
"We're going to start evaluating how to reopen it as soon as possible," Burnham said.

In a Truth Social post, President Trump praised the response of the Coast Guard and other law enforcement agencies for "doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana."
The American Heritage was built in 2015 and is operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The Associated Press reports that the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. The tanker specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semisolid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.
CBS News has reached out to the tanker's owner for comment.

title: Port of New Orleans sues tanker that hit riverboat cruise for $1 million
summary: The port asked a judge to seize and sell the tanker that hit a riverboat cruise to cover the costs of repairs.
story: The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of the asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship on the Mississippi River yesterday. In a lawsuit reviewed by CBS News, the port said the tanker was at fault for the incident and that the collision caused more than $1 million in damage to port property.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with the much smaller American Heritage passenger boat while it was docked at the port's Thalia Street Terminal on Friday afternoon. There were an estimated 129 passengers, plus crew members, aboard the cruise ship at the time of the collision, Port NOLA said Friday. Everyone aboard both vessels was accounted for, and there were no fatalities or critical injuries reported, though the cruise ship was left on its side and largely submerged in water.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court late Friday, names the tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management Pte, Ltd.
The full extent of the damage is still being assessed, according to the lawsuit, and the port is seeking money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.
The lawsuit asked that the tanker be seized and sold to pay for the damage.

The lawsuit alleges that the tanker and companies failed "to use all available means to avoid the risk of" colliding with the stationary riverboat, noting that a presumption of fault arises when a ship hits a stationary object.
The collision "occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or careless of the" ship and operating companies, the lawsuit alleged.
Owner Nave Shipping and management company Thome Ship Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment from CBS News about the lawsuit.

Thome posted a statement on Saturday morning about the incident, confirming the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt is safe and accounted for. It said the tanker had been separated from the riverboat and is stably anchored for damage assessments.

"OSM Thome is fully complying with the local authorities as they carry out the necessary investigations," the company said. "We would like to extend our sincere gratitude to all parties and personnel who responded to this incident with urgency and humanity."
The lawsuit also notes that further parties may be identified and added to the legal proceeding as the investigation into the incident continues.

title: U.S. loses measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, researchers with knowledge of the decision confirmed to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. The agency is set to hold a news conference on Tuesday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continue to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. New York and Wisconsin have each reported one death.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that the disease's spread can be sustained, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshhold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 did not get vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.

Some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated for measles, so they rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading. Awan said that these groups of people will bear "the brunt of the consequences" of increased measles spread.
"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.

title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights
summary: The rare nationwide ground stop lasted about five hours on Friday. An update to the network connecting the air traffic control system caused a reboot, crash and outage, sources told CBS News.
story: Federal airspace is operating normally after a nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights threw the aviation industry into turmoil Friday. Officials said the issue stemmed from a "telecommunication outage."
The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours.
As of 7:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, the airspace was operating as normal and being closely tracked, senior government sources familiar with the situation told CBS News.

"Operations are slowly returning to normal this morning. Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a social media post on Saturday. "We are in close coordination with the airlines to support the ongoing recovery."
He warned that travelers will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition crews.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," he said. "To our air traffic controllers, pilots, and flight crews who are working around the clock: the nation thanks you for your professionalism and dedication to the flying public."
There are more than 2,000 delays and more than 3,800 cancellations in the U.S. on Saturday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.

Delta Air Lines led the way with 640 cancellations, while United had 530 and American had 488. Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, Chicago O'Hare International Airport and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport were most affected by the cancellations on Saturday morning. There were also about 1,400 flights delayed.
Preliminary investigation indicates routers caused outage
Duffy said Friday that routers became overloaded with data and began to provide inconsistent information.
"Because of that, we shut the system down," Duffy said, noting the air traffic control system is "incredibly old."
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Friday's briefing that new security patches introduced into the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers.

The FAA's preliminary investigation has led the agency to believe the issue was limited to Cisco 600 series routers that were manufactured between 2001 and 2006, senior government sources told CBS News. The sources said the faulty equipment has been identified and isolated.

The sources said the routers essentially got overwhelmed and started feeding out-of-sync data packets into the larger air traffic control system. That causes static over voice communication lines and can cause screens to flash or go to black.

Sources told CBS News they are receiving conflicting information about the cause of the issue. Multiple sources said Friday that an update to the private communications network that connects the U.S. air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage.
Officials call for emergency funding to modernize ATC

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, known as FTI, is the communications backbone that connects air traffic control centers and other FAA facilities. It supports the transmission of essential voice communications and operational data used to manage air traffic. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The FAA awarded Harris Corp., the predecessor to L3Harris, a contract to modernize, operate and manage the network in July 2002.
A November 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review described the FTI network as obsolete and said it depended on an older communications technology known as TDM.

The review also warned that the technology was no longer supported by the telecommunications infrastructure on which it relied and that an unexpected failure could leave individual FAA facilities, or even an entire regional air traffic control center, disconnected from the broader network.
There has been frustration with L3Harris's communication and response, sources told CBS News.
On Friday night, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.
"But you will have more of these," Duffy said during the news conference. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."

Mullin argued that the incident demonstrated why he believed piecemeal modernization was insufficient and said the Trump administration wants a complete replacement of the air traffic control system, at an estimated cost of $50 billion.
"No indication" of cyber attack or threat, Mullin says

Mullin told reporters in an earlier briefing outside the White House Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."

"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."
Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global Microsoft outage.

"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said during the news briefing with Duffy. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."
Chaos for travelers

According to the flight tracking site Flightradar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began. Planes were able to land safely, Mullin said, but with no aircraft able to take off again, delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."

Overall, 9,159 flights were cancelled and 7,190 were delayed on Friday, according to FlightAware. It was the second-worst travel day for airlines this year: A massive snowstorm on Jan. 25, 2026 led to 11,607 flight cancellations.

In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.
