title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
summary: A U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
story: A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.

The 41-year-old suspect hasn't been publicly identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
The officer was caught in a sting operation and arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, the official said. He is expected to be charged Sunday or Monday.

The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."
Speaking to reporters Wednesday in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had "nothing to do with" the detention of the U.S. soldier.

In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.

The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive," although it seems none of the participants expect any immediate breakthroughs, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejecting European demands for an immediate ceasefire.

U.K. police said the arrest was not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations," meaning it appears to be unrelated to the recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, which officials have said is linked to Iran. The U.S. military last month removed its bombers from that base after a security incident that led to the arrests of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national in late September. There are U.S. troops stationed at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at RAF Fairford. One of the suspects is in custody in New York. However, the other two are not in custody at this time, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
summary: Pope Leo declared Peru his "homeland" as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit​, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor.
story: Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.

Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.

Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.

In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.
"That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.
Popemania descends on Peru, where Leo lived and served for decades

The visit to Peru marked the final leg of Leo's three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that Leo, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. He has said it was here that he learned "what it means to be a shepherd." As a dual citizen of the U.S. and Peru, he's the first pope from each country.
"We love him so much because he's worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all," said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who held a pope plush doll made by her niece as she waited for Leo to arrive.

In preparation for the pope's visit, a huge 46-foot statue of the pontiff was unveiled in the port of El Callao. Baristas in Lima, the capital, were offering cappuccinos decorated with the image of the pope.
"My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy," said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo's
secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast.
Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of "Lived Religion in Latin America," said the trip was a "return to his origins, without any doubt."
"Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born," he said.

With hands raised and voices lifted in song, hundreds awaited the pope's arrival in Lima in front of the presidential palace. "Long live Christ!" the crowd sang, following a Catholic choir on the stage.
Popemania also hit Chiclayo, where Leo arrives on Friday. Leo is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on T-shirts, baseball hats and even bobblehead dolls.

Over the coming days, Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including at the nearby sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a city that is a hub of Afro-Peruvian culture, and where the pope often visited to pray to the saint of his devotion.

Since Leo knows his adopted country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral Thursday "on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people."
Pope to honor Peru's Indigenous peoples in the Amazon

The pope will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon, to celebrate Mass. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Peru's Indigenous peoples.

"The Amazon is a place where critical issues affecting development — such as the environmental crisis, the exclusion of Indigenous peoples, various forms of violence, and extreme poverty — all intersect," said Pérez.

Leo will also meet with popular groups of faithful and representatives of local traditions in Cusco — the capital of the Inca Empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and an important cultural
destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu.
The pope will celebrate Mass in Cusco's main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.
Pope arrives in Peru about one month after undergoing lung cancer surgery

The pope's arrival in Peru comes about one month after he underwent surgery in Italy to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, during which surgeons confirmed he had lung cancer. The Vatican announced at the time that the 71-year-old had been diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, and that the surgery had been successful.
Just two weeks after he underwent the surgery, doctors cleared him to make the South American trip, which started in Uruguay and took him to Argentina.
During an address in Uruguay last weekend, the pope used his own experience with cancer to push for access to universal healthcare.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness, and I received care for which I am grateful," the pope said. " … Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society."
At the start of his trip, the pope also confirmed that he voted by mail in the U.S. midterm elections in Chicago, the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election.

title: What to know as "super El Niño" conditions take shape
summary: Here's what to know about El Niño, the powerful climate pattern impacting weather across the globe.
story: El Niño has become especially powerful this year, with "super El Niño" conditions now officially taking shape.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center announced Thursday that the phenomenon, which affects weather and climate around the world, has intensified and continues to strengthen. Its effects through next spring may even be considered historic, the agency said.
Here's everything to know about El Niño:
What is El Niño?
El Niño is a climate pattern defined by warming waters in a specific region of the Pacific Ocean near the equator. It occurs every two to seven years and usually lasts between nine and 12 months.

When El Niño is active, a large portion of the world gets warmer, too. In September, researchers at the University of Chicago predicted that an estimated 451,000 more people would die worldwide during this year's El Niño, compared with a typical year, because of excessive heat exposure.

The impacts of El Niño vary in different parts of the world, adjusting hurricane frequencies, altering sea levels, and at times triggering mass flooding or severe drought as well as seasonal snowfall amounts that depart from historical averages.
Fishing and agricultural industries often feel tangible consequences of those changes, as do utilities that depend on rainfall and wind to generate power.
A "super" El Niño

Hype has swirled around the phrase "super" El Niño, which describes an El Niño climate pattern that is particularly strong and impactful. It isn't an official term, though, and neither NOAA nor the World Meteorological Organization recognizes it. Instead, both agencies categorize this year's El Niño as "very strong."

NOAA determines that an El Niño event is taking place when El Niño conditions are detected in the tropical Pacific for at least a three-month period, five times in a row. If sea surface temperatures in that region rise 0.5 degrees Celsius, or more, above average, an El Niño event is declared.

As of Nov. 12, sea surface temperature anomalies topped 4 degrees Celsius as El Niño strengthened and its conditions continued to spread, according to NOAA's Climate Prediction Center. If temperatures rise to 2 degrees or more above average for five three-month periods in a row, the event will be considered a "very strong" El Niño.
El Niño's impact on North America
Due to the warmer climate, the southern portion of North America tends to experience wetter conditions during an El Niño event, as more frequent storms move in from the Pacific Ocean.
But the northern portion of the continent is likely to see milder weather, with less precipitation through the winter months.

In the U.S., southern states should prepare for a stormier winter than usual. According to NOAA's winter outlook, those areas have higher chances of receiving precipitation in the form of rain or snow.
El Niño's impact worldwide

The northern portion of South America and central Africa are typically drier through the winter months during El Niño, while Australia and southern Asia also tend to experience drier conditions with less shower and storm activity. Drought risks are elevated in areas where drier weather is expected.

Wetter conditions will materialize in certain regions, including eastern Asia and the southern portion of South America, both of which are forecast to receive more precipitation as a result of El Niño. Moisture could potentially help improve drought conditions in some of those areas, but it also carries risks for severe flooding.

El Niño's contrasting impacts on Central and South America have raised concerns this year, as a mix of drought and record precipitation devastated agriculture and prompted multiple countries to declare national emergencies.
How El Niño affects hurricanes
How El Niño affected hurricane seasons in both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans this year was one of the more obvious examples of its influence.

In the Atlantic, an El Niño tends to create conditions that hamper the development of tropical storms, while the opposite set of conditions encourages their formation in the Pacific. It played a key role in the Atlantic basin's record-low tropical storm and hurricane activity this year, and, at the same time, contributed to the Pacific season's record intensity.

Meteorologists watch for movement of Saharan dust in the atmosphere off the coast of western Africa to predict tropical activity in the Atlantic basin. When an El Niño climate is present, drier conditions enhance Saharan dust, which decreases the potential for tropical activity.

In the Pacific, warmer waters caused by El Niño help create the ideal fuel for storm systems to erupt and become tropical storms or hurricanes. In the Western Pacific, where tropical cyclones are referred to as typhoons, these systems are more likely to become hazardous "super typhoons" during El Niño, at times bringing catastrophic impacts to parts of eastern Asia.

Weather agencies have tracked 32 typhoons so far in 2026. Super Typhoon Sinlaku in April and Super Typhoon Champi in October tied as the strongest typhoons of the year in the Western Pacific, both reaching Category 5-equivalent strength with sustained winds of up to 185 mph.

The Eastern Pacific has seen 21 named tropical systems this year. Some brought large waves to the West Coast of the U.S., eroding luxury beaches. In the Central Pacific, Hawaii has seen five named tropical systems make close passes, bringing heavy rainfall, strong winds and flash flooding.

El Niño's strength often dictates how dramatically it impacts global weather. This year's is among the strongest on record, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has predicted that it will most likely stick around through March. That means there are still months of potential repercussions ahead.

El Niño events are becoming stronger and longer over time, with scientists linking the current conditions to this year's record heat. Some recent El Niño events happened from 2023 to 2024, 2018 to 2019, 2014 to 2016, 2009 to 2010, and 2004 to 2005. In 2015, only 12 named tropical systems were tracked in the Atlantic while the Eastern Pacific saw 18 named systems, similar to this year.

title: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
summary: Far from the opposition American tech giants face, it's smooth sailing for the Chinese AI firms racing to catch up, and hoping to overtake them.
story: Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest.

Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind.

The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom.
The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now.

This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, China spy scandal
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, China spy scandal
Baletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive.
"It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area."

A short drive away, CBS News was able to see what all that wind power will soon be feeding. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are taking part in the construction project to create one of the biggest data centers anywhere in the world.

We drove miles down new roads with multistory data centers going up on either side. Even from the road it was easy to spot the countless racks that will hold servers, semi-conductor chips and cooling and exhaust fans.

There are dozens of data centers being built in Inner Mongolia, more than any other part of the vast nation. The reason they have chosen Ulanqab is because it offers cheap, abundant energy. Fossil fuels are still the main source of power here, but they also use renewables, including wind and solar.

Ulanqab is one of the most consistently windy locations in the province. The climate is also cold all year, which helps keep cooling costs down, and land and labor are more affordable in the remote region.
Experts cited by the Financial Times say data centers in China are built at about one-fifth of the costs incurred in the U.S., not least due to the much higher land and labor costs.

As many as 30,000 workers have been brought in from across China to help build the AI hub, and in a country experiencing an economic downturn and high youth unemployment, these mass infrastructure projects are very much welcome.

"Development is the best thing, especially when it provides job opportunities for many young people," a local businesswoman who sets up a lunchtime food stall outside the construction site told CBS News.

While data centers in the U.S. face major community opposition, which could be emboldened by the "blue wave" of the Democrats' stunning midterm election performance, there are few hurdles for Chinese developers.

While China's government doesn't generally tolerate protests of any kind, and it tightly controls messaging across all media, a United Nations survey last year found that as many as 80% of people in the country support data center construction. At least two-thirds of Chinese people use AI in their day-to-day life, as many embrace the technology and the infrastructure behind it.
Under President Xi Jinping, AI development has become a national strategic priority for China.

"There is no opposition to data centers in China. It's never heard of, whereas in the U.S., it has become a huge movement against data center building in neighborhoods," Henry Wang, founder and president of the Center For China and Globalization, told CBS News.

Huawei, Alibaba, Byte Dance, Deepseek, Baidu, Z.ai, ZData and VNET — China's biggest AI companies — are all active in Inner Mongolia. In areas where construction has finished, fences are up and grounds are landscaped, and avenues through the humming data centers have been named after the AI tech giants.
While Chinese firms' AI models are believed to be about six months behind their U.S. competitors, due largely to restrictions on the sale of high-end microchips, the gap is narrowing.
China has more than double the power generation capacity of the U.S., and some experts believe access to power, not chips, will ultimately be the deciding factor in the global race for AI dominance.
"Chips may not become the latest diving criteria," said Wang. "It may be that power is the bottleneck, and whoever goes through that first gets the advantage. And right now. China has the edge."

title: Ukraine says Starshield throttled again as U.S. pushes for a deal
summary: Ukraine says its ability to intercept Russian strikes is again hampered by speed restrictions on Musk's Starshield network amid U.S.-led diplomacy.
story: As President Trump's senior envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed Thursday in a snowy Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said connection issues with the Starlink satellite network were again affecting his country's ability to defend itself from incoming Russian missiles and drones.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces using Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink network, which was also impacted last month, were again facing a "systemic speed restriction."
Ukrainian interceptors, used to shoot down Russian weapons, have been losing their Starshield satellite guidance connection this week if they try to fly faster than about 100 miles per hour.

"Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant malfunctions in Starshield's operation over Ukraine's territory for several days now: along the entire front line and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory," Zelenskyy said in a social media post. "Ukrainian military personnel have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but a systemic speed restriction. For us, this primarily means a significant increase in the difficulty of intercepting Russian jet-powered drones."

A Ukrainian official confirmed the restrictions to CBS News, saying "the speed limitations as of now are on Ukrainian occupied territories and across the contact line. The contact line is the first line of our defense and the first point for interception of Russian drones. It started gradually 3 days ago and now it's 100%."

Overnight, Russian drones hit an apartment building in Kyiv, killing one woman, according to authorities, while more energy infrastructure was hit in Rivne in Ukraine's northwest, leaving more people in the dark and cold as temperatures fall.
Earlier this week, a Russian strike in the Odesa region killed three people, and multiple strikes across the country caused energy grid disruptions.

"Starshield services must be restored urgently for Ukraine to keep its soldiers connected, to protect its citizens and to defend its territory," European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said at a news conference in Brussels.

Zelenskyy did not blame anyone for Ukrainian forces' latest problems with the Starshield system. However, one Ukrainian source told CBS News they "are certain" that SpaceX implemented the restrictions, as officials in both the U.S. and Ukraine said was the case during last month's outage.

People familiar with the matter told CBS News that Elon Musk himself made the decision to reduce Starshield service in Ukraine last month, after multiple conversations with Trump administration officials.

As both sides carried on with their daily attacks — Russia said more than 70 Ukrainian drones were intercepted Thursday, including several headed for Moscow —   Witkoff and Kushner carried on with their shuttle diplomacy.

Their meeting with Putin in Moscow came after the first round of U.S.-brokered talks between the two countries since February concluded on Wednesday with an announcement of plans for a new prisoner exchange and a commitment to keep talking, but nothing to suggest a wider peace deal could be in the offing.

Speaking after the two-day talks, Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser, said he wanted European countries to be involved in the peace process, something both Ukraine and its European partners have long pushed for.

Russia, however, accuses America's European NATO allies of being a party to the war Putin launched more than a decade ago, and ramped up significantly with the ongoing full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Speaking Wednesday, Kushner said the U.S. envoys would "see if we can get the Europeans added to the format, so we can make this a multilateral format."
He said "the only way to get this done is to have them by our side."

During the same briefing after the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky made Moscow's position on Europe clear, telling reporters: "We do not really understand what there is to discuss with them, and they haven't offered a single proposal."

Major hurdles to a peace deal remain, including Putin's demand for Ukraine to surrender all of its eastern Donbas region —   roughly 20% of Ukraine's overall territory — including some areas Russian forces haven't managed to wrest control of by force. He also wants guarantees that European countries will back off from involvement in Ukraine's security going forward, while Kyiv has long sought membership in the NATO alliance.
Witkoff and Kushner were set to fly from Moscow to Dublin, Ireland, later Thursday to meet with Zelenskyy for further discussions.

Zelenskyy, in Dublin ahead of the U.S. envoys' arrival to attend a European Political Community Summit with fellow leaders, again noted the Starshield restrictions Thursday, and he alleged that "Putin has told people close to him he wants to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities — Kyiv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and other cities."

"If someone in America is making decisions that essentially treat Ukrainian territories as if they don't belong to Ukraine, then that tells us where things are heading," Zelenskyy said. "We must be clear and never, under any circumstances, recognize the Russian occupation of Ukrainian territory."

title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6, health authorities say
summary: An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Hamas-controlled Health Ministry said.
story: An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Health Ministry said Thursday. The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck "a senior Hamas terrorist" and other militants "while they were operating within Nasser Hospital," without providing evidence.
Israel accuses Hamas and its allies of using hospitals as cover for military activity.
In the statement, the Israeli military said Hamas was using the hospital as "a command center for military and terrorist activities."

The Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgery department and that a doctor was among the dead. An Associated Press journalist at the scene said parts of the building's second floor were destroyed.

Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in the Palestinian territory, where healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by the yearslong war.

Israeli forces have previously attacked and raided Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.

The war started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government but whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton visited the Egyptian side of the border with southern Gaza this week, hoping to use his celebrity status to raise awareness of conditions inside the Palestinian enclave. In a statement posted on social media he condemned Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide — an allegation made by United Nations experts but vehemently rejected by Israel.
Hamilton said he saw "walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in," referring to Gazans, for whom the territory had become, in his words "like an open-air prison."

He said there were "food trucks lined up ready to go" into Gaza at the Rafah border crossing, "but they're regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics center, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs, even footballs for kids.Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. No excuse."

Axios reported last week that President Trump, in a phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the U.S. midterm elections, pushed the Israeli leader to take steps to implement a Gaza peace plan laid out by Mr. Trump. The nature of that call and Mr. Trump's remarks have not been confirmed by the White House.

Mr. Trump's special envoy Jared Kushner directly linked a lack of progress on the rehabilitation of the war-torn Gaza Strip and on the peace effort to Israel's recent elections, which delivered a sigificant loss for Netanyahu.

Kushner's remarks, a rare criticism of Netanyahu's government by a senior Trump administration official over his Gaza policy, came after the Israeli leader rejected the U.S. plan touted by Mr. Trump as a "historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other groups in Gaza." Netanyahu vowed there would be no withdrawal of Israel's military from Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
U.S. efforts to advance the plan to disarm Hamas and open the way for investment to rebuild Gaza have stalled amid disagreements with Israel and Hamas over the proposal.

title: China fines a company over a Dove chocolate "situationship" ad
summary: China has fined a company what amounts to about $120,000 over an ad it created for Dove chocolate featuring a woman in a "situationship," saying it promoted the "wrong views on marriage and relationships."
story: Chinese authorities have fined a company the equivalent of about $120,000 over an advertisement it created for American chocolate brand Dove that featured a woman in a "situationship," saying on Thursday it promoted the "wrong views on marriage and relationships."
The video, first posted online in August, showed a woman getting chocolates from a man with whom she was in a "situationship" after her boyfriend ignored her.
The clip caused a stir online in China, with some social media users saying it promoted infidelity, prompting Dove to issue an apology.

Zongzheng Food — the company that created the ad and that operates a Dove store on Chinese e-commerce platform Kuaishou — was fined 800,000 yuan ($120,000) last month, Shanghai authorities said on Thursday.

The ad "packaged being unfaithful in a relationship as a 'sweet experience,' promoting wrong views on marriage and relationships and violating good social customs," the Shanghai Municipal Market Supervision Administration said in a statement.
China is facing a demographic crisis after its birth rate halved over the past decade, and in response authorities have heavily promoted traditional family structures.
Marriage registrations from January to September were down 9.8% year-over-year, reaching just 4.6 million, data from China's civil affairs ministry showed last week.
Dove, which is owned by McLean, Virginia-based Mars Inc., said in its apology in August that the ad didn't follow its content review process and was "clearly inappropriate."
Dove "bears responsibility" for all content posted to its official channels, the chocolate brand said on social media platform Weibo.
Chinese authorities have previously rebuked companies for platforming romantic relationships deemed inappropriate.
In May, Chinese consumer electronics company OPPO said it "severely punished" multiple executives over an ad joking about infidelity, which authorities publicly condemned.

title: Princess Diana’s legendary White House dance with John Travolta almost didn’t happen
summary: Princess Diana danced with Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and Ronald Reagan that evening, but it took coaxing to get John Travolta onto the floor.
story: "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, reveals the story behind Princess Diana's famous dance with John Travolta and showcases her iconic velvet gown.
John Travolta had all the right moves, but when the chance to dance with Princess Diana came along, even Hollywood's smoothest dancer got cold feet.

The Princess of Wales and the actor lit up the White House ballroom in 1985, creating one of the most unforgettable moments in royal and Hollywood history. Diana was attending a White House dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan and first lady Nancy Reagan when she took a spin with the heartthrob.

More than four decades later, their legendary dance is being celebrated at "Princess Diana: Love, Life, Legacy — A Life of Giving," an exhibition at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. More than 700 artifacts connected to Diana's life are on display.
PRINCESS DIANA, HOT DOGS AND A PRESIDENTIAL MATCHMAKING ATTEMPT: ICONIC ROYAL VISITS TO AMERICA
American actor John Travolta dancing with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House, Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Glasshouse Images)

The collection, presented through a partnership between the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute (RRPFI) and Renae Plant's Princess Diana Museum, features the velvet gown designed by Victor Edelstein that Diana wore that night.
But the iconic dance nearly didn't happen.

Princess Diana's "Travolta" dress is a highlight of the exhibition dedicated to the late Princess of Wales and her warm friendship with the Reagans. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"In preparation for the state dinner, the Marine Band that was going to perform the music during the dinner was told to rehearse music from 'Saturday Night Fever,'" Melissa Giller, chief marketing and cultural programming officer at RRPFI, told Fox News Digital.
WATCH: PRINCESS DIANA'S ICONIC DANCE WITH TRAVOLTA GETS NEW SPOTLIGHT

"The social secretary, Gahl Burt, she orchestrated it after speaking with Mrs. Reagan that after the dancing began, Gahl would walk up to John Travolta and tap him on the shoulder and encourage him to have a dance with Princess Diana," Giller said. "Now through the whole evening, Princess Diana danced with Ronald Reagan. She danced with Clint Eastwood. She danced with Tom Selleck and many others."
But when it came time for Travolta to step onto the dance floor with Diana, he needed some coaxing.
President Ronald Reagan dances with Princess Diana in Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"When it was time, Gahl Burt walked up to John Travolta and tapped him on the shoulder," Giller said. "He was actually a bit hesitant. He didn't know if it was something he should do. But after some encouragement, he went up and asked the princess to dance."

Prince Charles and Princess Diana met President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985, during an official visit to the United States. (Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images)
Travolta mustered the courage and approached Diana. The two then waltzed across the checkered floor to music from "Saturday Night Fever."
"They ended up dancing for 15 minutes," Giller said with a smile.
President Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan welcome Princess Diana and Prince Charles at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 1985. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Every presidential library archive has a photo that's the most requested by the public. President Nixon's library is the photo of Elvis meeting President Nixon. And one of our most requested photos is the one of Princess Diana dancing with John Travolta."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Princess Diana is seen here with John Travolta in the Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., at a dinner for Prince Charles and Princess Diana of the United Kingdom on Nov. 9, 1985. (Alamy Live News.)
Travolta later admitted he was nervous before approaching Diana.

"I didn't think they'd ask me to dance with her," he told Esquire Mexico in 2021. "I had the great privilege and honor of doing so, and I thought, 'There must be a reason for doing this and I better give it my all.’ That meant lead the dance well and make sure we had fun. That was the easy part, but just the fact of greeting Diana appropriately, being confident and asking her to dance was a complicated task."
President and Mrs. Reagan welcome Prince Charles and Princess Diana to the White House on Nov. 9, 1985. (Bettmann Archive)
The "Grease" star also recalled how special it was to dance with Diana.
John Travolta later revealed that dancing with Princess Diana was one of the highlights of his life. (John Shelley Collection/Avalon/Getty Images)

"Think of the setting. We were at the White House. It's midnight. The stage is like a dream. I approach her, touch her elbow, invite her to dance," he said. "She spins around and gives me that captivating smile, just a little sad, and accepts my invitation. And there we were, dancing together as if it were a fairytale."
In the 2021 interview, Travolta also recalled his disbelief over the once-in-a-lifetime encounter.
Princess Diana's childhood keepsakes on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
"Who could imagine that something like this is going to happen to you one day? I was smart enough to register it in my memory as a very special, magical moment."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
John Travolta and Princess Diana danced for 15 minutes. (Pete Souza/The White House via Getty Images)
Travolta also told Dutch television station Één that it was Nancy who told him Diana wanted to dance with him.

"[She] said, 'It is her wish,'" the actor recalled. "At midnight, I had to tap her on her shoulder, and I had to say, 'Would you care to dance?' She turned around and dipped her head in that Lady Diana way, and we were off for 15 minutes dancing."
Princess Diana's Versace dress. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"I'll never forget it," he continued. "I'm so honored that I was able to experience this, and I know for a fact that it was her highlight of being in the United States; it was her favorite moment. So I feel I made her life better, she made my life better, and I'm very sorry that she's not here."

Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing a cream lace gown with a scalloped neckline designed by Murray Arbeid and the Lover's Knot diamond and pearl tiara, smiles as she attends a dinner at the British Ambassador's Residence in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 11, 1985. (Getty Images)
During a 2016 appearance on "Good Morning America," Travolta was asked if there was anything from the 1980s that he'd like to bring back to the 2010s. He said he'd love to dance with Diana again.
"That was one of the highlights of my life, so that's probably the best moment of the '80s."
Princess Diana's honeymoon shoes and hat on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
Giller noted that the Prince and Princess of Wales maintained a close friendship with the Reagans.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
The former Prince Charles is seen here attending a dinner with President Ronald Reagan and his wife Nancy at the White House in Washington, D.C. (Jean-Louis Atlan/Sygma)

"When Princess Diana got married to Prince Charles, Ronald Reagan, as President of the United States, could not go because the assassination attempt happened a few months ago and he was [still] recovering," Giller explained. "So, Mrs. Reagan went on behalf of President Reagan, as well as the United States. And I think that sort of bonded her with Princess Diana, although of course, Mrs. Reagan was much older than Princess Diana."
"They shared a kinship, especially once Princess Diana became a mother," Giller said. "You can see that in [their] letters and their relationship."
Princess Diana's "final goodbye" dress was designed for the Princess of Wales but never worn before her tragic death in August 1997. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
The exhibition features letters Nancy and Diana wrote to each other over the years, as well as gifts the Reagans received from the Prince and Princess of Wales.
Princess Diana with Nancy Reagan at the White House in 1985. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Giller said the exhibition aims to show visitors the woman behind the royal title, highlighting Diana's humanitarian work and influence beyond her relationship with the Reagans.
"Diana: Love Life Legacy — A Life of Giving" showcases more than 700 original artifacts from Princess Diana's extraordinary life. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)

"This isn't just an exhibition about dresses and shoes and jewelry," she said. "This is an exhibition about a woman who truly cared about her family, about her people, about all people, not just those in Europe, but around the world."

Princess Diana's famous "Caring Dress" from the Princess Diana Museum is also on display. (Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute)
The exhibition, which opened Nov. 7, runs through May 31, 2027.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Below Deck’ star arrested after brawl leaves 17-year-old dead
summary: João Franco, the former "Below Deck Mediterranean" star, and his brother claim self-defense after their arrest in Turkey after a fatal brawl.
story: "Below Deck Mediterranean" star João Franco was arrested after a brawl. (Greg Endries/Bravo/NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images)
Former reality star João Franco and his brother were arrested in Turkey after a fistfight outside a clothing store that left a 17-year-old dead.

In CCTV video obtained by Page Six, the former "Below Deck" star and his brother, Carlos Franco, are seen leaving a store in the Bodrum district of Muğla Nov. 7 with an employee following closely behind them.
Carlos appears to throw the first punch, after which more employees rush out of the store.
At first, João is seemingly trying to de-escalate the situation, often placing himself between his brother and the store employees, before appearing to get involved and throw punches himself.
'BELOW DECK' CAPTAIN SANDY SAYS SHE AND WIFE LOST 'ALL OF OUR MONEY' IN ALLEGED $1.6M CONTRACTOR SCAM
João Franco and his brother were arrested in Turkey after a fight that resulted in the death of a teenager. (Fred Jagueneau/Bravo via Getty Images)
The fight escalated to the point one of the men appeared to grab a nearby stool, seemingly to throw it at Carlos and João.
The Associated Press, citing the Demiroren News Agency, reported that 17-year-old Muhammet Koyabakan fell during the fight and hit his head on the ground. Koyabakan later died in the hospital.
João seemingly tried to de-escalate the situation several times. (Mark Rogers/Bravo via Getty Images)

João and his brother were initially detained and were later arrested. While it is unclear what charges they face, the Demiroren News Agency reported they told police they acted out of self-defense and denied hitting Koyabakan.
According to the news agency, João and his brother were intoxicated and swearing during an argument, which then escalated into a physical fight.

title: Former Miss USA contestant warns aspiring beauty queens she wouldn’t touch Miss Universe ‘with a 10-foot pole’
summary: The TLC documentary "Crown of Deceit" explores pageant scandal allegations, and Taylor Hale details her experience competing as Miss Michigan USA and what followed.
story: Miss Michigan 2021 winner Taylor Hale tells Fox News Digital she'd steer clear of Miss Universe, raising doubts about the international pageant.
The crown may look glamorous, but one former Miss USA contestant is warning aspiring beauty queens what's waiting beyond the national competition may not be worth the risk.
Taylor Hale, who was crowned Miss Michigan USA in 2021, isn't discouraging young women from competing, but she has a stark warning about chasing the Miss Universe dream.

"I hope you win your state pageant. I hope you are highly competitive at Miss USA," she told Fox News Digital ahead of the premiere of TLC's documentary, "Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal."
FORMER MISS NORTH CAROLINA USA SAYS CONSERVATIVE CHRISTIAN VALUES PLAYED ROLE IN LOSING CROWN

Taylor Hale, who competed in Miss USA in 2021, called for sweeping changes at Miss Universe, saying the organization should be "burned to the ground and then rebuilt from the ashes." (Matt Winkelmeyer/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

"And I hope that gets enough eyes on you so that you can achieve whatever it is outside of being Miss USA. Because as Miss USA, you have to go to Miss Universe, and that is a whole other ball game that I wouldn't want to touch with a 10-foot pole."
Hale said she still supports women competing on the national stage.
"I really, really like the new director. I think Thom Brodeur is a really great director. He cares about the women and the well-being of all the girls, teen and miss," she said.
WATCH: FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT HAS WARNING FOR FUTURE MISS UNIVERSE HOPEFULS
But she cautioned that winning a national title shouldn't mean surrendering control of what comes next.
"So, chase your dream, pursue the dream, but also understand that you have to have some ownership and real directorship of where you're going to go afterwards," Hale said.
"Because I don't know if Miss USA at Miss Universe is going to fulfill the fantasy anymore."
ARREST WARRANT FOR MISS UNIVERSE CO-OWNER ISSUED AFTER COURT NO-SHOW IN FRAUD CASE
Taylor Hale praised changes at Miss USA but questioned whether competing at Miss Universe still offers young women the opportunities they hope to gain from pageantry. (TLC/Taylor Hale)
When Fox News Digital asked whether the organizations could regain contestants' trust, Hale said Miss USA has made strides toward greater transparency.
However, she said Miss Universe requires more sweeping changes.
"Miss Universe has to, I think, be burned to the ground and then rebuilt from the ashes," she said.
WATCH: FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT SAYS MISS UNIVERSE MUST BE 'BURNED TO THE GROUND' AND REBUILT AFTER SCANDALS
She added that new leadership and management would be necessary to restore her confidence in the global competition.
MISS MEXICO SPEAKS OUT AFTER HEATED CONFRONTATION WITH MISS UNIVERSE EXECUTIVE GOES VIRAL

While competing as Miss Michigan USA in 2021, Hale said she experienced sexual harassment from Max Sebrechts, vice president of Miss USA at the time, the morning after she failed to advance to the finals.

After declining an invitation Sebrechts allegedly sent through a social media direct message to visit his presidential suite, Hale said he approached her at a hotel and twice initiated unwanted, overly intimate embraces. Sebrechts has denied all allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against him by former pageant contestants.
Former Miss USA contestant Taylor Hale accused former pageant executive Max Sebrechts of sexual harassment. He denied the allegations. (Justin Baker/Getty Images)
Hale said she wasn't the only contestant to receive his message, calling the experience "so offensive … icky and infuriating."
She added, "You can do every single thing right and still be put in a position where, 'OK, great, now I have to deal with this on the backend.'"
Hale said she immediately reported the incident and was promised a meeting with the general counsel for WME-IMG, the entertainment company then associated with the pageant organization.
However, she said pageant leadership did not provide her with answers before sending a mass email six weeks later announcing Sebrechts' departure.
Alexis Fagan-Williams, a Miss Michigan USA 2023 and a "Big Brother" winner, and Miss Michigan USA 2021 Taylor Hale attend the Jovani NYFW Show. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for Jovani Fashion)

Hale called for more accountability, stronger financial backing and major corporate sponsors willing to invest in contestants' safety rather than simply attaching their names to the pageant's glamour.
"We need more sponsors that are not just charitable, but actually invested in real business practices," Hale said.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Hale pointed to Halle Berry as an example of the opportunities pageants can provide, arguing that young women shouldn't have to choose between pursuing those opportunities and feeling protected.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Miss USA Organization and the Miss Universe Organization for comment.
"Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal" is available to stream on TLC and HBO Max. (TLC )

The three-part documentary, "Crown of Deceit: Inside the Miss Universe Scandal," examines allegations of rigged competitions, financial turmoil, lawsuits and a battle over who controls the Miss Universe Organization.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The docuseries also explores the controversy surrounding the 2025 Miss Universe pageant, held in November 2025 in Thailand, according to a news release. The competition faced a series of scandals, including confrontations between contestants and pageant executives, last-minute judge resignations and accusations that the competition was rigged.
Omar Harfouch, a Miss Universe judge who made headlines when he abruptly resigned just before the 2025 pageant, appears in the documentary.

Harfouch resigned after accusing pageant organizers of rigging the competition, alleging that the top 30 finalists had been selected before the event began. The Miss Universe Organization has denied his accusations.

Thai business tycoon Jakkaphong "Anne" Jakrajutatip appears at a Miss Universe event in Bangkok. She was reportedly convicted in a fraud case involving a corporate bond investment worth approximately $951,927. (AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit)

Jakkaphong "Anne" Jakrajutatip, the founder of JKN Global Group, which co-owns the Miss Universe pageant, was sentenced to two years in prison after being convicted in a fraud case involving a corporate bond investment worth approximately $951,927, the Bangkok Post reported.
The Bangkok South Kwaeng Court handed down the sentence Dec. 26, 2025, while Jakrajutatip was absent, according to the outlet. Jakrajutatip reportedly remains at large.

The docuseries also examines Miss Universe President and co-owner Raul Rocha, whose bank accounts were frozen as part of a criminal investigation into alleged drug, weapons and fuel trafficking, according to a December 2025 report by The Associated Press.
Neither Rocha nor the Miss Universe Organization responded to the AP's requests for comment about the allegations or investigation at the time, the outlet reported.

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton get unexpected help enforcing strict rule for George at elite school: experts
summary: Prince George's Eton College smartphone ban aligns with Prince William and Kate Middleton's strict no-internet phone policy for their children.
story: Royal author Hugo Vickers explains why Prince George could find freedom, privacy and a sense of normalcy at Eton College despite his future as Britain's king.
Prince William and Kate Middleton are reportedly giving Eton College's smartphone ban the royal thumbs-up, especially for their eldest son, Prince George.
The 13-year-old began his studies at the prestigious boarding school in September, where first-year Etonians are banned from using smartphones, according to The Telegraph.
Instead, Year 9 students like George are issued basic "brick phones" with no internet access, limiting communication with their parents to calls and texts outside school hours.
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON COULD SEEK 'GENTLEMAN'S AGREEMENT' TO PROTECT PRINCE GEORGE AT ETON: EXPERTS
Eton College said the decision to ban smartphones for first-year students is intended "to balance the benefits and challenges that technology brings to schools."
Eton reportedly tightened restrictions on first-year students' school-issued iPads in September 2026 in response parental concerns about gaming and internet browsing.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, and Prince William, Prince of Wales, walk with their 13-year-old son, Prince George of Wales, as he arrives for his first day at Eton College Sept. 8, 2026, in Berkshire, England. (Adrian Dennis/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Eton College and Kensington Palace for comment.
In 2025, William told actor Eugene Levy on the Apple TV+ series "The Reluctant Traveler" that "none of our children have any phones, which we’re very strict about."

Prince George arrives for his first day at Eton College in Eton, west of London, on Sept. 8, 2026. Prince William and Catherine accompany him as headmaster Simon Henderson and provost Nicholas Coleridge greet the family. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
That same year, William told Brazilian TV host Luciano Huck during the 2025 Earthshot Prize events in Brazil that it had been "really hard" to protect his children from the harms of social media.
WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE AT ETON COLLEGE COULD LOOK VERY DIFFERENT: EXPERT

"Our children don't have phones," he explained at the time. "I think when George moves on to secondary school, then maybe he might have a phone that has no internet access. And, to be honest, it's getting to a point where it's become a little bit of a, like, tense issue.

"But I think he understands why," William continued. "We communicate why we don't think it's right. And, again, I think it's the internet access I have a problem with. I think children can access too much stuff they don't need to see online, and, so, having a phone and text message, the old sort of 'brick phone' as they call them, I think that's fine."
A view of Eton College, Eton, Berkshire, June 1962. (Archive Photos/Getty Images)

"It has been rumored that William and Kate were having battles with George over having a smartphone with internet access," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. "Usage could get him into trouble but also allow him access to views on the royal family, good and bad, which may worry him.
Kate Middleton and Prince George at Eton College. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"It is now becoming more common practice for schools to ban smartphone usage during school days, and parents want age-appropriate locks on internet technology."
British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that Eton's smartphone policy is "music to Prince William and Princess Catherine's ears."
Eton College Chapel is the main site of worship for students at Eton College, a famous English boys' school. (Mark Kerrison/In Pictures via Getty Images)
"Prince William and Princess Catherine restrict smart devices to protect their children from internet safety risks," she explained.

"A healthy rule of accessing only 'brick phones' at Eton only enables essential communication and calls and texts at home. The couple take great comfort in knowing that Prince George will not be wasting his time gaming, 'doom-scrolling,' or accessing inappropriate online content.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The Prince and Princess of Wales, seen here on the Isle of Mull, western Scotland, April 30, 2025, agreed that their eldest, Prince George, would attend Eton College. (Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images)

"Prince George has never owned a smartphone," Chard continued. "He will be more than happy with a brick phone. As Princess Catherine has shared, smartphones can create an emotional disconnection. Prince George has years of smartphone access ahead of him and certainly will not go without."

Eton College, a world-renowned all-boys boarding school, was founded in 1440 by King Henry VI. It serves students between the ages of 13 and 18. About 1,350 students attend Eton, where they live in 25 boarding houses, each housing approximately 55 pupils, according to the school's website. People magazine reported that tuition was about $80,000 for the 2025-26 academic year.
A view of Eton College, founded by King Henry VI (Archive Photos/Getty Images)

William and his younger brother, Prince Harry, attended Eton, making them both "Old Etonians." Princess Diana's father, John Spencer, and brother, Charles Spencer, also attended the school, as did Queen Elizabeth II's cousins, the Duke of Kent, the Duke of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent.
Prince William signs in on his first day at Eton College Sept. 6, 1995. (Anwar Hussein/WireImage)

Hugo Vickers, author of "Behind Closed Doors" and a fellow "Old Etonian," told Fox News Digital that Eton College's use of "brick phones" is "sensible." Vickers has written several books about the British royal family.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Behind Closed Doors: The Tragic, Untold Story of the Duchess of Windsor" by Hugo Vickers is available now. (Pegasus Books)
"In my day, most of our communication was by writing a letter home," he said with a smile.
Prince William stands at Eton College in Eton, United Kingdom, wearing a waistcoat as a member of the elite society group called "Pop." (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)

"And there was about, if I remember rightly, about four telephone boxes planted at different places around the school. On a Sunday morning, if you wanted to ring your parents, you had to get there, and then you'd have to queue up while other people were in there. It sounds very archaic now.
"And sometimes you never got into the telephone box because it's time to go to chapel or something.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Students from Eton College in the Mound Stand react to Harrow students during a cricket match between Eton and Harrow at Lord's Cricket Ground in London, England, May 10, 2024. (Philip Brown/Getty Images)

"So, I think the whole thing about communicating with parents is a whole new concept," Vickers continued. "Basic communication with parents is a good thing, but, of course, to get the full advantage of the school, it's probably better not to be linking to things all over the world via internet."
Melanie Sanderson, managing editor of The Good Schools Guide, told People magazine that Eton College's phone decision "was very much welcomed by parents."
A young Prince Harry at Eton College (Tim Graham/Getty Images)
"And the boys are so busy, they don't have time to be sat on their beds scrolling TikTok," she said.

According to reports, Prince George of Wales is proud to follow in his father's footsteps. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

George was recently on Eton's "Long Leave," a 16-day break that ended Nov. 8. The royal family lives at Forest Lodge in Windsor. When George returns to Eton, the school's restrictions on first-year students' smartphones could offer some additional privacy, although older students and parents may still have access to the devices.

Boys make their way to classes at Eton College, date unknown. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)

"I do know that when George and his siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis … if one of them was going to play a match at a neighboring school, the headmaster would send out a message saying … 'Please, no photographs, no posting,'" Vickers said.

"And the parents would respect that because they're all well brought up. … We never saw any pictures of them at other schools. Nothing was ever leaked because people respect William and Catherine very much."

title: ‘Saved by the Bell’ star Tiffani Thiessen says she needs hip replacement at 52 after painful diagnosis
summary: Tiffani Thiessen revealed a torn labrum and hip dysplasia diagnosis on a podcast, joking she's "basically a German shepherd" ahead of hip replacement.
story: Tiffani Thiessen revealed she had been diagnosed with hip dysplasia and a torn labrum, which caused significant hip pain. (Axelle Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Tiffani Thiessen's active lifestyle hit a painful roadblock after the "Saved by the Bell" star learned she was dealing with more than just the usual aches and pains.
The 52-year-old actress shared her diagnosis and revealed she has to have a hip replacement during an appearance on the "Breaking Bread with Tom Papa" podcast.
"I was a dancer when I was younger, which was a good thing," Thiessen explained. "I have a torn labrum. That's one issue I have.
"This is what happens. Just wait. You guys just wait," she jokingly warned. "And then I found out going to my second opinion that I'm basically a German shepherd. I have hip dysplasia."
'SAVED BY THE BELL' STAR TIFFANI THIESSEN 'FELL IN LOVE' WITH ICE PLUNGING
Tiffani Thiessen attends the 2018 Creative Arts Emmy Awards at Microsoft Theater Sept. 8, 2018, in Los Angeles. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Thiessen claimed her flexibility as a child, which helped her to dance, might have caused her hip issues.
"I hear that hip replacements aren't as bad as knee and shoulder," she added.
Thiessen's painful condition eventually forced her to put one of her favorite pastimes on hold.
"My doctor didn't say it was pickleball, but it probably hasn't helped," she admitted. "I have not been able to play in the last couple weeks because my hip's been so bad."

Thiessen often plays alongside her son, who started playing less than a year ago.

The "Saved by the Bell" star said her hip problems forced her to take a break from playing pickleball, a sport she enjoyed with her son. (NBCU Photo Bank)

Thiessen began modeling and appearing in commercials as a child, winning the Miss Junior America title in 1987. Her big break came in 1989 when she landed the role of Kelly Kapowski on "Saved by the Bell." The character quickly became a fan favorite, helping establish Thiessen as a teen idol.

Tiffani Thiessen admitted that as she got older, she focused less on landing specific roles or winning awards and more on continuing to work in Hollywood. (Aaron Rapoport/Getty Images)
Decades after becoming a household name, Thiessen revealed that her biggest career goal had little to do with fame or recognition.

"It's more just wanting to continue to have the opportunity to do it," she said. "That's what it is for me now. It's not so much specific, ‘I want this or this award or this type of film or work with this type of person.’ I mean, I have a lot of those.

"But, it's more, the main thing is just getting to still do it," Thiessen added. "As we get older, that starts to get smaller. And, so, the fact that I get to still do what I love is really what is most important to me."

Shawn Mendes divided social media with a "Free Palestine" post on Thursday. (Redferns)

title: Randy Travis’ wife says doctors gave country legend 1% chance of survival before miraculous comeback
summary: Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.
story: Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.
Randy Travis' life was turned upside down by a devastating health crisis that doctors gave him just a 1% chance of surviving, according to his wife, Mary.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the country legend — whose new 12-track album, "Same Old Way," is out now — and his wife, Mary, reflected on that life-changing ordeal more than a decade ago, explained how hope and faith played a pivotal role in his recovery, and shared how his determination helped him rebuild his life and reconnect with music.

"They had already told us he had 1% chance of survival. And that was the first couple of days in the hospital," Mary said. "So here we are, five and a half months later, he's still here. He's still improving. We went through the second brain surgery. He came through that with flying colors. The first one is when they said he's not, you know, he doesn't have any chance. But, you know, once you get over those and you start seeing the glimmers of hope and the hand of God on the whole thing."
RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY
Randy Travis' wife, Mary, says the country legend was given a 1% chance of survival in 2013. (Getty Images for the Grand Ole Opry)

The "Forever and Ever, Amen" singer was hospitalized in 2013 for congestive heart failure tied to viral cardiomyopathy. He subsequently suffered a massive stroke that left him with partial paralysis and affected his speech. What began as a trip to seek treatment for congestion became a five-and-a-half-month hospital stay, followed by years of rehabilitation.

"We went through three years of rehab every single day, so we were very quiet and out of the limelight, if you will," she added. "We, you know, we were at home. We went to rehab every day for about three years."
Travis won many awards throughout his 40 years in the music industry, including seven Grammy Awards. (Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images)

Eventually, Mary said, Travis "got tired" of the constant rehabilitation and decided to "go live life." Their trips back to Nashville helped renew their hope that he could once again be involved in the music he loved.
WATCH: RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

Travis has since found new ways to share his music and connect with fans. In May 2024, he released "Where That Came From," using AI technology to recreate his signature singing voice. His "More Life" tour continued through 2026, with Travis appearing alongside Mary while guest vocalist James Dupré and his longtime band perform his hits.
VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY
Mary previously told Fox News Digital that Randy's health crisis cemented their relationship. (Amy E. Price/Getty Images)

Now, with the release of his first album of original material in more than 18 years — featuring 12 previously unreleased songs recorded between 1986 and 2013 and restored by his longtime producer, Kyle Lehning — Mary is reflecting on the determination and gratitude that carried her husband through his toughest moments.
CELINE DION BREAKS DOWN ONSTAGE DURING EMOTIONAL RETURN AFTER 6-YEAR HIATUS

"Just being with this guy has been such an inspiration to me because, going through even the tough times in the hospital, the nurses would come in and cut him or stick him or poke him or do whatever, and they'd walk out the door. And if he wasn't in his coma and he was aware, he’d say, ‘Thank you.’ That was Randy Travis," she said. "And they'd turn around and look like, you got to be kidding me, you know. But that was Randy Travis."
Randy Travis, Mary Travis and James Dupré visit the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, Tenn., on March 5, 2025. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
That same spirit, she said, followed him into rehabilitation and remains evident today, even as aphasia continues to affect his ability to communicate.

"I have pictures of him there in the rehab center and he's smiling. He's laughing. He’s giving it all he's got. Randy Travis hasn't changed. And that's still the man that I get to sit beside right now," she said. "He still has that, that love for life, the love for people."

For Mary, the release of "Same Old Way" is especially emotional because it represents an opportunity they once weren't sure would ever come again. Before his stroke, she said, they assumed there would be many more albums and years of making music ahead.
BILLY RAY CYRUS CHEATED DEATH DURING SEPSIS, VOCAL PARALYSIS BATTLE BEFORE STAGING MUSIC COMEBACK
Travis' new album, "Same Old Way," was released Nov. 13. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"It's really an emotional thing, because 18 years ago when he put out his last one, we thought that the world was an oyster and there was gonna be so many more," she said. "But the stroke happened, it was 13 years ago, and everything changed."

"Thirteen years ago, we had no idea, based on where we were then, when we were in the hospital, that we would have this opportunity. So, in a way, it’s a miracle," she added. "I get emotional when I think about it, just because I wanted to hear his voice so bad again."
Randy Travis and James Dupre perform during the Volunteer Jam: A Musical Salute to Charlie Daniels at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., on Aug. 18, 2021. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Hearing those recordings, Mary explained, offers listeners a chance to experience Travis' voice at different stages of his life — and gives the couple another reason to appreciate how far he has come.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Life is so precious and so fragile, but it’s so wonderful also. And to be able to do something like this, it’s pretty monumental," she said. "It doesn't happen often that somebody has the opportunity to do this after a life-changing moment."

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

title: Jim Caviezel says he’ll ‘always’ be disappointed he isn’t in ‘Passion’ follow-up, hasn’t talked to Mel Gibson
summary: Jim Caviezel reveals his disappointment over not returning as Jesus in Mel Gibson's "Resurrection of the Christ" and why "Ghost Soldier" won out.
story: The "Ghost Soldier" actor told Fox News Digital why he decided to play Jesus in 2004's "Passion of the Christ."
Jim Caviezel said he’ll always be disappointed that he wasn’t able to return as Jesus Christ in Mel Gibson’s upcoming "Resurrection of the Christ."
"Always will be disappointment with that one. Always will be, but I wouldn't have been able to do this film," he told Fox News Digital of his new movie "Ghost Soldier," which was released on Nov. 11.

"A friend of mine said, ‘I think you're going to do well. You have to look at each film as, can you move on? Because you have this one moment,’" he said. "My initials were JC. I was 33 years old, and I couldn't get that out of my head. And I felt like I had been prepared my life to go through this. But if I said ‘No,’ there's no going back."
'THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST' RETURNS TO THEATERS IN 4K WITH A 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' SNEAK PEEK

Caviezel said he "couldn't live with it, so I took the film knowing that it was going to do a lot of detriment. Not much has changed in 2,000 years. Jesus is as controversial now than he's ever been. Always will be this way. And so, but I like to engage in that."
The characters in "Ghost Soldier" taught him the "warrior spirit. And it was the same application when we did ‘The Passion.’"

MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION SEQUEL

He added, "What we did on that movie, they can’t touch it. Nothing. When I’m dead and gone, that’s an annuity. People are going to keep coming back and finding God, and I did my job."

In "Ghost Soldier," which was released on Veterans Day, Caviezel plays a former Green Beret, and he said he drew on his decades-long relationship with the Navy SEALs for the part.

Jim Caviezel attending a screening of "Ghost Soldier" at Naval Air Station North Island in Coronado, California. (Getty Images for Sony Pictures)

title: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor forced to retire as health battle threatens hearing

Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor announced he is "retiring from playing the drums" and stepping away from the band due to health concerns.
The band released a statement on their official Instagram, noting his retirement comes on the heels of "a worsening of his recently diagnosed tinnitus."

"This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make," Taylor said in the statement. "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors."
He went on to say that "figuring out the timing of all of this has not been easy, but I’m going out on a real high."
Roger Taylor, drummer for Duran Duran, announced he is retiring from playing drums. (Virginia Turbett/Redferns)
THE OFFSPRING GUITARIST KEVIN ‘NOODLES’ WASSERMAN STEPS AWAY FROM TOURING OVER ‘SERIOUS HEALTH ISSUE’

He noted that the band "just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour," after which they headlined a show at BST Hyde Park for the second time, returned to record in the studio with guitarist Nile Rodgers and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

"I couldn’t have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I’ll treasure forever," he added. "I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John."
Taylor said it was a difficult decision to leave the band but that it was time to listen to his body. (Chris Walter/WireImage)

The statement highlighted Taylor's contributions to the band's success, noting he "has been at the heart of Duran Duran’s sound across two remarkable chapters," first in its "era-defining early records" and then again when the original line-up reunited in 2001.
After coming back together in 2001, the group released six more chart-topping albums, with Taylor "performing with them to millions of fans around the world."
Taylor made the decision to leave the band "after careful consideration" and by listening to medical advice. (Dave Benett/Getty Images for Xerjoff and Duran Duran)
"After careful consideration and medical advice, he has decided that protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first," the statement read.

Fellow band members Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and John Taylor also shared their thoughts, calling Taylor "our brother," and crediting his drumming for helping "define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning."

Taylor returned to perform with the band in 2001 following a breakup in the 1980s. (TV Times via Getty Images)

Duran Duran formed in the late 1970s, releasing their self-titled debut album in 1981 and quickly making a name for themselves as a group ready to push the boundaries. Duran Duran released their debut album in 1981. (Michael Putland/Getty Images)

Despite their success, the band split in the mid-1980s, with two members, including Taylor, pursuing solo projects. However, they came back together in 2001 and released an album with all five original members from the '80s in 2004.
