Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats seize on midterm wins to push massive minimum wage hikes, but economists see trouble ahead
summary: Josh Shapiro says he wants to more than double Pennsylvania's minimum wage and codify abortion rights with the new Democratic trifecta.
story: Research Director at the Employment Policies Institute, Rebekah Paxton, warns local officials about raising the minimum wage as Alameda County advances the highest mandate in U.S. history.

Democrats are pushing major minimum-wage increases after their midterm victories, but economists warn the proposals could come with unintended consequences for small businesses and inexperienced workers.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is pledging to more than double his state's $7.25 minimum wage, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is calling for a federal increase as Democrats make affordability a central part of their governing agenda.

The renewed push comes as Seattle, which has one of the nation's highest minimum wages, faces concerns about rising business costs and employment opportunities, raising questions about the tradeoffs of higher wage mandates.

"We’re going to more than double Pennsylvania‘s minimum wage," Shapiro wrote in an X post this month. "Codify abortion rights into our state Constitution. Fund mass transit. Build more housing. These are the commonsense things that Pennsylvanians want done.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro speaks during a re-election campaign kickoff event in Philadelphia, Pa., Jan. 8, 2026. (Rachel Wisniewski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"And with a Democratic trifecta, we will deliver on all of them."

Shapiro's proposal would raise Pennsylvania's minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, an increase of roughly 107%, prompting questions about how small businesses would absorb the additional labor costs.

Tom Savidge, an economist with the American Institute for Economic Research, warned in an interview with Fox News Digital that steep wage increases could force small businesses to raise prices, reduce workers' hours or cut back on hiring.

"A federal minimum wage hike will worsen the affordability crisis," Savidge told Fox News Digital. "A one-size-fits-all mandate ignores regional differences in wages and business costs. It risks higher prices, fewer hours and fewer jobs, especially for inexperienced workers. Politicians can mandate higher wages, but they cannot mandate that businesses can afford to pay them.

"Small businesses employing minimum-wage workers cannot absorb such a sharp increase without adjusting elsewhere," he added. "Some may raise prices, cut hours or stop hiring. A higher minimum wage means little to workers who cannot find a job."
The debate comes as Democrats seek to deliver on campaign promises to make life more affordable, even as businesses in cities with higher minimum wages report growing financial pressures.

Seattle, where the minimum wage is $21.30 an hour and will rise to $22.14 in January, offers one example of the economic questions surrounding such policies. While proponents have asserted that minimum wage increases will be a boon to employees, some Seattle business owners have previously raised concerns about facing additional cost burdens, KOMO News reported in December 2025.

Rising labor costs have been among the financial pressures cited by Seattle restaurant owners who have closed locations, along with higher food prices, declining customer demand and other operating expenses, Fox News Digital previously reported.

A January survey by The Intentionalist found that 67% of 136 independent small businesses surveyed in Seattle and surrounding Washington communities reported greater financial strain than during the pandemic, with respondents pointing to rising labor costs, rent, insurance and weaker customer demand.

A 2022 study published in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that Seattle's 2015 and 2016 minimum-wage increases boosted pay for longer-tenured workers but reduced hours worked, particularly among less experienced employees, and limited opportunities for people entering low-wage jobs.

However, in a separate 2017 study by University of California, Berkeley, researchers found that Seattle's earlier minimum-wage increases raised wages in the food service industry without a statistically significant decline in restaurant employment.
Savidge went on to say that steep minimum wage increases often benefit major corporations over Main Street businesses.

"Higher minimum wages can favor big corporations over small businesses," he explained. "Large corporations can spread higher labor costs across more sales, invest in automation or relocate operations. Small businesses have fewer options."
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE
Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, at the Democratic National Convention, speaks with activists from New Hampshire at a delegation breakfast Aug. 21, 2024 in Chicago. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Despite concerns about the potential economic consequences, Shapiro has made raising Pennsylvania's minimum wage one of his first priorities after Democrats won control of both chambers of the state legislature.

"Half a million workers in Pennsylvania still make less than $15 an hour. You can’t live off of that in 2026," Shapiro said. "Now, we’re finally able to change that. The very first bill that I will sign into law with our new Democratic majority this January will be to raise our minimum wage and make sure every Pennsylvania worker has a livable wage. It’s long overdue."
He made the comments after Democrats secured a trifecta in Harrisburg in the 2026 midterms after flipping the Pennsylvania state Senate.
$25 AN HOUR? MAJOR CITIES EYE MASSIVE WAGE HIKES AS LABOR ACTIVISTS SEEK FEDERAL MANDATE
When reached for comment, Shapiro's office referred Fox News Digital to the governor’s comments on raising the minimum wage during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon released on Sunday.

"Some of your viewers and listeners are going to think it's crazy, but job No. 1 is going to be raise the minimum wage to 15 bucks an hour, and now your listeners are like, 'What do you mean 15 bucks an hour?'" Shapiro said during the interview.

"Everybody's at 15 bucks an hour. Well, we're not in Pennsylvania. We've been stuck at $7.25 an hour for decades, right? Because the Republicans in the state senate, every time we've sent a bill over there, have blocked it."
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker speaks during a news conference at the UI Health Mile Square Health Center Feb. 28, 2025. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
The minimum wage push is also gaining traction beyond Pennsylvania.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who signed legislation in 2019 gradually raising his state's minimum wage to $15 an hour, is now calling on Congress to increase the federal minimum wage as part of his post-election economic agenda.

"Americans made their voices heard, and this is an opportunity for Congress to immediately address the challenges of working people – higher wages, lower costs, rooting out corruption," Pritzker said in a statement. "The people of Illinois cannot afford to wait."
AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?
Savidge told Fox News Digital that Pritzker and Shapiro's minimum wage proposals "risk giving large corporations a competitive advantage while squeezing out smaller competitors."
Critics question whether higher wage mandates translate into better overall economic outcomes, particularly for workers with little job experience.
Adam Gorcyca, a policy researcher at the Illinois Policy Institute, warned that employers may respond to higher labor costs by reducing hours, limiting hiring or raising prices.

"Mandating higher wages doesn't immediately guarantee workers will take home more money," Gorcyca added. "Employers often respond to these policies by cutting back hours, slowing hiring or raising prices. It can help select workers, while also making it harder for entry-level or younger workers."
Gorcyca also questioned whether Illinois' minimum wage increases had delivered broader employment gains, pointing to the state's slow pandemic recovery as evidence of its economic struggles.

"In Illinois, Gov. JB Pritzker passed a minimum wage hike in 2019, slowly increasing the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025," he said. "While he has campaigned that it was the ‘right thing to do,’ the state doesn’t have a stronger labor market for workers. In fact, Illinois was one of the slowest to recover from the pandemic."
Pritzker's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Tuesday.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The push is also emerging as a priority for congressional Democrats.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Monday that the federal minimum wage needs to be raised and that he plans to discuss the issue with members of both chambers of Congress.
"It's a conversation that I look forward to having with not simply the members of the House Democratic caucus, but with the Senate as well, to see what is possible," Jeffries said.
"It certainly needs to be increased. It's a disgrace that the minimum wage hasn't been raised in 20 years and is currently $7.25 per hour."

title: Massie's push to impeach Hegseth splits constituents in his own backyard: 'Pure spite'
summary: Northern Kentucky residents offer sharply divided takes on Thomas Massie's push to impeach Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and his true motives.
story: Northern Kentucky voters talked to Fox News Digital and gave differing opinions of their firebrand libertarian representative, who was defeated in the Republican primary and will leave office.

KENTON COUNTY, Ky. — Rep. Thomas Massie's push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war drew sharply different reactions from northern Kentucky residents interviewed by Fox News Digital.
The residents offered competing assessments of the outgoing Republican congressman and whether his latest confrontation with the Trump administration reflects principle or political payback.

Fox News Digital visited Covington, the population center of Massie’s district, along with Newport, Erlanger and other communities across the river from Cincinnati, to ask residents about their outgoing congressman and his efforts to impeach the Pentagon chief.
TRUMP DEFENDS PENTAGON CHIEF AS MASSIE TARGETS HIM: 'HEGSETH SHOULD BE PRAISED, NOT IMPEACHED'
Richard Hassebrock, a Covington resident who said he has not always agreed with Massie, welcomed the impeachment effort.
"I'm not always a huge fan of Thomas Massie, but on this point I am," Hassebrock told Fox News Digital.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon Nov. 10 in Arlington, Va. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging he violated the Constitution by waging war in Iran without congressional authorization, among other charges. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Craig Cuskey, who works in the Covington area but lives just outside the bounds of Massie’s district in Louisville, described the impeachment push as "pure spite" and "petty," saying his opinion of the congressman had deteriorated.

The contrasting reactions came after House Republicans voted to refer Massie's impeachment effort against Hegseth to committee, adding another confrontation to the Kentucky Republican's long-running disagreements with President Donald Trump and his party's leadership.
Democrats poised to take the gavel in January, however, signaled they will likely take up Massie’s mantle and seek the Pentagon chief’s impeachment.
Hassebrock said he was disappointed by Massie's electoral defeat and praised the congressman's independence.
"He stands up for himself. He stands up to what he believes in. He's got principles unlike 99% of the other congresspeople out there," he said.
Rilla, a Fort Wright resident who provided only her first name, offered a more complicated assessment.
"I think he's just trying to get back at Trump," she said, adding she had been proud of Massie for standing up to the president and was disappointed by his defeat.
7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS
Rilla said she opposed the Iran war, particularly the prospect of military action without congressional involvement.
"I don't think anyone should just go in and declare war without Congress being a part of it," she said.
Phil Wiseman, an Independence resident, said he doubted the impeachment effort would accomplish much, even as he questioned the administration's military strategy.
"I don't see a definable outcome," Wiseman said. "And if you're going to fight a war, there needs to be a definable outcome."

Wiseman said he identifies as a "RINO," a term often used derisively by conservatives for "Republican in name only," and voted for an independent instead of supporting Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, the Trump-endorsed Republican who defeated Massie in Kentucky's primary earlier this year.
He said his family has discussed Hegseth, noting that his father was a 27-year military veteran and his son served in the Marine Corps.
"We all had the same discussion," he said. "Who is advising him? Because this [war] is very ill-thought-out and not well-planned."
Wiseman compared that aspect of the Iran conflict to how the U.S. previously became mired in Afghanistan.
"So, I seriously question the military advisors that are giving them this advice, or maybe they gave them contrary advice, and it was ignored," he said.
Anthony Tuemler of Covington supported impeachment and accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution through his conduct of the war.
Tuemler's assessment of Massie was similarly mixed. Although he said he was glad the congressman was leaving office, he credited Massie with speaking up when he believed it was necessary.
"I'm glad he's gone," Tuemler said of Massie. "But the only thing I'm distressed about or sorry about is, like, when it came time to say the right things, Massie was the one who did it."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Randall Thompson of Newport, dressed in a military uniform for Veterans Day as he walked with his children near Covington's Mainstrasse Village corridor, said he supports the defense secretary and pointed to their shared military experience in the Middle East.
"I support the troops and Pete Hegseth," Thompson said, adding off-camera that he was in the same area of Iraq as the former Fox News host when they were both deployed.
Cuskey also defended Hegseth, saying he had initially been skeptical of his nomination but had grown more impressed with his performance.
"I think, for his background, he's done a remarkable job," Cuskey said, arguing that Hegseth was carrying out directives from the commander in chief.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has voiced support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, while other Democrats have signaled plans to revisit his conduct when they take control of Congress in January.

Some lawmakers are also eyeing investigations and potential impeachment proceedings involving other senior Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan, setting the stage for a broader confrontation between congressional Democrats and the White House.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Blue wave meets ballot box surprises as voters split on abortion, voter ID and billionaire taxes
summary: Voters in three states approved voter ID measures, while California rejected a billionaire wealth tax and Idaho turned down a proposal to expand abortion rights.
story: Americans from across the country shared their midterm voting decisions with Fox News Digital, driven by everything from President Donald Trump to abortion, immigration enforcement and gun rights. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

While Democrats’ midterm sweep dominated election night, voters in several states delivered consequential — and sometimes crosscutting — verdicts on voter ID, abortion access, taxes and English-language laws.
But the down-ballot decisions largely unfolded beneath the shadow of the GOP’s crushing losses, offering a separate look at the policy priorities voters chose to elevate in their states.
Read on to learn more about some of the most significant ballot measure results that will be shaping the lives of thousands of Americans.
New voter ID voting requirements
More than a dozen states held ballot measures on Election Day that were related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
DEMOCRATS ‘DIVORCED FROM VOTERS’ AS 5 STATES BACK CITIZEN-ONLY VOTING, BOLSTERING GOP PUSH

Voters in Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio all voted to pass voter ID requirements, even as talks among federal lawmakers have stalled on the issue, showcasing that the issue remains a point of public interest.

In North Carolina, the state has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018. But with the adoption of a constitutional amendment in a 59.6% to 40.3% vote, the Tar Heel State expanded the requirement to all forms of voting.

Similarly, in Ohio, voters passed Issue 3 by a 65.3% to 34.6% vote. Although Ohio already had preexisting in-person voter ID laws, Issue 3 codified the requirement in the state’s constitution, making it harder to overturn later.

Finally, in Nevada, Question 7 passed by a 62.1% to 37.8% vote, establishing a constitutional amendment to enact the state’s first voter ID requirement. It compels voters to show ID when voting in person and, for mail and absentee ballots, asks voters to provide the last four digits of their driver's license or Social Security number.
English is the official language of Idaho
The Idaho Capitol building in Boise, Idaho. (Getty Images)
EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In Idaho, voters approved HJR6 in a 63.1% to 36.8% outcome, a measure that makes English the official language of the state, codifying it for use in public proceedings with a constitutional amendment.
English had already been made Idaho’s official language through statute since 2007.

State Rep. Dale Hawkins, one of the champions behind HJR6, called it reflective of efforts by the Trump administration to make English the official language of the United States through executive order.
"Our current administration signed an executive order doing this for the entire United States, so we are just in line with what’s going on," Hawkins said in public remarks.
In an interview with local media, Hawkins also cited a concern that many newcomers to the U.S. had, in his view, overlooked the country’s linguistic identity.

"One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive," Hawkins told the Idaho Capital Sun.
Voters reject a ‘viability’ right to abortion

Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of the Susan B. Anthony List, speaks as she introduces former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence at the National Press Club Nov. 30, 2021, in Washington, D.C. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)
DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

Alongside their English language constitutional amendment, voters in Idaho rejected Proposition 1, which would have created a right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability, except in cases of medical emergency.

In the words of the proposition, it "would support creating a right to abortion before fetal viability — defined as a fetus’ ability to survive without extraordinary medical measures — and after fetal viability in cases of medical emergency; providing protections against professional discipline and civil and criminal liability for healthcare providers; and codifying a statutory reproductive right to freedom and privacy."
Proposition 1 failed with a 55.9% to 44.0% outcome.
Had it been successful, the measure would have greatly reduced the state’s current limits on abortion except to save the life of a pregnant woman or in cases of rape or incest.

To onlookers like Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, the outcome demonstrates that protecting life in the womb remains a priority and an ongoing contest at the state level.

"We are incredibly grateful for Stop Prop 1 and all who stood up to defend the unborn. This is a hard-fought win and an example to pro-life voters, candidates and elected officials across the country. … Voters were not fooled because pro-life leaders spoke up boldly to expose this initiative," Dannenfelser said in a statement.
Socialist-backed 5% tax for billionaires goes up in smoke
California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a group of DSA supporters. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images; Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

In California, voters rejected the implementation of a 5% billionaire tax that carried the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The measure, Proposition 40, failed by a vote of 52.4% to 47.5%.
The proposition would have applied a 5% tax on assets like businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property while excluding select pensions, real estate and retirement accounts.
To prevent billionaires from simply leaving the state, Proposition 40 was designed to retroactively apply to billionaires who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026.
The DSA framed the measure as a way to distribute wealth and as a kind of scaled-up version of a progressive tax, a tax that scales relative to income.

"We have the money in California to pay for the quality schools and healthcare that we need. It just needs to be transferred from the wrong pockets to the right ones. We can do that by taxing the rich," according to a slide presentation.
Notably, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40, arguing it would lessen California’s competitiveness relative to other states.
California rejects voter ID
California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks while campaigning for Senate candidate Chris Pappas at Exeter Town Hall on Oct. 17, 2026, in Exeter, N.H. (John Tully/Getty Images)
Voters in California also rejected Proposition 39, a proposed constitutional amendment that would have required ID for in-person voting and checks for the state’s voter registration lists.
Like Nevada's Question 7, it also would have asked absentee voters to provide the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number before securing a mail-in ballot.
The measure failed in a 60.5% to 39.4% vote.
Ahead of Election Day, Gov. Newsom characterized Proposition 39 as an extension of efforts to restrict access to voting rights.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Trump and his MAGA allies tried to rig our elections once, and California voters shut them down with Prop 50. Prop 39 is just their latest attempt to silence us, because they know they can’t win in California in a fair fight. It’s voter suppression, full stop, and Californians will vote it down in November," Newsom said in a statement.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Democrat flips Alaska governor's mansion after Trump-backed GOP infighting
summary: President Trump endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson for Alaska governor, but bitter GOP infighting and ranked-choice voting complicated the race to succeed Mike Dunleavy.
story: After a midterm rally in Alaska, President Donald Trump told Fox News' Matt Finn, 'We are looking into" Dan Sullivan, an independent challenger who goes by the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won Alaska's gubernatorial election, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson and flipping the governor's mansion.
The Associated Press called the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, Friday evening. He is the first Democratic governor in Alaska since 1998.
Alaska's gubernatorial election became an unusual contest as Republicans battled among themselves over who should succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred from seeking a third consecutive term.
A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS
Former State Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat from Alaska, during the What's Next conference in Denver, Colo., Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Wilson, a conservative activist and former political operative, received President Donald Trump's endorsement during a campaign in which multiple Republicans competed for the governor's office.
Trump publicly criticized fellow Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, accusing them of dividing conservative voters and potentially jeopardizing the party's hold on the governorship.
Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor, and Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, remained part of the Republican field, creating a complicated general election contest.
ALASKAN POLITICAL SCION HOPES TO HOLD ONTO STATE'S SINGLE HOUSE SEAT
Alaska gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson was the only Trump-endorsed candidate in the race despite being one of three Republican options. (Courtesy: Bernadette Wilson for Governor)
Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, emerged as the Democratic contender, seeking to return his party to the governor's mansion after Dunleavy's two terms.
The election unfolded under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and those ballots are redistributed according to voters' next preferences. The process continues until a candidate secures a majority among continuing ballots.
The system has added an unusual dynamic to Alaska politics, allowing multiple candidates from the same party to compete in the general election without a traditional partisan runoff.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy speaks at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, in October 2026. President Trump endorsed GOP gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson at this rally, but Dunleavy did not offer an endorsement for any candidate. (Nathaniel Wilder/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The contest also came as Alaska remained a reliably Republican state in presidential elections despite occasionally electing Democrats and independents to statewide office.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Rep Lauren Boebert projected to lose House seat in another Democratic flip
summary: Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., lost her congressional seat to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher. Boebert, an ally of President Trump, was seeking a fourth term.
story: Incoming House Minority Leader Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, discusses the GOP’s agenda during the post-midterm election lame-duck session, Democrats’ lawfare threats and his priorities as House GOP leader on ‘Hannity.’
GOP firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., is projected to lose her seat in the House to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.
The Associated Press made the call in the razor-thin race Friday afternoon in favor of Laubacher, who maintained her slim 48.7% lead over Boebert’s 47.9% once 99% of the ballots had been counted.
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., arrives to a Republican caucus meeting at the U.S. Capitol September 13, 2023, in Washington, DC.  (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
GOP SENATOR SAYS REPUBLICANS CAN 'FORGET 2028' AS PARTY LOOKS TO RECLAIM UPPER CHAMBER
Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris came in third with a little more than 3% of the vote.
Laubacher is projected to win Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, according to the AP.
Boebert was running for her fourth term in the state. She served her first two terms in Colorado’s third district and was running for her second term in the state’s fourth district.
2026 MIDTERMS: PRIMARIES, KEY RACES AND ELECTION RESULTS
The 39-year-old congresswoman’s loss comes amid a blue wave that saw Democrats flip seats in Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Democrats now have 256 seats in the House of Representatives to Republicans’ 169. A party needs 218 for a majority.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Several races nationwide remain uncalled nearly two weeks after Election Day.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Former CIA Director John Brennan's son arrested after FBI uncovers dozens of alleged child porn images
summary: Kyle Brennan, 40, son of former CIA Director John Brennan, was arrested on a federal child pornography charge after an FBI investigation, prosecutors say.
story: An image shows former CIA Director John Brennan in front of a Central Intelligence Agency crest. (William B. Plowman/NBC/NBC Newswire/NBCUniversal via Getty Images; Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was arrested for allegedly possessing child pornography, Fox News has learned.
Kyle Brennan, 40, was charged with transportation of child pornography, according to a federal complaint.
The case originated when Adobe CyberTipline reports flagged accounts linked to Brennan for uploading illicit files involving minors.

In April and June 2024, Adobe submitted two reports to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) regarding an account allegedly used to upload suspected child sexual abuse material.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS BLUE STATE'S LAW PROHIBITING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS ON THE JOB

Former CIA Director John Brennan speaks during a forum on election security, "2020 Vision: Intelligence and the U.S. Presidential Election" at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., Oct. 30, 2019. (Joshua Roberts/Reuters)
The FBI's Washington field office is involved in the investigation.

Around April 7, 2024, three files were uploaded to the Adobe account. A review of the files indicated a file that appeared to be a morphed image combining the face of a minor girl, later identified as a 12-year-old, with the naked body of another minor, federal prosecutors said.
Comcast records showed that the IP address used to upload the files was registered to Kyle Brennan at an address in Warrenton, Virginia, where he lives.
Records from Apple later confirmed that the private relay account was registered to Brennan, authorities said.
DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS
President Barack Obama in the East Room of the White House in Washington, announcing he was nominating John Brennan, right, as CIA director. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis via Getty Images)
In July 2024, authorities searched Brennan's home and seized his iPhone.
The case was referred to the FBI in October, and a judge signed off on a warrant so investigators could examine the records and seize Brennan's phone.

On Friday, an FBI analysis of the iPhone, which was named "Kyle’s iphone (2)" contained a photograph of Brennan’s Virginia driver’s license and revealed approximately 88 images depicting girls under the age of 18 engaged in sexually explicit conduct, prosecutors said.
One image appeared to be a "fully nude, pubescent minor girl on a locker bench," the complaint states.

"The girl’s wrists and ankles were bound and her mouth was gagged," it said.

The Justice Department is investigating John Brennan, who served under former President Barack Obama, regarding his role in the 2017 Intelligence Community Assessment (ICA) on Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election.
Fox News Digital has reached out to a representative for John Brennan and the Justice Department for comment.

title: Schumer's leadership rival reveals major Senate rule change he'd pursue if elected
summary: Chuck Schumer faces a rare contested Senate leadership race as Chris Van Hollen pushes to abolish the filibuster and shake up Democratic strategy.
story: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., tells Fox News Digital at What's Next conference that he’s running to lead Senate Democrats because voters called for change.
DENVER — A mile above much of the country, and leagues away from Washington, D.C., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is facing a progressive rebellion that threatens his grip on power.
The challenge is being led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has served under Schumer since 2017. And he is willing to go further than Schumer ever has on one issue: terminating the filibuster.

Years ago, Schumer tried and failed to narrowly change the Senate’s rule to pass a sweeping voting rights package. Republicans have toyed with it over the last two years, but never pulled the trigger.
SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE
Van Hollen said, "We need democracy in the United States Senate, and that means allowing, ultimately, a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people.
"So, that means 51 votes. So, my personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic … provision. It's not in our Constitution," Van Hollen added.
"It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people."

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, says he has the votes to remain leader and guide the party’s incoming majority. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Van Hollen announced his challenge against Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, Thursday night after a listening campaign with Senate Democrats. It presents a rare opportunity for Senate Democrats since there hasn’t been a contested Democratic leadership election since 1994.
Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump.

"I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, where Democratic leaders, strategists and activists gathered to debate the party’s direction after its midterm wins.
Van Hollen framed his challenge to Schumer as a response to voters’ calls for change after Democrats’ sweeping wins and President Donald Trump’s policies.
"I did discuss this with Senator Schumer," Van Hollen told Fox News Digital. "We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice."
DEMS ADMIT UNCOMFORTABLE ELECTION SWEEP TRUTH AS PARTY DESCEND ON DENVER TO SHAPE 2028 WITHOUT A FRONTRUNNER
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver Nov. 13, 2026, as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)
Voters "chose change," he said, adding that the Democratic caucus needs "new ideas" and "a different way of governing."

Van Hollen has also criticized Schumer for limiting votes on legislation popular with Democrats, including a bill to boost unions. He said the incoming majority should pass the bills candidates campaigned on and challenge Trump to respond.
"We shouldn’t wait to hear what President Trump may or may not do," Van Hollen said. "We should answer the call of the American people."
Toppling Schumer will be an uphill climb. As the incumbent leader, he has an established network of support and can offer colleagues leadership posts.

Either candidate will need 28 votes in the secret ballot contest expected in early December or 29 if Democrats win Alaska, where ballots are still being counted in the Senate race between Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
THE MISTAKE NEWLY ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS
A protest sign calling for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. to step aside as Democrats debate who should lead the party. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Some What’s Next attendees said Van Hollen could deliver the Senate leadership shake-up they want.
"We definitely want change. We don’t want to go back to the way things have been. This is a turning point for our country," Jenny, a Denver resident, said, adding it was time for Schumer to go.
"This is the time for us to really, really go after what is right for everyone, not the status quo."
Ara, also of Denver, was optimistic about Van Hollen’s chances, saying she believes he already has significant support.
"I think there’s a really good chance," Ara told Fox News Digital. "I think there were a lot of people that were already willing to support him. So I feel very good about this," she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Zoe said Van Hollen’s willingness to stand up for his constituents is the kind of fight young people want from their representatives.

"He goes out there, and he puts his body on the line for his constituents. And I think that’s what we’re looking for, the kind of fight we’re looking for from our representatives as young people," Zoe told Fox News Digital.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Pete Hegseth impeachment effort dies in the House as absent Democrats couldn't beat the traffic
summary: Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided becoming only the third cabinet secretary ever impeached after 11 absent Democrats failed to reach the House floor.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports the latest on Democratic Party divisions over leadership post-midterms.
Most of America bemoans political gridlock in the nation’s capital. DC area commuters deplore the city’s transit gridlock.

But Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth may now be a fan of DC’s legendary traffic snarls. It appears that crosstown traffic may have prevented him from becoming only the third Cabinet secretary ever impeached by the House of Representatives.
The House voted 211-204 this week to divert an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Hegseth.
House Republicans moved to block a straight, up-or-down vote on impeachment.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., speaks on impeaching U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Instead, Republicans forced a vote on sending the articles to the Judiciary Committee.
That’s where they’d go to die. If the House failed to sidetrack the articles, Members would have then voted on actual impeachment.

If a simple majority voted to impeach, Hegseth would join 19th century Secretary of War William Belknap and former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas as the only Cabinet Members impeached by the House.
But DC’s streetside congestion altered the parliamentary traffic on the House floor.
All Democrats said they were intent on impeaching Hegseth.
But Republicans faced an attendance problem.
Seven of their Members were missing. The vote on sending the impeachment articles to committee was tight. The tally read 204-204 at one point.

By rule, tie votes fail. That would have compelled a vote on actual impeachment. But a few more Republicans trickled in. The absent Democrats never did. Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) presided over the vote.
He gaveled it closed at 211 yeas to send the articles to the committee and 204 votes against.
That was it. The Hegseth impeachment quest was dead. Eleven Democrats missed the roll call.
It’s about the math.
Flip four votes and Hegseth would have been impeached, 208-207.
HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS
And, had all 11 truant Democrats made it to the U.S. Capitol and voted, it’s likely the House would have impeached Hegseth 215-211. Even eight Democrats would have made it 212-211.
However, thanks to the Democrats’ attendance issue, Republicans were able to tap the brakes on the impeachment interstate.
The failure to impeach Hegseth is now fueling road rage in the Democratic Party.
"Shame on them for not showing up," said Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.).
"I don't make excuses for colleagues who don't show up on such an important vote," said Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.).
Democrats can’t beat Republicans if they can’t beat the traffic.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., arrives for the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee deposition of former Attorney General Pam Bondi about the Jeffrey Epstein files, in Rayburn building on Friday, May 29, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) is one of the most outspoken Democrats when it comes to her disdain for Hegseth.
But Stansbury grew defensive when questioned by colleague Bill Melugin about missing the vote.

"I was trapped right there at that street corner because there was a police motorcade moving busses off of the campus. And I physically was trapped right at that corner in my vehicle, in traffic because the police had shut down traffic," said Stansbury.
"Why not come here sooner, though?" followed up Melugin.
HEGSETH COULD FACE NEW IMPEACHMENT PUSH OVER UKRAINE AID, LAWMAKERS WARN
"I did and I was trapped in my vehicle because of a police motorcade," said Stansbury.
Maybe. Maybe not.

The Constitution’s "Speech or Debate" clause exempts lawmakers from police interference when "going to and from" the Capitol for "their attendance at the Session of their Respective Houses." It’s kind of like diplomatic immunity.

A few years ago, Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) was supposed to preside over a brief House session in the middle of a recess. Traffic heading into DC from Northern Virginia was stopped because of an incident. Beyer was the only Member scheduled to be present in the House chamber that day. So Beyer identified himself to a police officer who proceeded to let him through.
Over the years, other lawmakers have asserted the Speech or Debate clause as a reason to bypass unrelated police activity and get to Capitol Hill.

Reps. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) and Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.) also said they were stuck in traffic. However, Rep. Lou Correa (D-Calif.) was out for a medical procedure. Rep. Steve Horsford (D-Nev.) missed the vote because of a personal emergency. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) was in the Golden State.
DC’s traffic interfered with parliamentary traffic again on Thursday morning.
The House took an early Thursday morning vote related to a veterans bill.
The House adopted the motion, 271-135. But the House gaveled down the vote with 26 Members absent. The reason? Some Members were again stymied from making it to the Capitol.

Emergency room physician Matt Lambert killed one person at a gym, shot six people and engaged in a standoff with cops before turning the gun on himself. Initially reported as an "active shooter" incident, District of Columbia police locked down major parts of the city, stalling traffic.
A member of the National Guard stands in Washington, D.C., where a gunman opened fire in a gym on Thursday, November 12. (Brooke Curto for Fox News Digital)
And that’s why some lawmakers missed Thursday’s roll call. They were marooned in traffic.
Shifting gears, Rep. Eric Sorensen (D-Ill.) in fact made that procedural vote on the floor. When the vote began, a gentle breeze blew across the Capitol plaza. Then a mist enveloped the Capitol.
Later, a few heavier drops. Then the sun broke through the clouds. But reverted to overcast. It was a dank morning in Washington.
"I want to know what the weather is," yours truly shouted at Sorensen as he skipped down the House steps toward a group of reporters waiting below.
Sorensen is a meteorologist who worked for decades at TV stations in Texas and Illinois before coming to Washington in 2023.
Sorensen pivoted immediately into weatherman mode.
"We've got increasing showers guys. Much cooler temperatures for the weekend," said Sorensen, replicating the precise forecast for Washington, DC over the next few days.
The meteorologist-turned-lawmaker gestured to his right as though looking at a phantom map of the Midwest, projected against a green screen in a TV studio.

"As God is my witness, I cannot talk about the weather without moving my hands," said Sorensen. "I talk about high pressure. It's high pressure right here in the midsection of the country. And it's moving in our direction for the next week."
After the election, the political weather forecast would seem good for Democrats right now. Supposedly balmy days and comfortable nights. A political "high", if you will.
"So is there a high-pressure system moving here for the Democratic Caucus?" yours truly asked.
"No. It's low pressure, man. It's low pressure going into the next Congress. We’ve just got to keep everybody together," he replied.

But is a high-pressure system really in the long-range forecast for Democrats? Or will a political "low" bring storms and atmospheric volatility — especially if progressive and centrist Democrats tangle with one another?
"I thought high pressure was a good thing," said your trusty reporter. "No subtropical systems coming in. No clipper system."

"As a meteorologist, I'm not in production. I'm in promotion," said Sorensen of potential Democratic storm systems which might emerge on the horizon. "With a complicated issue like the weather, I was able to help connect with people every day for 22 years. But here, this is the most complicated mechanism in the United States. We’ve got to get better at communicating what we do for the people."

DC traffic has already stymied Democrats over the past few days. Tornadic political storm systems may brew inside the Democratic Caucus. And that’s to say nothing about transportation and just getting people to the Hill.

Traffic and weather. And if the internal Democratic fisticuffs turn ugly, well, may show that on sports. Right along with the hockey fights.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Two top Trump Cabinet officials go to war over China spy scandal amid explosive accusations: report
summary: A White House Situation Room meeting erupted after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy tied to chip diversions was revealed.
story: Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo outlines the national security concerns rising from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy on ‘The Story.’

A White House Situation Room meeting reportedly turned into a blowout between two of President Donald Trump's Cabinet secretaries after news broke that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspect Chinese spy.

Tempers apparently boiled over regarding claims Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick dragged his feet on placing restrictions on a company run by a suspected Chinese spy with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, even after the Cabinet official received an intel memo informing him of the potential threat.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly confronted Lutnick about that in the meeting, and other Cabinet officials took Bessent's side, according to Axios.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick before an event with President Donald Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook in the Oval Office of the White House on Aug. 6, 2025, in Washington, D.C.  (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Trump has for months called to place companies suspected of supplying China with Nvidia's complex AI chips on what is called the Entity List, a Department of Commerce export control list that identifies companies the U.S. government believes pose a serious risk to national security.
A SPY TOOK OUT NVIDIA’S CEO; HERE’S HOW AMERICA STILL WINS THE AI RACE
Three times — in May, August and last Thursday — Trump approved taking action against companies believed to be diverting Nvidia chips to China, according to Axios.

One of those companies is Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is reportedly one of Nvidia's largest customers. Suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, with whom the former Nvidia CEO admitted to having an affair, is an executive at Megaspeed.
Lutnick was accused of slow-rolling in putting Megaspeed on the Entity List, which prompted Bessent to lose his patience.

When the news of Jensen Huang's affair broke, Lutnick, Bessent, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reportedly convened in the Situation Room.
Bessent confronted Lutnick about why the export controls had not already been put into place, and others in the room took Bessent's side, according to the Axios report.
REBECCA GRANT: JENSEN HUANG OWES AMERICA AN APOLOGY, AND NVIDIA OWES INVESTORS ANSWERS
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the Nvidia GTC global AI conference in San Jose, Calif., March 17, 2026. (Reuters/File)
Lutnick said he would have to discuss it with the president despite Trump's May and August orders to proceed.
The group then met with Trump later in the day at the Oval Office. The president reportedly gave the order again, saying, "Let's get it done."
Still, Lutnick wouldn't proceed.
"I'll develop some options and come back," he said. The group replied that Trump's decision was final and that Lutnick must "go f---ing execute."

Lutnick is at the center of the scandal, especially after it was revealed he received a memo informing him about U.S. intelligence that Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and still did nothing to put the company she ran on the Entity List.
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
Commerce Secretary Lutnick, President Donald Trump and Secretary of the Treasury Bessent, (Getty Images)
CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS
A spokesperson for the Commerce Department didn't directly address the report of Lutnick's confrontation with Bessent.
"The Department of Commerce and the Department of the Treasury have a great working relationship and are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda," Kristen Eichamer told Fox News.
She also said Lutnick has proactively decided to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions on the matter. A hearing is scheduled for Dec. 10.
Bessent appeared on CNBC's "Sqwuak Box" Thursday morning, where he was asked about the reported blowout.

He said there was coordination between the various agencies about putting Megaspeed on the Entity List but then referred further questions to the Commerce Department and Bureau of Industry and Security.
"You will have to ask them about their internal proceedings," Bessent said.
US ATTORNEY WARNS CHINESE ESPIONAGE IS 'EXTREMELY PERVASIVE,' SAYS BEIJING 'PLAYING THE LONG GAME'
Jensen Huang resigned from his post as Nvidia CEO Thursday morning, and the company has reportedly opened an investigation into the affair.
The Treasury Department and White House did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Schumer's former ally mounts leadership challenge as Democrats face rare internal power struggle
summary: Senate Democrats face their first contested leadership race since 1994 as Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer with Bernie Sanders' backing.
story: Fox News senior congressional correspondent Chad Pergram joins 'Fox & Friends' as Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen mounts a challenge against New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leadership.
Senate Democrats are getting an opportunity they haven’t had in decades: a different option for who their leader could be.

Even before the blue wave crashed over Republicans and Democrats emerged with a commanding majority in the Senate, the rumblings for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to step aside were there.

Now, he’s got a challenger in Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., a familiar face in Washington, D.C., who framed his bid against Schumer as one answering the call for change voters demanded. It’ll be the first time that a Senate Democratic leadership race will be contested since 1994.
DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer arrives at the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 2026. Newly elected members of the 120th Congress arrive for the first day of new member orientation after Democrats flipped both chambers in the midterm elections. (Getty Images)

Van Hollen’s emergence, at 67, as the lone challenger to Schumer, 75, comes after lawmakers and candidates demanded a change in Democratic leadership before the election. That call has only intensified in the week after Democrats won the midterms, with Van Hollen interpreting the seismic political shift as an indictment of President Donald Trump that can only be acted on if Senate Democrats go in a new direction.
The challenge is already dividing Senate Democrats.
In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen didn’t offer a sharp policy contrast to Schumer, and cast doubt on Democrats’ ability to pass key progressive desires, like Medicare for All.

"But it should be very clear: While, you know, voters have rejected the Trump policies, they’ve not yet hired Democrats — they’ve given us a chance, we have to earn their trust," Van Hollen said. "My view is that you can’t earn that trust with old leadership. You need to move on to new leadership."

Van Hollen acknowledged that he was an "underdog," but revealed during the interview that he had over 10 Senate Democrats in his corner and believed more were to come. Right now, either lawmaker will need 28 secret ballot votes to win the job — that could bump up to 29 if Democrats flip Alaska, where ballots are still being counted in the Senate race between Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. And it could get messy over the next few weeks before the early December, closed-door election.

And he’s got the backing of the progressive standard-bearer in the Senate: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and new faces of the progressive movement, like Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who Van Hollen endorsed early on in his campaign, and Peggy Flanagan, who said on X that Van Hollen was the "leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind."
VAN HOLLEN CHALLENGES SCHUMER FOR SENATE LEADERSHIP AFTER DEMOCRATIC ELECTION SWEEP
Ultimately, either candidate's success will likely break down on how well they both work with and push back against President Donald Trump.

Early in Trump’s second term, Van Hollen won praise from progressives when he traveled to El Salvador for a welfare check on Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident who was mistakenly deported by the administration.

But Schumer has dealt with Trump for years, and told the Washington Sun that his strategy heading into the new Congress will be to put bill after bill on the floor, like restoring Obamacare subsidies or banning insider trading, and dare Republicans to vote them down — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., used a similar strategy over the last two years.
"In a certain sense, it’s a win-win. I’d rather get things done, but it’s not going to stop us," Schumer said. "We are going to move forward with or without Trump, with or without the Republicans."
Despite the demands for change, Van Hollen is very much a creature of Washington, having served in Congress since 2003.

He’s the son of diplomats, and served in House Democratic leadership under former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. He was chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the House Democrats’ campaign arm, for two cycles, and was quickly tapped by Schumer to lead the Senate’s campaign operation when he ascended to the upper chamber in 2017.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., and Rep. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speak to the media during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Feb. 11, 2010, in Washington, D.C. The lawmakers were set to introduce a bill aimed at offsetting a recent Supreme Court ruling that allowed unlimited spending by corporations and unions during elections. (Getty Images)

And he spent his entire career in the Senate behind Schumer, who first became leader in 2017, and he has rarely broken with him on key votes. He has, however, emerged as a staunch critic of Israel and criticized Schumer’s ties to the crypto industry and meddling in Democratic primaries.

He currently serves on four committees in the Senate: Appropriations, Foreign Relations, Budget and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs, and throughout his career in Congress has focused on budget issues and foreign affairs.
Still, outside progressive groups are beginning to back him.
The progressive Sunrise Movement is all in on Van Hollen. The organization announced its support for the lawmaker on Bluesky, and wrote, "Young people voted for change on election night."

"Chuck Schumer can’t give us that, but Chris Van Hollen might," they said. "The truth is, the ‘blue tsunami’ could easily become the blue mirage in the wrong hands. And Schumer’s hands are too full of billionaires’ money to hold young people’s future."

Another progressive group, the 50501 protest movement, also declared its support for Van Hollen Thursday night in a post on Bluesky, urging voters to pressure their senators to "vote Chris, NOT CHUCK."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There are a bevy of other outside groups that have opposed Schumer, including Indivisible, MoveOn and the Working Families Party, and the 600,000-member International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers sent the top Democrat a letter demanding he step aside.
But Schumer has remained confident about retaining his position.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," Schumer said on X. "I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."
His allies have leaned into sports metaphors to describe why he should keep the job, with both Sens. Angus King, I-Maine, and Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., comparing it to a successful manager in baseball.
"When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract," Gallego said.Fox News Digital reached out for comment from both Schumer and Van Hollen.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Ford privacy promise raises questions about your car data
summary: Ford's new privacy promise pledges not to sell driving data to insurers or brokers, but disabling connected car data sharing could cost you key features.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Norway's confirmation that Chinese-owned rental cars recorded military data on 'Fox Report.'

Your car probably knows more about you than you realize. It can track where you drive, how fast you go and whether something under the hood needs attention. Depending on the vehicle, that information may also travel back to the manufacturer. And, chances are, you haven't spent much time thinking about who gets to see it.

Now, Ford wants to put those privacy concerns in the spotlight. On Nov. 2, the automaker announced a new Ford privacy promise designed to give drivers more transparency and control over their personal information. The company also says it won't sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

That sounds encouraging. But there's a catch worth understanding. Turning off certain data-sharing settings could also mean losing some of the connected features you've come to rely on. So, how much privacy can you get without giving up the technology you paid for?
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Ford's new privacy promise gives drivers more information about how their vehicles collect and share personal data, but disabling certain settings could limit connected features. (Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What is Ford's new privacy promise?

Ford says its new privacy initiative will make it easier for drivers to understand what information their vehicles collect and how the company uses it. The automaker has also launched a dedicated data and privacy website where owners can learn about their options. The announcement centers on several commitments.

Ford says it designs its products with privacy in mind and wants customers to have clearer information about their choices. It also promises to respect the privacy settings drivers select. Perhaps the biggest commitment involves what happens to driving information. Ford specifically says it does not sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

However, that promise does not mean Ford stops collecting connected vehicle data altogether. The company still uses information from equipped vehicles to operate services and improve its technology. Ford's chief privacy officer, Kristin Jones, explained to TechCrunch that the company wants to build greater trust by helping customers understand its data practices.

The effort comes as Ford prepares to introduce more connected vehicles, including models built on its upcoming universal electric vehicle platform. Importantly, many of Ford's privacy controls already existed. The new initiative focuses on making those controls easier to understand and find.
What information can your Ford collect?
Modern Ford vehicles can generate a surprising amount of information. Exactly what gets collected depends on your model, its connected features and the privacy settings you select.
For example, Ford says equipped connected vehicles may share information about:

Vehicle location: Precise location information that can support navigation and roadside assistance.Driving behavior: Information about speed, braking and how the vehicle is operated.Vehicle health: Diagnostic information, including tire pressure, fuel levels and possible mechanical problems.Vehicle identification: Details such as your vehicle identification number (VIN) and software information.
Vehicle location: Precise location information that can support navigation and roadside assistance.
Driving behavior: Information about speed, braking and how the vehicle is operated.
Vehicle health: Diagnostic information, including tire pressure, fuel levels and possible mechanical problems.
Vehicle identification: Details such as your vehicle identification number (VIN) and software information.

There are practical benefits to some of this sharing. Vehicle diagnostics can help identify maintenance problems earlier. Location information can support roadside assistance or help you find your parked car. Ford also says it may use connected vehicle data to improve future technologies.

With your consent, certain information can support personalization and relevant offers. Still, your driving habits can reveal personal details about your daily routine. That's why understanding which settings are enabled deserves your attention.
Why Ford's privacy promise comes at a critical time

Ford's announcement follows increased scrutiny of how automakers handle customer information. On Oct. 29, a coalition of 36 attorneys general announced a $220 million settlement with General Motors over allegations involving drivers' personal information. The states alleged that GM collected and sold driving behavior and location data to third parties, including data brokers that supplied information to insurance companies.

According to the state attorneys general, some insurers used that information when calculating insurance rates. The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative, express consent before collecting or disclosing covered driving and location data.

GM previously discontinued its Smart Driver program. The case shows why vehicle privacy has become such a sensitive issue. Drivers may agree to connected features without fully understanding how much information those systems collect.

We've explored similar concerns in our CyberGuy article, "Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move?" Insurance monitoring programs can offer savings, but drivers should understand what information they are agreeing to share. Against that backdrop, Ford's public commitment could help set expectations for how automakers handle sensitive driving information.
The privacy tradeoff that could affect your Ford's features

Ford says customers can turn off connected vehicle data sharing. However, doing so may affect some of the features that make newer vehicles convenient. Depending on your Ford model, equipment and which settings you disable, you could lose access to:

Remote start: Starting your vehicle through the Ford app.Connected navigation: Receiving real-time traffic information and other online navigation services.Vehicle location: Checking where your car is parked through the app.BlueCruise: Using Ford's available hands-free highway driving assistance system.Software updates: Receiving certain vehicle updates over the air.Connected roadside assistance: Accessing services that depend on a vehicle data connection or location sharing.
Remote start: Starting your vehicle through the Ford app.
Connected navigation: Receiving real-time traffic information and other online navigation services.
Vehicle location: Checking where your car is parked through the app.
BlueCruise: Using Ford's available hands-free highway driving assistance system.
Software updates: Receiving certain vehicle updates over the air.
Connected roadside assistance: Accessing services that depend on a vehicle data connection or location sharing.

The exact impact depends on which settings you disable and the technology installed in your vehicle. Turning off all vehicle connectivity can affect more features than changing individual data-sharing preferences. Some features can continue working even when connected vehicle data sharing is disabled. Ford says features such as Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility can continue working without sharing connected vehicle data with Ford. Local Bluetooth connections and regular radio playback can also remain available.

Of course, availability depends on your vehicle's equipment and software. Before turning anything off, check which services your particular Ford needs. Disabling one optional sharing preference does not automatically disable every connected feature. And remember, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto use smartphone technology. Your phone and its apps may have their own data collection settings that you'll want to review separately.
How to change your Ford's privacy settings

Ford gives owners several ways to review their data-sharing preferences. You can manage vehicle connectivity through the car's touchscreen. The Ford app and your online Ford account provide additional controls for certain uses of your information.
Start with the vehicle parked safely. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built in 2018 or later review their connected vehicle settings.

On your vehicle's center touchscreen, open Settings.Look for Vehicle Connectivity or the available Privacy and Data Sharing settings.Review the available options for Vehicle Data, Driving Data and Vehicle Location.Turn off any optional sharing you do not want enabled.Read any warning that appears before confirming a change.
On your vehicle's center touchscreen, open Settings.
Look for Vehicle Connectivity or the available Privacy and Data Sharing settings.
Review the available options for Vehicle Data, Driving Data and Vehicle Location.
Turn off any optional sharing you do not want enabled.
Read any warning that appears before confirming a change.

Menu names and available controls vary by Ford model and infotainment system. If you want to stop sharing connected vehicle data with Ford, the company says to find Vehicle Connectivity in your vehicle's settings and turn it off. However, this broader change can limit connected services and other features. Ford provides additional guidance through its official privacy settings page.
GM WANTS DRIVERS TO TAKE THEIR EYES OFF THE ROAD BY 2028
Ford says it does not sell customers' driving behavior data to insurance companies or data brokers as it introduces a new vehicle privacy initiative. (John Keeble/Getty Images)
You can also adjust certain information-sharing preferences through the Ford app on your smartphone.

Open the Ford app.Tap the account icon on the home screen.Scroll to Settings and select Legal and privacy.Tap Privacy and data sharing.Select Set Preferences under Manage Data with Ford or Manage Data with Third Parties.Under Manage Data with Ford, review the available Personalization and Marketing settings for vehicle and driving data.Adjust the preferences you want to change.
Open the Ford app.
Tap the account icon on the home screen.
Scroll to Settings and select Legal and privacy.
Tap Privacy and data sharing.
Select Set Preferences under Manage Data with Ford or Manage Data with Third Parties.
Under Manage Data with Ford, review the available Personalization and Marketing settings for vehicle and driving data.
Adjust the preferences you want to change.

Ford also provides controls related to Google Maps in the app and certain preferred dealer notifications. Keep in mind that the app's personalization and marketing controls are separate from the vehicle's main connectivity controls. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. If you own more than one Ford, review each vehicle's settings separately.

You may also want to find out what personal information Ford already holds. The company provides options to request access to personal data and seek corrections or deletion, subject to applicable privacy laws and exceptions. You can find those options through Ford's privacy notice.

If you're selling or trading in your Ford, perform a factory reset to remove stored personal information from the vehicle. Ford says this can erase saved addresses, connected accounts and programmed garage door opener codes. You should also make sure the vehicle is disconnected from your Ford account. Depending on its connectivity equipment, you may need to remove the vehicle's VIN from your account as well. Simply deleting the Ford app will not stop vehicle data sharing. However, that reset will not erase data the company already received. Any request to delete that information must be handled separately.
Does Ford's promise mean your data stays completely private?

There's an important point worth keeping in mind. Ford's commitment about selling driving behavior data to brokers and insurers is specific. It does not prohibit every form of data collection or disclosure. Ford's privacy notice describes circumstances in which information may be shared with service providers or other parties. It also addresses disclosures made in response to valid legal requests.

Meanwhile, Ford offers personalization and marketing settings that deserve a separate review. And even though Ford says it doesn't sell driving behavior data to insurance companies, that doesn't mean an insurer can't collect information about how you drive through a separate smartphone app or a voluntary insurance monitoring program.

There are also exceptions to Ford's privacy controls. The company says it may collect vehicle location data in certain circumstances even when location sharing is turned off. These can include legal requirements, emergencies and protection of property. Vehicles equipped with the Ford Security Package may also share location information when a Theft Alert is triggered.

So even with Ford's new promise, I would still encourage drivers to examine their individual settings. A company can make a meaningful privacy commitment while continuing to collect information needed for its services. And if you're shopping for a new vehicle, consider privacy before making the purchase.
What this means to you

If you own a newer Ford, this announcement gives you a good reason to check your privacy settings. You may discover that your vehicle shares more information than you expected. You might also find settings you can disable without affecting the features you enjoy. However, you should understand the tradeoff before switching off all connectivity. Losing remote access or other useful services could be inconvenient, especially if you rely on them regularly.

The same advice applies if you drive another brand. Take a few minutes to find your manufacturer's privacy settings and learn what information your vehicle shares. You can explore the broader privacy concerns in our article, What your car knows about you and could be telling the world. Ultimately, knowing what your car collects gives you a better chance of controlling your personal information.
DATA BROKERS DON'T JUST COLLECT FACTS. THEY GUESS ABOUT YOU

Ford owners can adjust vehicle data-sharing settings to protect their privacy, though turning off connectivity may affect remote start, navigation and other features. (Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I like seeing Ford make a public commitment about protecting driving data. Especially after what we've learned about how vehicle information can end up in the hands of insurance companies. But here's what I keep coming back to. When you spend tens of thousands of dollars on a vehicle, how much of your personal information should you have to share to enjoy the features you already paid for? I understand why Ford needs certain data to make connected technology work. Real-time traffic updates can be useful.

So can getting an alert before a mechanical problem leaves you stranded. But I also think automakers need to make privacy choices much easier to understand. Drivers shouldn't have to dig through complicated menus to figure out what's happening with their information. Ford's promise is encouraging, and I hope other manufacturers pay attention. The real test will be how well these commitments hold up as vehicles become even more connected.

Would you sacrifice features like remote start or live navigation to keep your driving data private, or should automakers be required to offer those conveniences without collecting so much personal information? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
