"This matter shows that partnerships are essential to protect our countries and I want to express my thanks to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command for their outstanding work," Patel said.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Mojtaba Khamenei aide's chilling '40 years' warning surfaces amid US push for Iran deal
summary: Mohsen Rezaei once warned that ceasefire talks could last decades, as JD Vance reportedly reached out to him about resuming U.S.-Iran peace talks.
story: Fox News senior strategic analyst Ret. Gen. Jack Keane discusses reports that Vice President JD Vance contacted an Iranian hard-liner at President Donald Trump’s direction. Keane argues that Iran is not serious about reaching a deal and would not comply with one.

Iran's top security official, who reportedly received a letter from Vice President JD Vance about resuming peace talks, warned in a resurfaced interview that wartime negotiations with Tehran could drag on for decades, and during which both sides should "be prepared to fight."

Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), now serves as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and acts as a key aide to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He also helped shape Tehran's military strategy during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq War.
That eight-year conflict ended after Iran's then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, accepted a U.N.-brokered cease-fire that he famously likened to drinking from a "poisoned chalice."
JD VANCE RETURNS TO WASHINGTON AFTER 16 HOURS OF IRAN PEACE TALKS COLLAPSE IN PAKISTAN

Senior Iranian general Mohsen Rezaei issues a direct threat against President Donald Trump as the U.S. repositions aircraft carrier amid rising tensions with Tehran, according to reports. (Ayoub Ghaderi/YJC/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS)

"Ceasefire means an unfinished war," Rezaei had said of the war in a 2006 interview with the Iranian publication Baztab. An English translation of the interview is preserved by George Washington University's National Security Archive.
Asked whether both sides would remain in their positions and begin talks, Rezaei replied: "Yes. Negotiations can take 30 to 40 years and during that time Iran and Iraq should be prepared to fight."
Two decades after suggesting negotiations could drag on for years, Washington has reportedly been seeking talks with Rezaei, a key power player in Iran’s current military leadership.
Vance sent him a letter proposing renewed peace talks between the United States and Iran in October, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Iran said it had received a letter from Vance but had not responded, according to Iranian state media. The semi-official Tasnim News Agency said Iran was awaiting U.S. compliance with its conditions, warning that "any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable."
TRUMP SAYS IRAN DEAL ‘LARGELY NEGOTIATED’ AS 84-DAY WAR NEARS POSSIBLE END
President Donald Trump

In June, President Donald Trump had posted a warning on Truth Social that Iran had taken too long to come to terms and would "pay the price," while on Monday, he also said that Iran wanted a deal but warned that another U.S. strike could be about five times as large as the previous.
"We could knock it out fast, or we could knock it out over a short, not a long period of time," Trump said during a C-SPAN interview on "Washington Journal Primetime."
"I can tell you that Iran would like to make a deal, and we'll find out whether that'll happen," Trump said of the current timeframe.

Rezaei however, has continued to maintain a defiant stance toward Washington, writing on X on Nov. 9: "The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government," he wrote before adding that "Washington flails like a desperate gambler."
"FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.
"Stop denying the West Asian NEW ORDER. Time to SURRENDER to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out," he said.
Following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, Rezaei also claimed Iran had defeated Washington militarily and politically.
He warned of a "devastating response" to another attack and declared it was time for Washington to "SURRENDER."
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY'

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) generals and commanders, Mohsen Rezaei (2nd L), Ali Fadavi (3rd L), Ahmad Vahidi (2nd R), and Hassan Hassanzadeh (R) attend a memorial ceremony for IRGC commanders, nuclear scientists, and civilians killed in the Iran-Israel war at the Imam Khomeini Grand Mosque in downtown Tehran, Iran, on July 2, 2025. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Rezaei also rejected reports of ongoing U.S.-Iran negotiations or any planned meeting in Qatar, accusing Washington of spreading false claims to ease economic pressure and lower oil prices. He reiterated that Tehran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its seven conditions were met.
Rezaei has spent more than four decades in Iran's defense establishment. He commanded the IRGC from 1981 to 1997, overseeing operations during the Iran-Iraq War.
In the 2006 Baztab interview, Rezaei also detailed how Iranian leaders distinguished their public rhetoric from military strategy.
Although Khomeini and other Iranian officials called for "fighting till Saddam is toppled" and "until the nuisance is eradicated," Rezaei said Tehran's actual strategy was "fighting up to a victory."
At the time, Iran's battlefield gains, he suggested, were meant to strengthen Tehran's negotiating position rather than achieve total conquest.
IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES

Commanders and members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps meet with Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran, Iran, on Aug. 17, 2023. (Office of the Iranian Supreme Leader/WANA (West Asia News Agency)/Reuters)
"The world did not pay attention to the slogans," Rezaei said in the interview, adding that foreign governments and intelligence agencies focused on Iranian leaders' actions and diplomatic positions.
Rezaei also said Iran had struggled to turn battlefield gains into diplomatic victories because it lacked international alliances and influence at the United Nations.

Rezaei has since faced U.S. sanctions and international scrutiny. The Trump administration first sanctioned him Jan. 10, 2020, under an executive order targeting senior Iranian officials appointed by the supreme leader.
Rezaei had also been accused of involvement in the July 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Interpol approved an Argentine request for a Red Notice against Rezaei in 2007 in connection with the bombing.

title: TV anchor found dead with gunshot wound to head, officials arrest husband
summary: The broadcaster’s husband claimed he was playing with a firearm when it discharged inside their home, according to a provincial official
story: Rabiya Ahsan, 41, was found dead inside her Pakistan home. Her husband claimed a gun accidentally discharged while he was playing with it, according to officials.
The husband of a TV anchor was arrested in Pakistan Sunday after his wife was found dead with a gunshot wound to the head, according to officials.
Rabiya Ahsan, 41, was allegedly killed inside her home in Rawalpindi, according to Punjab Information Minister Azma Zahid Bokhari.

Ahsan worked as a program host for 92 News, where she established herself as a dedicated journalist alongside senior colleagues. She also frequently posted videos about national affairs on social media.
Officials identified her husband as Ahsan Tahir Khan, who claimed he was playing with a firearm in the home when it accidentally discharged, Bokhari said.
POPULAR TV HOST, MEDIA STAR FACES HANGING AFTER CONVICTION IN MAJOR SYNTHETIC DRUG TRAFFICKING CASE
News anchor Rabiya Ahsan speaks in a video recorded before she was found fatally shot Sunday. (@rabiyaahsanofficial/Instagram)

Khan reportedly works as a civil service officer at the Overseas Pakistanis Foundation, a government agency that supports citizens living abroad, according to local outlet The Express Tribune, citing police sources.
Police are preparing to pursue a murder case against the suspect, according to the report.
Rawalpindi police also confirmed in a post on X that a woman was killed in a Sunday shooting but did not immediately identify her.
Authorities said officers seized the suspected weapon in connection with the husband's arrest.
Ahsan's body was also transferred to a hospital for a postmortem examination.
HUSBAND CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER REALTOR WIFE FOUND SHOT DEAD INSIDE HOME IN WEALTHY VIRGINIA COUNTY
Ahsan was found dead in her home in Pakistan over the weekend.  (@Rabiya_Ahsan/X)
The news of her death sparked an outpouring of grief across Pakistan's journalism community.
"I am deeply saddened to learn that our ex-colleague anchorperson Rabiya Ahsan is no longer with us," one former colleague said on X.
The Pakistani presidency also expressed sadness over the killing and called for a transparent investigation to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
"The First Lady has expressed deep sadness over the killing of journalist Rabia Ahsan and strongly condemned the violence," the statement read, referring to First Lady Aseefa Bhutto-Zardari.
DALLAS PUBLIC DEFENDER’S CHIEF INVESTIGATOR CHARGED WITH WIFE’S MURDER AFTER BLOODY APARTMENT DISCOVERY
Rabiya Ahsan, 41, addresses viewers in a social media video recorded before her death. (@Rabiya_Ahsan/X)
She also voiced concern over what she described as a "disturbing pattern" of professional women being targeted and allegedly killed by their husbands in the same metropolitan area.

"Such incidents demand serious attention and accountability. Women must be able to live and work without fear for their lives," the Pakistani presidency said.

title: Riot-torn France struggles with chaos at home as Macron eyes military mission thousands of miles away
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron's Lebanon military force plan hits resistance from Italy as Marco Rubio floats a civilian alternative to UNIFIL.
story: As Israeli and Lebanese military officials meet in Washington for rare Pentagon-mediated talks, Ahmed Sharawi of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies warns Hezbollah’s grip on Lebanon continues to undermine hopes for a broader agreement.

French President Emmanuel Macron is pushing ahead with plans for a new European military presence in Lebanon while struggling with mounting political and economic turmoil at home, even as the initiative encounters resistance from a key European partner and Washington considers an alternative that may not require troops.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that he had discussed the future of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) with Macron, suggesting that a replacement monitoring mechanism could be civilian rather than military.
"It doesn't have to be a military mission. It could be a civilian mission," Rubio said in remarks published Tuesday.

Rubio explained that the administration is seeking a credible mechanism to verify arrangements under which Israeli forces withdraw from designated areas, the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) assume control and the Iran-backed terrorist group Hezbollah is prevented from returning.
RUBIO ANNOUNCES FRAMEWORK DEAL BETWEEN ISRAEL AND LEBANON AS EXPERTS WARN IRAN WILL FIGHT TO SABOTAGE IT

Soldiers from the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon UNIFIL attend a ceremony marking the International Day of UN Peacekeepers in Naqoura, Lebanon, May 29, 2025. (Ali Hashisho/Xinhua via Getty Images)
He suggested France could play a constructive role but emphasized that any arrangement would require agreement from both Lebanon and Israel.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz also made clear that Washington has no intention of preserving the existing peacekeeping mission.

"UNIFIL in its current form will not continue, and it must not continue — we are working with our international partners to draw down the mission and ensure that the Lebanese people can choose their own future and to ensure that the Lebanese Armed Forces can secure the nation’s future," Waltz told Fox News Digital.
MACRON UNDER FIRE OVER IRAN, HEZBOLLAH POLICY AS TRUMP ADMIN HOSTS ISRAEL-LEBANON TALKS
French President Emmanuel Macron reviews the troops during his visit to the nuclear submarine navy base of Ile Longue in Crozon, France, March 2, 2026 (Yoan Valat /Pool via Reuters)

The French initiative, meanwhile, envisions a multinational force potentially involving thousands of European troops to support the Lebanese army as UNIFIL prepares to end its nearly five-decade mission. The proposed force's final size, mandate and participating countries remain unconfirmed.

However, Italy, which previously joined France in calling for an international coalition following UNIFIL's withdrawal, does not support deploying its troops under the proposal currently advanced by Paris, three sources with knowledge of the discussions told Fox News Digital.
The initiative comes as Macron faces growing domestic pressure, with France experiencing widespread demonstrations over rising living costs, wages and deteriorating public services.
The unrest has further complicated the government's efforts to pass its 2027 budget, as mounting debt and political divisions limit its room to maneuver, Reuters reported Nov. 5.

Against that backdrop, France's proposed deployment raises questions about the financial and military resources Paris could commit to another overseas mission, particularly without firm support from its European partners.

Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy for Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, argued that replacing UNIFIL with another international military force risks repeating the shortcomings of the existing mission.

"UNIFIL’s mandate should end as scheduled. Hezbollah built up its military presence in southern Lebanon with international peacekeepers already on the ground. Keeping troops there under a new mandate would repeat an approach that failed to prevent that buildup. The basis for what comes next should be the U.S.-brokered agreement Israel and Lebanon reached in June. France can help both sides put it into practice and move further," Rodan-Benzaquen told Fox News Digital.
FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio sits with France's Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot during the G7 foreign ministers summit at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris to discuss support for Ukraine and stabilization efforts in the Middle East. Nov. 9, 2026. (Christophe Petit Tesson / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
The question of who would conduct such inspections has already proved contentious.

The United States and Israel had previously opposed France serving as a third-party verifier of Hezbollah's disarmament, according to an Aug. 7 Reuters report citing Lebanese officials and foreign diplomats. A Lebanese official also told Reuters that Beirut had rejected an earlier proposal involving private security companies.
The challenges extend beyond diplomatic disagreements.
According to a Congressional Research Service assessment updated November 9, Hezbollah continues to refuse disarmament while Israeli forces maintain positions in southern Lebanon.
IS THE IRAN-BACKED TERRORIST MOVEMENT HEZBOLLAH ON THE ROPES IN LEBANON?

A protester holds a rock to throw at police as a kiosk burns during a demonstration near Place de la République, as the Gilets Jaunes join students for a weekend of action on October 17, 2026, in Paris, France. (Carl Court/Getty Images)

A U.S.-brokered framework agreement reached in June linked a phased Israeli withdrawal to the verified disarmament of armed groups and the deployment of Lebanese forces. But implementation has stalled beyond the initial pilot areas, and negotiations in October ended without agreement.
Rather than committing additional troops, Rodan-Benzaquen argued that Paris should focus on using its diplomatic influence to strengthen the Lebanese government's efforts to disarm Hezbollah.

"France’s greatest leverage is notably in Beirut. The Lebanese cabinet has already outlawed Hezbollah’s military activity. Paris should work with the Lebanese government to press disarming Hezbollah. Israel needs credible evidence that Hezbollah cannot return to an area its troops are eventually leaving. Beirut needs confidence that once its army secures that area, the agreed Israeli withdrawal will eventually follow. That is where French diplomacy can make a difference."
The debate follows the August 2025 Security Council resolution extending UNIFIL's mandate for a final time, until December 31, 2026, with an orderly withdrawal authorized over the following year.

Washington backed terminating the mission amid longstanding concerns about its inability to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining a military presence in southern Lebanon. France, by contrast, has warned against leaving a security vacuum.
PENTAGON HOSTS FIRST-EVER ISRAELI–LEBANESE MILITARY TALKS AIMED AT CURBING HEZBOLLAH

United Nations peacekeeping force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) vehicles drive along the main road leading to Lebanon's southern town of Naqura close to the border with Israel on October 27, 2022.  (Photo by Mahmoud Zayyat/ AFP/Getty Images)

In a previous Security Council statement, the French Mission to the U.N. said: "France will support UNIFIL until the expiration of its mandate. It will contribute to defining the future international engagement in Lebanon, in support of its sovereignty and the implementation of resolution 1701."

U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told Fox News Digital that Secretary-General António Guterres presented three options for a future U.N. presence in June, but the Security Council has not formally selected one.
He added that the U.N. is aware of discussions about a possible non-U.N. military presence in southern Lebanon but is not directly involved in those negotiations.

With UNIFIL's mandate approaching expiration, France faces the challenge of securing agreement not only on which countries would contribute personnel, but also on what those forces would be authorized to do in a country where Hezbollah remains armed and Israeli troops have yet to fully withdraw.

A member of the Spanish UNIFIL peacekeeper forces stands in front of the rubble of destroyed buildings during a patrol in the southern Lebanese village of Borj El Mlouk, near the border with Israel, on January 7, 2025. (ANWAR AMRO/AFP via Getty Images)

The Italian government has not responded to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Requests for comment were also sent to the State Department, Spanish and Lebanese authorities.

title: Trump meets key Iran war mediator as UAE reveals major oil export surge despite conflict
summary: Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House as Marco Rubio warns Iran negotiations are far from a breakthrough amid Strait of Hormuz chaos.
story: Reporting from Abu Dhabi, Fox News Digital examines how the UAE is navigating disruptions to global energy supplies.

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — President Donald Trump met Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, on Monday at the White House as diplomatic efforts to end the war with Iran continue, even as Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns that negotiations remain far from a breakthrough and Tehran signals a willingness to negotiate without yielding to pressure.

The competing messages come as the Strait of Hormuz remains a major source of global economic disruption and regional governments push for a diplomatic solution to a conflict that has subjected Gulf countries to thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks.
Speaking to reporters Sunday before departing for a G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris, Rubio said there had been little progress in negotiations and rejected the terms put forward by Tehran.
"I wouldn't say we're on the verge of a breakthrough," Rubio said.
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY'
Cargo is loaded at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. (Amr Alfiky/Reuters)
He emphasized that Trump prefers a diplomatic settlement but described Iran's demands as unrealistic.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that Tehran was prepared to negotiate an end to what he described as a prolonged state of neither war nor peace.

"We can negotiate with dignity and resolve the issue with dignity. We favor dialogue and negotiations," Pezeshkian said, according to Anadolu Agency on November 9, citing an Iranian presidential statement.
He said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed officials to end the uncertainty but insisted that Iran would not surrender to coercion.

Trump, meanwhile, signaled Sunday that he was not seeking another escalation. In an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes," the president said he saw no reason to intensify the war with Iran while maintaining that the Strait of Hormuz was open.

Mediators have been discussing a two-day proposal under which the United States would lift its naval blockade and release some frozen Iranian funds. Tehran would then take steps toward renewed nuclear inspections and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before broader negotiations resumed, according to Axios on November 9.
The proposal has not been accepted by Washington, and significant differences remain over the terms of any agreement.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
A satellite image shows the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, vital for global energy supply. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Nowhere are the consequences of the diplomatic stalemate clearer than in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow shipping corridor connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.

Before the war, the equivalent of roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption and more than one-fifth of global liquefied natural gas trade passed through the waterway, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, making it one of the world's most strategically important maritime routes.
Since the conflict began, Iranian attacks, shipping restrictions and U.S. military operations have severely disrupted commercial traffic.
Despite the American naval presence, attacks on commercial vessels have continued.

Reuters reported Monday that tanker attacks in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz had accelerated sharply in October and continued into November. Iranian authorities also claimed that a tanker had struck a mine east of the strait on Sunday.

In an interview with Fox News Digital at the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi, Amos Hochstein, a former senior adviser to President Joe Biden and now managing partner at TWG Global, challenged claims that the strait had effectively reopened.
HORMUZ CRISIS HIDES A DEEPER OIL THREAT THAT COULD OUTLAST THE WAR
A view of the Port of Fujairah as U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, on May 6, 2026. (REUTERS)
"There has been a hot conflict in the Strait of Hormuz on almost a nightly basis. Tankers are getting fired on, tankers are getting hit," Hochstein said.
"If you need a heavy U.S. military presence just to let an oil tanker go through, to me that's the definition of not open," he told Fox News Digital.
Hochstein argued that the extraordinary security measures required to protect commercial vessels demonstrate that normal navigation has not been restored.
Higher insurance premiums, the danger of additional attacks and restrictions on maritime traffic have continued to burden the global economy.

His assessment contrasts with the more optimistic picture offered by U.S. Central Command. In late October, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of CENTCOM, said American forces had cleared primary shipping routes of Iranian mines and assisted thousands of commercial vessels transiting the waterway.
According to a CENTCOM statement reported October 25, more than 3,000 commercial vessels had successfully transited Hormuz with American military support over the preceding six months.
But for Hochstein, the ability of military forces to escort ships does not mean the commercial risks have disappeared.

He suggested that negotiations could proceed on separate tracks, with Washington concentrating on Iran's nuclear program while Gulf governments take a greater role in discussions over freedom of navigation and maritime security.

"Maybe the Gulf allies themselves should be the ones that are managing that part of the negotiation on the [strait] while the United States would manage the negotiations ... on the nuclear front," Hochstein told Fox News Digital.

Dr. Angela Wilkinson, CEO of the World Energy Council, said the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the need to rethink global energy markets, which have traditionally prioritized efficiency over resilience.
"Efficiency is not enough. We have to have resilience," Wilkinson told Fox News Digital at ADIPEC.
"What we at the World Energy Council recommend is that we rebalance energy," she said, advocating solutions that address energy security, affordability and sustainability simultaneously.
"We have escalating logistics costs, but we've got new vulnerabilities of interdependency. And that's what we're navigating our way through."
TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION

Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the UAE Federal National Council's Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks to Fox News Digital in Abu Dhabi about the Iranian threat, regional security and prospects for diplomacy. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
For the UAE, the disruption has accelerated efforts to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
The Emirates has invested in alternative routes, particularly its pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait, allowing some oil exports to bypass the contested shipping corridor.
Al Nuaimi said the country had substantially increased its oil exports since the war began.

"We want the Strait of Hormuz to be open, to be respected according to international law, but we don't wait and make our country and our people hostages to others. … Before the war started on February 28th, we used to export 3.1, 3.2 million barrels a day. Now we are exporting almost 4.4."
UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei also said at ADIPEC on November 2 that the country's exports had, at times, exceeded prewar levels.
The country is also investing in new export routes, overseas storage capacity and shipping infrastructure to strengthen its ability to withstand future disruptions.
Hochstein praised the UAE and Saudi Arabia for anticipating the risks associated with dependence on a single maritime route.
"You can create alternative pathways and infrastructure, but those are redundancies," he said.
IS THIS TRUMP’S LAST ‘LAST CHANCE?' CEASELESS STRING OF BROKEN CEASEFIRES FUELS DOUBT OVER IRAN DEAL

Attendees gather at ADIPEC 2026, one of the world's largest energy conferences, held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Nov. 2–5, 2026, as industry leaders discuss global energy security, technological innovation and the growing role of artificial intelligence. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
His point was that alternative infrastructure can reduce the economic impact of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but cannot entirely replace the waterway.
The wider consequences have been felt across international energy markets, with increased shipping costs and supply disruptions affecting consumers far beyond the Middle East.

In a separate exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the Emirati research center B'huth, argued that the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz amounts to a separate economic war with consequences far beyond the region.

"The third war was Iran's war on global economy by blocking the Strait of Hormuz," Baharoon said. "And they've affected people in the Philippines, in India, in Brazil that has nothing to do with this conflict."

He argued that the disruption has exposed the vulnerability of countries dependent on a single shipping corridor, reinforcing the need for alternative pipelines, transportation networks and supply chains.
"And part of resilience is that you will not have only one outlet," he said.
Baharoon stressed that those investments were not simply emergency responses to the war but part of a longer-term effort to strengthen regional connectivity.
"The war might have accelerated the plans, but the plans have always been there," he said.
Even if Hormuz fully reopens, he argued, the region will still need more routes for international trade.

Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on Aug. 10, 2026. (Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images)
"We need more access, we'll need more supply chains. And we need them to be not only durable, resilient, but also redundant."
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

title: Gunman who killed 6 in Poland's Krakow square dies in hospital after police shootout
summary: The Krakow shooter, 24, died Monday after police shot him during Saturday's mass shooting that killed six and wounded 15 in the historic square.
story: The death toll rises following the mass shooting in Krakow’s Main Market Square after three people were found dead inside the gunman’s home. Polish authorities also say two police officers were injured during the shooting.
The gunman who killed six people and wounded 15 others in a shooting at a crowded square in Poland died Monday after being shot by police during the attack, authorities said.
The 24-year-old suspect had been hospitalized in critical condition since Saturday's shooting in Krakow and underwent several operations before his death.
Polish prosecutors have opened an investigation into the killings and attempted killings, including attacks on police officers, as a possible terrorist offense.

Emergency responders gather after a deadly shooting on November 7, 2026 in the Main Market Square of Krakow, Poland. At least five were killed and more were injured in the incident. (Omar Marques/Getty Images)
Authorities said the gunman held far-right views, though investigators have not publicly established a motive for the attack.
TEEN WEARING HELMET CAMERA KILLS WORKER AT POLISH SCHOOL AMID FEARS OF COPYCAT ATTACKS

Police also discovered the bodies of the suspect's mother, father and sister at the family's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, roughly 93 miles northeast of Krakow, per reporting from The Associated Press. The three are believed to have died from gunshot wounds, though authorities have not confirmed the circumstances of their deaths.

Emergency responders gather after a deadly shooting on November 7, 2026, in the Main Market Square of Krakow, Poland. At least five were killed and more were injured in the incident. (Omar Marques/Getty Images)
The suspect, who was wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into Krakow's historic Main Square on Saturday before opening fire, according to authorities.
A woman reacts at the site of a shooting near the main market square of Krakow, Poland, November 7, 2026. (REUTERS/Jakub Porzycki TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY)
Four women and two men were killed, including a British man and an Austrian woman. Five foreign nationals were among the wounded.

title: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop
summary: Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.
story: Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.

By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.

A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.
What caused the ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.
Why disruptions continued Saturday

Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.
But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.
Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”
Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.
In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.

Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the  system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.
Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.
“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.
Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”
With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.
There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare
Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.
In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

title: FAA ground stop throws college football into chaos, while the NFL is safe
summary: A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several pro and college teams across multiple sports.
story: A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several teams across multiple sports.
Follow along for live coverage.

Multiple games in college football had to be rescheduled to accommodate new travel plans, while a handful of NBA teams changed their flights as a result of the ground stop. Every NFL game, meanwhile, will be played as scheduled, as all road teams were scheduled to travel Saturday.
A few backup referees for the NFL

Every NFL game will stick to its original start time, a league spokesman confirmed to NBC News. Teams playing Sunday typically do not travel until Saturday, meaning the league was largely unaffected by the Friday ground stop.
The New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions, who are playing in Munich, Germany, both traveled overseas well ahead of the stop.
While the league’s teams and players will arrive as scheduled, the NFL did have to modify officiating crews for Sunday’s games.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” a league spokesman said.

Three backup referees — Duane Heydt, Barry Anderson and Don Willard — will be used Sunday. Heydt was assigned to a game in New Orleans and Anderson to one in Tennessee, while Willard will be the side judge for games in both Indianapolis and Cincinnati. (The kickoffs in those two games are more than seven hours apart, and the stadiums are separated by less than 120 miles.)
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise,” the league spokesman said.
Many college football games have been pushed back
Travel plans for more than a dozen teams were affected by the stoppage, according to The Athletic.
Some schools opted to fly out on Saturday morning for games scheduled the same day, while others — including the Alabama Crimson Tide playing at Vanderbilt — took a bus to their destination.
Several kickoffs were pushed back to later Saturday to accommodate new travel plans, including the games between Baylor and BYU, Arizona State and UCF, and Utah and Arizona.
The game between Oklahoma and Ole Miss, however, was pushed back to Sunday after Ole Miss couldn’t figure out its travel in time — and it drew a strong response from the Sooners.

“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution,” Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny said in a statement. “After multiple conversations with the league office, [SEC] Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”

Denny’s statement added: “Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight.”
No major issues for the NBA and NHL
A few NBA teams — such as the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Chicago Bulls — had to reschedule flights from Friday night to Saturday morning, but otherwise it’s largely business as usual for the league.
An NBA source confirmed to NBC News all games would take place as scheduled as of Saturday morning, though noted there were a lot of moving parts.

“Flights are late, get stuck on the runway, just like it does in the normal commercial world of flight, so it’s just part of it,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said before the team’s game Friday. “We’ve all been part of it. You just adapt.”

Atkinson’s star guard Donovan Mitchell was not enthused about the new plan, as Cleveland has a quick turnaround to another game Saturday.

“This is unprecedented,” Mitchell said Friday, per Cleveland.com’s Chris Fedor. “Back-to-back. Three-hour flight. It was already going to be a tough one. But if they say we have to play then we have to play.”
Mitchell added he would have liked for the game to be canceled.

The NHL, meanwhile, has not announced any changes to its schedule. The league had only two games on Friday night, allowing most teams to travel for their road games prior to the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to redevelop East Potomac golf course in D.C.
summary: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate its golf course.
story: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate its golf course.

The administration had previously announced plans to close what is effectively the entire area of East Potomac and Hains Point starting Sunday. But U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote that while litigation moves forward, the course, along with surrounding bike and walking paths, must remain open to the public “except for routine, temporary closures consistent with the Course’s historical operating practices, and except as needed to address articulated, imminent threats to public safety.”
Reyes wrote that closing the park would “irreparably harm” the plaintiffs — the Washington, D.C., Preservation League — who regularly use the park.

“It runs counter to the public interest in utilizing national parkland. And the Government has not plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings,” Reyes wrote.

Reyes’ order does not require the administration to continue operating the golf course, including features like the concession stand or pro shop, but does specify the administration “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course.”

The administration had argued the park had to close for repairs, including a seawall that needs mending that they argued is an “imminent threat to public safety.” The judge expressed skepticism at the argument, noting the National Park Service’s speed to cut down 400 trees in the area — an action Reyes at the time called “bad faith.”

“If public safety were at risk, NPS would have taken a step—any step—to address the safety issues it knew about. Recall that within just ten days, NPS was able to plan, muster the resources and staff, and execute felling over 400 healthy trees. So NPS was not without ability or resources. And presumably would not prioritize removing healthy trees over the public’s safety,” Reyes wrote.
President Donald Trump referred to the park as “trash island” just hours before the ruling, while criticizing Reyes.

“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The ruling came after a contentious day long hearing Friday where a lawyer for the government, Adam Gustafson, said the decision to close the park on Sunday was “distinct” from President Donald Trump’s declaration on social media that the East Potomac golf course would be closing for extensive renovations — on Sunday.

The president’s Oct. 18 announcement on Truth Social that the park’s three link-style golf courses would be transformed into one 18-hole championship style course is “not the same action” as the Interior Department’s decision to shut down a large part of the park that includes the golf course, Gustafson said.

The president has adopted several pet projects during his second term in office in an effort to modify Washington landmarks. He’s faced legal battles for some of them, including the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and a triumphal arch. Work on both has been blocked by judges.
The Supreme Court earlier this year allowed Trump to construct a ballroom on the White House grounds.
A Justice Department spokesperson, responding to Reyes’ ruling, said that the judge’s order would not stop development of a golf course.

“The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue. The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court,” the spokesperson said.

title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to redevelop East Potomac golf course in D.C.
summary: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate its golf course.
story: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate its golf course.

The administration had previously announced plans to close what is effectively the entire area of East Potomac and Hains Point starting Sunday. But U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote that while litigation moves forward, the course, along with surrounding bike and walking paths, must remain open to the public “except for routine, temporary closures consistent with the Course’s historical operating practices, and except as needed to address articulated, imminent threats to public safety.”
Reyes wrote that closing the park would “irreparably harm” the plaintiffs — the Washington, D.C., Preservation League — who regularly use the park.

“It runs counter to the public interest in utilizing national parkland. And the Government has not plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings,” Reyes wrote.

Reyes’ order does not require the administration to continue operating the golf course, including features like the concession stand or pro shop, but does specify the administration “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course.”

The administration had argued the park had to close for repairs, including a seawall that needs mending that they argued is an “imminent threat to public safety.” The judge expressed skepticism at the argument, noting the National Park Service’s speed to cut down 400 trees in the area — an action Reyes at the time called “bad faith.”

“If public safety were at risk, NPS would have taken a step—any step—to address the safety issues it knew about. Recall that within just ten days, NPS was able to plan, muster the resources and staff, and execute felling over 400 healthy trees. So NPS was not without ability or resources. And presumably would not prioritize removing healthy trees over the public’s safety,” Reyes wrote.
President Donald Trump referred to the park as “trash island” just hours before the ruling, while criticizing Reyes.

“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The ruling came after a contentious day long hearing Friday where a lawyer for the government, Adam Gustafson, said the decision to close the park on Sunday was “distinct” from President Donald Trump’s declaration on social media that the East Potomac golf course would be closing for extensive renovations — on Sunday.

The president’s Oct. 18 announcement on Truth Social that the park’s three link-style golf courses would be transformed into one 18-hole championship style course is “not the same action” as the Interior Department’s decision to shut down a large part of the park that includes the golf course, Gustafson said.

The president has adopted several pet projects during his second term in office in an effort to modify Washington landmarks. He’s faced legal battles for some of them, including the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and a triumphal arch. Work on both has been blocked by judges.
The Supreme Court earlier this year allowed Trump to construct a ballroom on the White House grounds.
A Justice Department spokesperson, responding to Reyes’ ruling, said that the judge’s order would not stop development of a golf course.

“The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue. The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court,” the spokesperson said.

title: Why Mary Peltola is on track to win in Alaska, even if ranked choice ballots come into play
summary: As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen.
story: As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan will hang on to his job.

His Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is on track to win the still-unresolved Senate race under either possible scenario — with an outright majority, or if the race goes to ranked choice ballots, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of outstanding and tabulated votes.

Peltola currently leads Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes. With 96% of the expected vote in, NBC News’ Decision Desk now believes Peltola is likely to win this race, though we may need to wait until Wednesday, Nov. 18, to know the final result.

If no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, Alaska determines a winner using ranked choice voting, in which the lowest-ranked candidates are eliminated one by one and their votes are redistributed according to each voter’s ranked preferences. If a voter did not rank the remaining candidates, their ballots are considered “exhausted” and are excluded from the final vote count.

Wednesday is Alaska’s deadline for final mail absentee ballots to be received by election officials, one reason why this close race has lingered for so long. Alaska reports its votes unevenly, and NBC News expects to see the remainder of these votes early next week.
Nov. 18 is also the day the state Division of Elections would run the ranked choice tabulation, if needed.

If Peltola receives over 50% of the vote, she will win the election without needing to go through the ranked choice tabulation process. She needs to win just 53.8% of the remaining ballots to clear this mark — a real possibility given her strength in recent vote reports. On Friday night, she received 58% of the newly reported votes.

Sullivan, the incumbent, has two separate paths to gain ground and win the election: making up the gap with first-choice rankings, or making up the gap via the ranked choice process. An NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the ballots already tabulated shows that the first route is highly improbable and that the second route is likely impossible.

The first route that Sullivan could use to come back would be passing Peltola in first-choice rankings. With approximately 12,000 votes outstanding, Sullivan would need to win around 92%  of those in order to tie with Peltola. That would amount to about 46 points better than he has performed in the vote counted so far, and far above the percentage either candidate has achieved in any batch of ballots received up to this point. On Friday night, he received just 38% of newly reported votes.
The second route for Sullivan to retake the lead is through the ranked choice process, but an analysis of the ballots shows why this route is effectively closed to him.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

There are currently 11,300 tallied ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan. Those ballots may be redistributed in the ranked choice process. With 4% of the total vote outstanding, the number of ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan could rise to around 12,000. For Sullivan to net 10,400 ballots out of a pool of 12,000 and close the gap with Peltola, he would need to win around 93% of redistributed votes.
However, even that steep figure is misleadingly optimistic for Sullivan because of what we already know about how people are ranking the candidates.
The Alaska Division of Elections posts a “Cast Vote Record” for the over-270,000 ballots currently tabulated. These records show exactly how each candidate is ranked on each ballot.

Our analysis of those ballots shows that Sullivan does gain some votes from the ranked choice process, receiving a large transfer of votes from voters who backed Republican Gerald Heikes, who is in third place. But the most important thing about these votes is that a large percentage of ballots from those who backed other candidates are “exhausted” in the ranked choice tabulation process.

Over 45% of voters who ranked Heikes, Dan J. Sullivan Jr. or a write-in candidate did not rank Peltola or Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a later choice, which means that these ballots will play no role in the ranked choice tabulation.
This ballot exhaustion means that there are far fewer than 12,000 ballots available for Sullivan to make up the gap of about 10,000 votes between him and Peltola in the ranked choice process.

If current rates are maintained, only about 6,600 ballots will actually be redistributed to the top two finishers in the ranked choice tabulation. If Sullivan is more than 6,600 votes behind Peltola’s first-choice margin after all ballots have been counted, it is mathematically impossible for the Republican incumbent to catch up to Peltola in the ranked choice tabulation.

The NBC News Decision Desk will need to assess the remaining ballots as they are received to determine if our standards are met to officially project the race, or whether the outcome will be determined by the ranked choice process carried out by the Alaska Division of Elections.

title: He was drafted as an NFL team’s future. It arrives now.
summary: Fernando Mendoza, the Heisman-winning quarterback selected No. 1 overall in last year’s NFL draft, takes over as starter for the Las Vegas Raiders. Will he turn around the franchise?
story: When Heisman Trophy-winning quarterback Fernando Mendoza was selected first overall by the Las Vegas Raiders in April’s NFL draft, he updated his biography on LinkedIn to say that he was “focused on preparation, growth and discipline.”
Emphasis on the first part.

It is a quirk of the NFL that teams historically race to draft a quarterback early, then play them as little as possible for much of their first season. Teams view the position as so demanding and the pro game so fast that they want their prized picks to prepare as much as possible before inheriting the pressure of an entire franchise.
Mendoza’s time to prepare ended Tuesday, nine games into his rookie season.
Now, the Raiders need him to produce.

Before Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline, Las Vegas (4-5) traded veteran starting quarterback Kirk Cousins and elevated Mendoza to starter ahead of Sunday’s Week 10 matchup against the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks (5-4). Cousins had thrown 20 touchdowns, the most by any quarterback to change teams midseason in NFL history, per NBC Sports research.

After starting 3-0, the Raiders have lost five of their last six games but still have what one playoff tracker pegged this week as a 15% chance to make what would be only the franchise’s third playoff appearance since 2003. Trading Cousins and elevating Mendoza “is no way to signify that we are punting on the season or looking forward to 2027,” Raiders general manager John Spytek said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“It’s something that [Mendoza] worked very hard for since the moment he walked into this building,” Spytek told reporters this week. “He passed every test. I want to stop short of saying he’s earned it, but he put us in a position where we had to make a really hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback.”

Mendoza is known as a quick study. While attending Cal, he spent his summers away from Berkeley interning at investment firms. In his first and only season at Indiana last fall, Mendoza picked up the Hoosiers’ offensive playbook so quickly that he led the perennial Big Ten doormat to a stunning national championship by using his arms and his feet.

Raiders coach Klint Kubiak, who as an offensive playcaller mentored Sam Darnold during last season’s Super Bowl run with the Seahawks, said that Cousins was “the right role model” for Mendoza to learn from and accelerate his acclimation to the NFL.

“It’s time to rally around Fernando,” center Tyler Linderbaum said. “Everyone has to step up and play for him. Obviously, it’s never easy being a rookie in that first game, but there’s 10 other guys on the field with him, there’s a whole defense, special teams unit, and just be there for him. Let him play with confidence. We’ve seen it every day in practice, the plays he can make.”

Mendoza’s only snaps to this point came Oct. 11 when he played late in a blowout loss to the New England Patriots and completed 6 of his 8 passes. Rookie debuts are inherently difficult; quarterbacks taken No. 1 overall are 5-23-1 in their first start since 1970, per NBC Sports research. Facing the Seahawks will make Mendoza’s big day even more challenging. Seattle leads the NFL in total defense, allowing just 244 yards per game.

Mendoza might not be under the most pressure of any Raiders player on Sunday, however. The team’s defense has allowed 30 or more points in each of its last six games, tied for the longest streak by a team in a season in NFL history.

“Fernando has done everything we’ve asked him to do in practice,” Kubiak said. “I think he’s exceeded those expectations, and we all know that live bullets Sunday is far different from practice. However, he showed us that he’s ready, not only physically, but mentally.”

title: FAA ground stop throws college football into chaos, while the NFL is safe
summary: A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several pro and college teams across multiple sports.
story: A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several teams across multiple sports.
Follow along for live coverage.

Multiple games in college football had to be rescheduled to accommodate new travel plans, while a handful of NBA teams changed their flights as a result of the ground stop. Every NFL game, meanwhile, will be played as scheduled, as all road teams were scheduled to travel Saturday.
A few backup referees for the NFL

Every NFL game will stick to its original start time, a league spokesman confirmed to NBC News. Teams playing Sunday typically do not travel until Saturday, meaning the league was largely unaffected by the Friday ground stop.
The New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions, who are playing in Munich, Germany, both traveled overseas well ahead of the stop.
While the league’s teams and players will arrive as scheduled, the NFL did have to modify officiating crews for Sunday’s games.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” a league spokesman said.

Three backup referees — Duane Heydt, Barry Anderson and Don Willard — will be used Sunday. Heydt was assigned to a game in New Orleans and Anderson to one in Tennessee, while Willard will be the side judge for games in both Indianapolis and Cincinnati. (The kickoffs in those two games are more than seven hours apart, and the stadiums are separated by less than 120 miles.)
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise,” the league spokesman said.
Many college football games have been pushed back
Travel plans for more than a dozen teams were affected by the stoppage, according to The Athletic.
Some schools opted to fly out on Saturday morning for games scheduled the same day, while others — including the Alabama Crimson Tide playing at Vanderbilt — took a bus to their destination.
Several kickoffs were pushed back to later Saturday to accommodate new travel plans, including the games between Baylor and BYU, Arizona State and UCF, and Utah and Arizona.
The game between Oklahoma and Ole Miss, however, was pushed back to Sunday after Ole Miss couldn’t figure out its travel in time — and it drew a strong response from the Sooners.

“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution,” Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny said in a statement. “After multiple conversations with the league office, [SEC] Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”

Denny’s statement added: “Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight.”
No major issues for the NBA and NHL
A few NBA teams — such as the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Chicago Bulls — had to reschedule flights from Friday night to Saturday morning, but otherwise it’s largely business as usual for the league.
An NBA source confirmed to NBC News all games would take place as scheduled as of Saturday morning, though noted there were a lot of moving parts.

“Flights are late, get stuck on the runway, just like it does in the normal commercial world of flight, so it’s just part of it,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said before the team’s game Friday. “We’ve all been part of it. You just adapt.”

Atkinson’s star guard Donovan Mitchell was not enthused about the new plan, as Cleveland has a quick turnaround to another game Saturday.

“This is unprecedented,” Mitchell said Friday, per Cleveland.com’s Chris Fedor. “Back-to-back. Three-hour flight. It was already going to be a tough one. But if they say we have to play then we have to play.”
Mitchell added he would have liked for the game to be canceled.

The NHL, meanwhile, has not announced any changes to its schedule. The league had only two games on Friday night, allowing most teams to travel for their road games prior to the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

title: Evacuation lifted after suspicious device found at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois
summary: A suspicious device at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, triggered a temporary evacuation request for those within a 1-mile radius, with events cancelled Friday.
story: A suspicious device at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, triggered a temporary evacuation request for those within a 1-mile radius, with events cancelled Friday.
An evacuation recommendation for those within that 1-mile radius after Friday afternoon’s discovery at the BioUrja Renewables facility was lifted Saturday, according to Peoria police.
Police and federal authorities said early Saturday that they had found a device deemed a “credible threat” and rendered it safe, without giving details as to its nature.
A search by federal, state and local authorities turned up no other devices, but an investigation into Friday’s discovery was ongoing, police said in a statement on Saturday.
“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said separately.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told NBC affiliate WEEK there was an “all hands on deck” response, saying: “A device has been identified. We know it’s a credible threat. We know it’s a bomb.”
​Presley told media that FBI personnel, along with local and state police, had determined a “suspicious package was a threat and rendered it safe.”
For Subscribers
Rep. Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., met with evacuees at Peoria Manual High School on Friday night.

“This is the designated shelter area for those that are impacted by the evacuation that’s going on just south of downtown Peoria,” he said in an update. “What we do need to make sure is that everybody’s making good decisions.
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker had urged locals to “follow directions from law enforcement and stay clear of the area.”
For Subscribers
Country music singer Jon Pardi was forced to cancel his show scheduled for Friday evening at the Peoria Civic Center.
“At the direction of the Chief of Police, tonight’s concert has been canceled due to an active local safety concern,” he posted on Instagram, adding that tickets would be refunded.
The weekend’s Illinois Comic Con at Peoria Civic Center canceled its Saturday events but said after the evacuation all-clear was issued that its Sunday plans were still scheduled.
Peoria’s Caterpillar Visitors Center, Riverfront Museum, Rhythm Kitchen Music Cafe, and Main Library and Lincoln Branch library were also closed on Saturday, those venues each said on Facebook.
Dozer Park, home of the minor league baseball team the Peoria Chiefs, also canceled a holiday event at the venue.

The nearby OSF HealthCare St. Francis Medical Center said it was “taking all appropriate precautions in response to the situation in downtown Peoria.” A statement said: “We will continue to monitor the situation and take any additional steps necessary to maintain a safe environment for those we serve and those who work at our facilities.”

In 2021, Houston-based BioUrja, which has described itself as an energy, agricultural and metals commodity trading company, purchased the former ADM (Archer-Daniels-Midland) ethanol production complex in Peoria. BioUrja CEO Amit Bhandari said at the time the facility would help it expand its presence in beverage-grade and highly-distilled industrial alcohol markets.
The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Weekend storm brings season’s first widespread freeze to millions across U.S.
summary: A departing storm brought more than a foot of snow to parts of New York State on Friday, while this weekend the nation will see its first widespread freeze event of the season.
story: A departing storm brought more than a foot of snow to parts of New York State on Friday, while this weekend the nation will see its first widespread freeze event of the season.

As of Friday morning in New York, 12.5 inches of snow had fallen in Hartwick, 12 inches in Burlington, 11.5 inches in Exeter Center and 10 inches in Cherry Valley. Multiple locations in the Catskills region of the state saw 3 to 7 inches of snow.
The morning’s wet snow will gradually taper off throughout the day, as rounds of rain were expected to impact the I-95 corridor from Philadelphia to New York.
Some minor coastal flooding was also possible in New Jersey along the Jersey Shore and up toward Cape May.

This storm will head out to sea Saturday, but cold northerly winds behind it will create lake-effect snow, rain showers and light snow across the Adirondacks, Berkshires, and Green and White Mountains in the Northeast.
The first big freeze

Another storm this weekend will bring the first below-freezing temperatures to millions around the country. Chicago will see wind chill temperatures on Saturday and Sunday of 24 and 27 degrees, with New York seeing 34 and 40 degrees, Atlanta seeing 31 and 32 degrees and Tallahassee, Florida, seeing 35 and 32 degree wind chill temperatures.

Frost and freeze alerts are in effect from eastern Oklahoma to the coastal Carolinas, stretching as far south as southern Alabama. Some of the cities under the frost and freeze alerts include Tulsa, Oklahoma; Little Rock, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Atlanta, Georgia, and Raleigh, North Carolina.
Parade of Pacific Storms

Meanwhile, on the West Coast, a storm on Friday coming in off the Pacific will bring heavy rain from northern Washington to southern California as heavy snow blankets the Sierra Nevada mountain range.
For southern California, some isolated thunderstorms are possible, including for the Los Angeles metro area.
Through Saturday, rainfall amounts will be up to 3 inches from northern California to southwestern Oregon.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
For the Sierra Nevada mountains, snowfall amounts will be as high as 12-18 inches above 6,000 feet elevation.
The active pattern will continue through the weekend, with the next storm system set to come into the Pacific Northwest Saturday night through Sunday.
Heavy rain for South Texas
On Sunday, Southeast Texas into western Louisiana will see heavy rain capable of producing some urban flooding.

Rainfall amounts will generally be 1-2 inches, but there could be some localized areas along the southeast Texas coast that could see 3-5 inches. The cities of Houston, Galveston, Beaumont, and Lake Charles could be impacted.
A few strong storms capable of damaging winds will also be possible for southeastern Texas on Sunday, stretching from Beaumont to Brownsville.

title: 100 pulled from water after tanker capsizes New Orleans riverboat
summary: A large tanker ship struck a riverboat with 191 passengers and crew members aboard in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River.
story: A large tanker ship struck a riverboat with 191 passengers and crew members aboard in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River.
First responders pulled roughly 100 people from the water, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said Saturday. Everyone aboard was accounted for, and no one died.
The American Heritage ship, managed by American Cruise Lines, was T-boned by the tanker while docked near the French Quarter, a spokesperson said in a statement.
Eight people remained hospitalized as of Saturday, including two in serious condition, said Jen Avegno, the deputy mayor for health and human services. The other six were stable.
Avegno said 32 people were taken to hospitals from the scene Friday, including 30 passengers and crew members and two responders. Two more people went to a hospital later to be evaluated.
Moreno called that fact that everyone survived “a miracle on the Mississippi.”
Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Saturday that initial reports pointed to a steering problem aboard the tanker. The cause of the collision remained under investigation.

The U.S. Coast Guard and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating. Some NTSB investigators had arrived in New Orleans by Saturday, and more team members were expected later in the day, Moreno said. A nationwide airport ground stop had delayed their arrival.

Trading Cousins and elevating Mendoza “is no way to signify that we are punting on the season or looking forward to 2027,” Raiders general manager John Spytek said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“It’s something that [Mendoza] worked very hard for since the moment he walked into this building,” Spytek told reporters this week. “He passed every test. I want to stop short of saying he’s earned it, but he put us in a position where we had to make a really hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback.”

Mendoza is known as a quick study. While attending Cal, he spent his summers away from Berkeley interning at investment firms. In his first and only season at Indiana last fall, Mendoza picked up the Hoosiers’ offensive playbook so quickly that he led the perennial Big Ten doormat to a stunning national championship by using his arms and his feet.

Raiders coach Klint Kubiak, who as an offensive playcaller mentored Sam Darnold during last season’s Super Bowl run with the Seahawks, said that Cousins was “the right role model” for Mendoza to learn from and accelerate his acclimation to the NFL.

“It’s time to rally around Fernando,” center Tyler Linderbaum said. “Everyone has to step up and play for him. Obviously, it’s never easy being a rookie in that first game, but there’s 10 other guys on the field with him, there’s a whole defense, special teams unit, and just be there for him. Let him play with confidence. We’ve seen it every day in practice, the plays he can make.”
